email_papers.title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization
email_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment. Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and evolving only one component is suboptimal---a harness tuned for one checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed harness. In light of this, we propose Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness proposer. Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step). The policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the policy's evolving failure modes. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings. Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. Self-HPO also improves reliability (Pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (Pass@k) over the base agent. Additionally, we show that with a stronger external model (e.g., Opus 4.8) as the harness proposer, the same framework yields a further performance boost.

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment.
Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and evolving only one component is suboptimal—a harness tuned for one checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed harness.
In light of this, we propose
Self-HPO
, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness proposer.
Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step).
The policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the policy’s evolving failure modes.
Across three coding benchmarks,
Self-HPO
consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B’s average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings.
Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains.
Self-HPO
also improves reliability (pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (pass@
k
k
) over the base agent.
Additionally, we show that with a stronger external model (
e.g.
, Opus 4.8) as the harness proposer, the same framework yields a further performance boost.
1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents have made rapid progress on complex, multi-step tasks such as software engineering
(
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2024
)
, web navigation
(
Zhou et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2024
;
Wei et al., 2025c
)
, and computer use
(
Xie et al., 2024
;
Agashe et al., 2025
)
.
Such an agent consists of two components: the policy model and its harness, which is the external scaffold that decides what the model observes, how its actions are executed, what feedback it receives, and when an episode terminates
(
Yao et al., 2023
;
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2024
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
.
Typically, the policy model defines the agent’s capability boundary, while the harness determines how these capabilities are elicited, hence the same model may succeed or fail on one problem depending on its harness
(
Le et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
.
There have been two main lines of research on improving such agents.
Harness optimization holds the policy fixed and searches over prompts, workflows, or agent code
(
Hu et al., 2024
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
, whereas policy optimization holds the harness fixed and updates the model from successful trajectories or verifiable rewards
(
Shao et al., 2024
;
Guo et al., 2025
;
Wei et al., 2025a
)
.
However, harness-only optimization cannot improve the underlying model, while policy-only training can learn only from the trajectories that its fixed harness elicits.
Although recent works begin to optimize both components
(
Kim et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026a
)
, they rely on an external harness proposer and face the challenge of a moving optimization target as the policy and its failure modes evolve, leaving self-driven evolution for coding agents underexplored.
In this work, we introduce
Self-HPO
, a framework for recursive self-improvement driven by the agent’s own policy.
As illustrated in Figure
1
,
Self-HPO
alternates harness optimization (H-step) with policy optimization under the optimized harness (P-step).
Harness optimization exposes and compensates for the weaknesses of the current policy, while policy optimization internalizes the elicited behaviors into the model and shifts the failures that the next harness should target.
Specifically, in the H-step, the current policy analyzes its failed trajectories and proposes harness revisions targeting its own failure modes, and selects the updated harness based on search-set performance (§
2.2
).
In the P-step, the policy is updated using reinforcement learning under the optimized harness (§
2.3
).
In the next H-step, the updated policy serves as the harness proposer, with hard tasks identified from the preceding P-step as the search set to keep harness search aligned with the policy’s evolving failure modes.
Figure 1:
Self-HPO
recursively improves the harness and policy using the agent itself.
Left:
In each H-step, the current policy proposes an improved harness, and each P-step then updates the policy through reinforcement learning with the optimized harness.
Right:
Average resolve rate over SWE-Bench Verified, SWE-Bench Multilingual, and SWE-Bench Pro along the H- and P-steps. Policy-only and Harness-only denote the RLVR
(
Peng et al., 2026
)
and Self-Harness
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
baselines.
We instantiate
Self-HPO
with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
as the base policy, and mini-SWE-agent
(
Yang et al., 2024
)
as the seed harness.
Across three coding benchmarks,
Self-HPO
consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only optimization, with the average resolve rate improving at every optimization step, as demonstrated in Figure
1
.
On SWE-Bench Verified
(
Chowdhury et al., 2024
)
, it improves the base resolve rate from 61.0% to 69.5%, with transferable gains on the out-of-distribution SWE-Bench Multilingual
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
and SWE-Bench Pro
(
Deng et al., 2025
)
.
Ablations further show that evolving the harness search set with hard tasks identified during policy learning yields better performance than reusing a fixed set.
We also extend
Self-HPO
to the external-model setup where Opus 4.8 is used as an external harness proposer, which further raises the resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified to 71.6%.
The main contributions of this work are as follows:
•
We propose
Self-HPO
, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, where the agent uses its own policy as the harness proposer and adapts harness search to the policy’s evolving failure modes.
•
We demonstrate that
Self-HPO
consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only baselines across three coding benchmarks, improving the average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings.
•
Our study shows that both optimized components of
Self-HPO
retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. We also find that
Self-HPO
not only improves reliability (pass@1) but also expands the capability frontier (pass@
k
k
) of the agent.

We study the problem of self-improving a coding agent’s own harness and policy. The harness changes which behaviors the current policy can reliably express, while a policy update changes the failures that the next harness should target.
As shown in Figure
2

each P-step then freezes this harness and updates the policy through reinforcement learning.
The updated policy becomes the next harness proposer, with hard tasks identified from the training process forming the next search set.
We call this alternating framework Harness-Policy Optimization (HPO) and implement it in two setups.
In the self-improving setup (
Self-HPO
), the evolving policy proposes its own harness candidates, so no separate proposer model is needed.
For reference, we also instantiate the same HPO loop with Opus 4.8 as a fixed external proposer.

3.1
Experimental Setup
Harness, model, and data.
All experiments use Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
as the base policy and mini-SWE-agent
(
Yao et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024
)
as the seed harness.
Following Orchard
(
Peng et al., 2026
)
, we construct a training set of 2,484 tasks from SWE-rebench
(
Badertdinov et al., 2025
)
, SWE-rebench V2
(
Badertdinov et al., 2026
)
, and Scale-SWE
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
, which is used for both harness search and policy optimization.
We perform two rounds of alternating harness and policy optimization based on the stopping criterion, with
K
=
6
K=6
harness candidates per H-step and 50 RL updates per P-step.
Appendix
A
describes the implementation details.
Benchmarks and evaluation metrics.
SWE-Bench Verified (SWE-Verified) contains 500 human-validated GitHub issues and is our primary benchmark
(
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Chowdhury et al., 2024
)
.
We further evaluate out-of-distribution performance on SWE-Bench Multilingual (SWE-Multi; 300 tasks)
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
and the public V2 set of SWE-Bench Pro (SWE-Pro; 642 tasks)
(
Deng et al., 2025
)
, covering other programming languages and more diverse repository-level tasks.
We report resolve rate, the percentage of tasks whose generated patches pass the benchmark verifier.
Main results are averaged over three evaluation runs (avg@3) with standard deviations.
Baselines.
We compare our method with policy-only and harness-only baselines under two setups, with the base agent as a reference.
In the
self-improving setup
, RLVR
(
Peng et al., 2026
)
updates the policy under the seed harness, whereas Self-Harness
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
optimizes the harness using the base policy as proposer without updating its weights.
Self-HPO alternates both updates and uses the current policy to propose harness changes.
In the
external-model setup
, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from resolved Opus 4.8 trajectories on the same training tasks, while Meta-Harness
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
uses Opus 4.8 to optimize the harness with the target policy fixed.
HPO combines external harness proposals with RL policy updates.

3.5
Case Studies
Harness evolution adds targeted controls around the existing agent loop.
Figure
5
contrasts the seed harness with the harness obtained after HPO’s second H-step.
The optimized harness retains the underlying model-query and command-execution loop, but intervenes before budget exhaustion and at submission.
First, it warns the model as the step or time limit approaches and prompts a best-effort submission before the episode ends with an empty result.
Second, a one-time empty-patch guard asks the model to include newly created files via
git add -N
.
Third, it delays the first submission that passes the empty-patch guard to prompt a check of API names and signatures against the repository and tests.
Finally, a fallback uses the sandbox’s Git diff when the submitted patch fails the apply check.
These changes target distinct ways in which useful repository edits can fail to become a valid submission.
They combine explicit runtime checks, such as detecting an empty patch, with behavioral guidance, such as requesting an interface check.
Harness optimization can therefore change execution and termination logic, in addition to prompts.

Conclusion
We introduced Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization.
The evolving policy proposes its own harness revisions, learns through RL under the selected harness, and supplies hard tasks for the next round of harness search.
Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only baselines, improving the average resolve rate from
57.8
%

to
64.8

Analyses further show that harness and policy improvements are complementary and that Self-HPO improves reliability (pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (pass@

Harness Proposer System Prompt
You are the harness optimizer for a fixed policy {P_t}. The search set contains {N}
hard training tasks that the policy never solved during the preceding P-step. The
parent harness is {H_best}, the current best harness. The starting harness of this search
solves {s}% of the search set under the frozen sampling configuration. Your goal is to design ONE new harness mechanism, of your own design,
that is added on top of the parent harness and solves more search-set tasks than the
parent.
CONSTRAINTS
- Keep every method of the parent harness verbatim and add exactly one new mechanism.
- The policy, sampling configuration (temperature 0.95, top-p 0.95), step limit,
maximum tokens, and verifier are frozen.
- Never inject reference patches or task-specific facts into the agent’s context; the
mechanism must compute its own signal at runtime.
EXPERIENCE (read it before designing; treat it as evidence, not a mandate)
- Candidates evaluated so far in this search: scores, code, and trajectories.
- Notes left by earlier proposals in this search.
Diagnostics computed from the starting harness’s runs on the search set:
- Coverage gap: the source files required by the reference fix versus the files the
agent touched.
- Precision gap: failures in which every required file was edited but the fix was
incorrect.
- Submission loss: failures in which a real source edit appears in the trajectory but
the final submitted patch is empty or malformed.
- Reference-fix archetypes (multi-file, signature change, new import, guard, error
handling, ...) versus what the agent produced.
Decide for yourself which failure is the largest and most reachable by a harness, or
find another one.
WORKFLOW
0. Review the experience: the earlier notes and every candidate evaluated so far.
For the most recent one, read the tasks it made worse and better than the starting
harness (trajectories and reference fixes), and work out why.
1. Read several failing trajectories and compare a few with the reference fix to form
your own hypothesis about the dominant failure cause.
2. Design a mechanism with a detectable trigger in the agent’s own state and a
concrete action: for example, intercept a submission and return feedback so that
the agent gets another turn to act on it, replace the submitted patch, or act at
any step.
3. Implement it in a copy of the parent harness. All repository access must go
through the sandbox environment.
4. Write a one-line purpose (diagnosed cause -> mechanism), append what you learned
this round to the notes, and stop. The search then checks that the candidate keeps
every parent method and fires on real sandbox tasks, and returns any failure to you
to fix.

RESCUE_TEXT
[BUDGET ALMOST EXHAUSTED -- STOP EXPLORING AND SUBMIT NOW]
You are nearly out of steps/time and have not submitted a patch. An empty result scores zero, but a focused best-effort edit can pass. Right now:
1. Decide the single most likely fix location from what you already know -- do NOT start new open-ended exploration.
2. Make that concrete edit to the source file (the smallest change that matches the PR’s literal request).
3. Immediately create and submit the patch, in SEPARATE commands:
git diff -- <the source files you modified> > patch.txt
echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch.txt
Do this in your next one or two commands.
(2) Empty-patch guard:
EMPTY_GUARD_TEXT
[YOUR SUBMISSION IS EMPTY -- it contains no source-code changes, so it cannot fix anything. Not finalized.]
You have not edited any source file yet (patch.txt is empty or has no diff hunks). Do NOT give up. Re-localize the bug:
1. Re-read the PR and grep for the exact symbol/message/flag it names.
2. Open the file where that symbol lives and make the concrete edit the PR requires.
3. IMPORTANT -- did your fix CREATE a NEW file (a brand-new module)? A plain `git diff` does NOT show untracked new files, so your patch looks empty even though the file exists. Stage new files first so they appear as additions:
cd /testbed && git add -N <the new file(s) you created>
4. Verify with `cd /testbed && git --no-pager diff` that a real change (or a `new file mode` hunk) now shows.
5. Then `cd /testbed && git diff -- <files> > patch.txt` and submit with:
echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch.txt
(3) Contract grounding:
GROUND_TEXT
[GROUND YOUR DIFF IN THE REPO’S EXISTING TESTS -- one-time check; your submission is NOT finalized yet]
The most common way this task is failed is submitting a patch that APPLIES cleanly but implements the WRONG contract -- a guessed function/option name, a signature the codebase never uses, a rename or new spelling that no caller expects, or an error/return shape different from what the code around it uses. Re-reading the PR will NOT catch this, because your reading of the PR is what produced the wrong contract. The codebase itself is the authority. The repo ships EXISTING tests that already exercise the code you touched and the API next to it -- they show the EXACT names, signatures, argument spellings, and error/return types the code is expected to have. Use them as ground truth now.
1. Print your changes and identify the concrete symbols you added or changed:
git --no-pager diff
List every NEW or RENAMED symbol/option/message string in your diff.
2. For each such symbol, search the repo’s tests and existing call sites for how that symbol -- and the nearest EXISTING sibling API -- is actually used:
grep -rn --include=’*.py’ -e ’<symbol>’ -e ’<sibling_api>’ . | head -40
Then OPEN and READ the specific test files that reference the area you changed (e.g. tests/ or test_*.py near your file) and note the exact spelling, call signature, and expected result/exception the codebase uses.
3. Confront your diff against what the tests/call sites actually expect. If you introduced a name, option spelling, signature, or error shape that NO existing test or caller uses -- while an existing convention does -- change your diff to MATCH the codebase’s convention. Do not invent a new API; conform to the one already there. Also confirm you did not MISS a behavior the tests imply is required.
4. If you changed anything, regenerate the patch:
git diff -- <the source files you modified> > patch.txt
and re-inspect patch.txt so it contains ONLY your intended source changes.
5. When your diff conforms to the codebase’s real contract, re-issue the EXACT submit command:
echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch.txt
This check happens only once -- after you re-submit, it goes through.

article.headline: 编码智能体让脚手架与策略交替自进化
article.lede: 微软研究提出 Self-HPO，让编码智能体用自身策略提出脚手架修改，并与强化学习交替迭代。
article.problem: LLM 编码智能体的性能同时取决于策略模型和连接环境的脚手架（harness）。只优化脚手架无法提升底层模型，只训练策略又只能学习固定脚手架诱发的轨迹；已有联合优化多依赖外部提议者，且策略变化后搜索目标会漂移。
article.method: Self-HPO 每一轮先固定策略，让当前策略分析自身失败轨迹并提出新的脚手架候选，在搜索集上选出最佳脚手架（H-step）。随后固定该脚手架，用 GRPO 加 BAR 的强化学习更新策略（P-step），并把本轮从未解决的任务作为下一轮搜索集。更新后的策略又成为下一轮的脚手架提议者。
article.results: 在 SWE-Bench Verified 上，Self-HPO 将 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 的 resolve rate 从 61.0% 提升到 69.5%；三个基准平均从 57.8% 到 64.8%，比 RLVR 高 2.9 个百分点。SWE-Bench Multilingual 和 SWE-Bench Pro 分别达到 59.7% 和 65.2%；改用 Opus 4.8 做外部提议者时，SWE-Bench Verified 达到 71.6%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把脚手架优化从一次性搜索变成与策略共同演化的闭环，为编码智能体的递归自我改进提供了不依赖外部提议者的路径。交叉评估还显示，H2 与 P2 联合带来 8.5 点提升，超过各自单独收益之和 6.9 点。
article.limitations: 论文只在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 与 mini-SWE-agent 上验证，训练和脚手架搜索仅用 Python 任务。提升也不均匀：Resolved 组 pass@1 下降 2.2 个百分点，案例中的 PR 意图提醒还出现误报。
article.figure_caption_zh: Self-HPO 总览：冻结策略在搜索集上分析失败并提出新脚手架，更新脚手架后策略通过强化学习演化，更新后的策略成为下一轮提议者，未解决任务构成下一轮搜索集。

figure.caption: {Overview of Self-HPO.} {Top ( ):} The frozen policy analyzes the agent's failures on the search set and proposes new harness candidates. {Bottom ( ):} With the updated harness, the policy evolves through reinforcement learning. The updated policy becomes the next harness proposer, while tasks never resolved during this form the next search set.

email_papers.title: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents
email_papers.abstract: Recursive language-model agents decompose tasks and delegate subtasks to child instances of the same policy, forming a tree of work. Training them, however, is hard: the final outcome is verifiable, but the self-invented intermediate subtasks are numerous and carry no ground truth. Existing methods score each node with a verifier or judge, which is costly at scale and blind to decomposition quality. We argue that a recursive agent must learn three coupled capabilities within one set of weights: decomposing problems into subtasks, solving them, and evaluating the outcomes, each requiring its own training signal. SERA (Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents) turns evaluation into a learned capability of the policy itself. Before delegating, the parent writes a rubric of weighted success criteria for each child subtask; a ranking objective against verified outcomes then trains rubric generation so that the criteria track genuine subtask success. In addition, a complementary leaf-coverage signal provides direct credit for task decomposition. Our central finding is that training the policy to generate aligned rubrics is what drives the gains: because the same weights both evaluate and execute, learning to judge subtasks sharpens the agent's ability to solve them. Notably, external supervision is also reduced: the judge is consulted only to train the rubric generator, while solving is trained against the agent's own rubric scores, which outperform direct use of the judge. Beyond training, the learned rubric doubles as an inference-time selector for tree search. On TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync, SERA improves over strong recursive-agent baselines by 5.38 and 13.14 points on average, and rubric-guided tree search at inference adds a further 2.43 points on TextWorld-Sync.

1
Introduction
Language-model agents are deployed on tasks that cannot be solved in a pass: multi-hop research questions require coordinating evidence across retrieval steps; repository-scale code changes involve interdependent edits. A natural response is to decompose the problem and delegate each piece to a child agent
(
Prasad et al., 2024
;
Schroeder et al., 2025
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
, turning one query into a tree of work where each child handles a focused subproblem in a fresh context. When the children are instances of the
same
policy, the system is
recursive
(
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
: a single set of weights drives every node. This is the design behind frontier coding and research agents
(
Anthropic, 2025
;
OpenAI, 2025
;
Tie et al., 2026
)
, and it composes across depth: a policy trained at shallow recursion generalises to deeper trees at inference
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
, making recursion a distinct axis of test-time scaling alongside longer chains of thought and wider sampling.
Training recursive agents is hard because supervision is scarce and unevenly distributed across the tree. The final outcome is typically verifiable (a research answer can be checked, code can be tested), but the intermediate subtasks the agent invents rarely admit a ground-truth check. The natural remedy is to score each node by its own success instead of broadcasting the root reward, using a verifier or an LLM judge (e.g.,
Gandhi et al., 2026
). This localises credit, but the resulting signal has three limitations. It is
coarse
: a binary per-node signal cannot separate a clean solution from a barely adequate one, or flag weak work inside a tree that still succeeds. It is
expensive
: a reliable signal at every node needs a verifier or judge call throughout the tree, which scales poorly. And it is
silent about decomposition
: rewarding whether subtasks were solved says nothing about whether they were the
right
subtasks to create, though that choice often decides whether the tree succeeds.
The root issue is structural: a recursive agent is not doing one thing but three. The same shared weights must
decompose
hard problems into tractable pieces,
solve
the subtasks that result, and
evaluate
whether delegated work was actually accomplished. Every child is a fresh instance of the parent, so all three functions live in a single policy. Training the agent well means giving each capability its own signal without the three interfering on shared parameters.
A self-invented subtask has no ground-truth check, so the agent must judge for itself whether it succeeded. We make this self-evaluation concrete with a
rubric
: when the parent delegates a subtask, it commits a short set of weighted natural-language success criteria for the child before the child runs, so they cannot be fitted to the trajectory they will later score. Applying the rubric to the child’s output yields a continuous, subtask-specific score in place of the coarse per-node signal.
However, a rubric helps only when its criteria align with subtask success. An untrained policy writes misaligned criteria, and using its scores as rewards helps little, inconsistently across tasks (§
4
). We therefore train rubric generation, but the signal for that training cannot be the task reward itself: since rubric generation and solving share weights, rewarding the rubric through task reward would let the two co-adapt, inflating rubric scores together without improvement. Instead, the signal comes from an external check: we score subtask rollouts with a verifier or judge and train the rubric to rank verified successes above failures. Importantly, the judge is used only here, never to reward nodes directly as common approaches do; the rubric provides the dense per-node signal itself, so external supervision is lighter overall. Grounded this way, shared weights become an asset: learning to judge subtasks reshapes how the policy solves them, which is our central empirical finding (§
4
).
A capability,
subtask decomposition
, is the choice of how to split a task into subproblems to delegate. We assign it a reward. In a solved tree, a delegation is credited by the fraction of the task’s leaf-level work its subtree covers, so a delegation that shoulders a large, well-scoped share of the solution scores high, while trivial hand-offs score near zero and delegations in failed trees score zero. This rewards the agent for using delegation to carry structural load, something no execution signal captures. The reward adds little on shallow, near-independent subtasks but helps when subtasks are interdependent, as in tasks with dependency chains, shared state, or coordination (§
4
).
Finally, since the learned rubric captures genuine subtask quality, it is useful beyond training. At inference we search the tree depth-first and select among candidate resolutions by rubric score, propagating the best upward. This further improves final task success without additional training (§
4.3
). The evaluation capability thus pays off as a reusable inference-time selector, a further scaling axis for recursive agents. We call the method
SERA
(Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents). Our contributions are as follows:
1.
A framing of recursive-agent training as learning three coupled capabilities (decomposing, solving, and evaluating subtasks) in a single shared policy, with evidence that each requires its own training signal (§
3
).
2.
A learned self-evaluation mechanism: policy-generated rubrics trained by a ranking objective against verified outcomes. We show that training rubric generation is what improves execution, that it reduces external supervision while outperforming direct use of the judge (§
3
).
3.
A leaf-coverage decomposition reward that credits a delegation by how much of the verified task it covers, with gains concentrated when subtasks are interdependent (§
3
).
4.
State-of-the-art results on TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync (§
4
), and the learned rubric as an inference-time selector for tree search, with further gains (§
4.3
).
2
Related Work
Recursive and multi-agent training.
Recursive and multi-agent scaffolds decompose tasks and route subproblems to child agents, scaling language-model agents at inference time
(
Prasad et al., 2024
;
Schroeder et al., 2025
)
, but most treat recursion as a fixed scaffold around a frozen model. Recent work instead trains agents to delegate, though largely at depth 1 with fixed or restricted workers: parallel delegation with reinforcement learning
(
Team et al., 2026b
)
and jointly trained organizer–worker systems
(
Sun et al., 2025
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
. Recursive Agent Optimization (RAO) is the closest prior work, combining recursion beyond depth 1, asynchronous subagent execution, and end-to-end RL training of both root agents and subagents
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
. We adopt this setting and use RAO as our primary baseline, but depart from it in the signal each node receives: RAO scores nodes with a binary success label from a verifier or judge and says nothing about decomposition quality, whereas SERA gives each node a trained continuous rubric and credits decomposition directly.
Dense rewards and process supervision for agents.
A large body of work densifies sparse outcome rewards with step- or process-level supervision, from process reward models
(
Lightman et al., 2024
)
to agentic variants that assign credit to intermediate actions
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
; these operate on flat, linear trajectories with the intermediate signal supplied by a separate critic or an additive decomposition of the return. Classical hierarchical RL such as options
(
Dietterich, 2000
)
and goal-conditioned hierarchies
(
Nachum et al., 2018
)
assigns credit across levels but assumes a fixed set of subtask types or hierarchy depth. In contrast, SERA operates on a dynamically generated tree where the hierarchy, the subtasks, and the evaluator are all produced by a single policy and vary from rollout to rollout.
Rubric-based reinforcement learning.
A separate question from where credit is assigned is what form the per-node signal takes. Rubrics extend RL beyond exactly verifiable domains by scoring outputs against generated criteria
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
. Because static rubrics saturate as the policy improves, recent work co-trains the rubric generator with the policy through per-step return decomposition
(
Tian et al., 2026
)
, alternating generator–judge optimization
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, or adversarial co-evolution
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
, with RubricEM the closest in domain family
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
. All assume flat or fixed-stage computation with a rubric model separate from the policy. SERA instead applies learned rubric generation to recursive, policy-invented subtasks whose topology varies across rollouts, uses the policy itself as the evaluator, and trains rubrics with a ranking objective anchored to verified outcomes. We find that the label-free discriminativeness signal favored in prior rubric learning degrades performance in a tree, where score spread reflects subtask-difficulty variation more than rubric quality (§
4.2
); relatedly, work documenting reward hacking under learned reward signals
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
motivates our verified-outcome anchoring.

Alternating optimization schedule
SERA jointly optimizes three objectives on shared parameters. Combining all three gradients in a single update risks instability, since the objectives can interfere and their scales differ. We instead alternate: each optimizer step activates exactly one objective, and the updates cycle in the fixed ratio

Alternation keeps the credit sources well separated, and the ratio can be adjusted per domain without changing the method. 4
Experiments
Benchmarks.
We evaluate on two benchmarks that differ in a property central to our method: whether intermediate subtasks can be verified independently.
TextCraft-Synth
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
is a procedural crafting environment requiring hierarchical planning, tool use, and recursive delegation, in which the agent crafts a target item by looking up recipes and delegating sub-crafts to child agents. Crucially, each subtask has a deterministic program verifier returning a binary pass/fail outcome, so SERA’s rubric training requires no external judge here. Tasks span four difficulty levels defined by recipe depth; we train on Medium and evaluate across all levels to test generalization.
TextWorld-Sync
is our multi-agent extension of TextWorldExpress
(
Jansen and Côté, 2023
)
, a shared-state text environment for evaluating coordination under constraints, with seven task families spanning dependency chains, resource conflicts, load balancing, and hierarchical decomposition. Unlike TextCraft, subtask outcomes are not independently verifiable; rubric training instead uses an LLM judge that provides binary success/failure labels for counterfactual rollouts, making this the benchmark that tests SERA’s ability to amortize a sparse external signal. On both benchmarks the verified outcome

Conclusion
We presented SERA, a method for training recursive language-model agents that casts training as three coupled capabilities: decomposing tasks into subtasks, solving them, and evaluating their outcomes. Each capability receives its own training signal, and the three are optimized by alternating updates on a single shared policy.
The central finding is that training the policy to generate its own evaluation rubrics, through a ranking objective anchored to verified outcomes, is what drives the largest performance gains. Since evaluation and execution share weights, learning to judge subtask quality directly improves how the agent solves them. This trained rubric also reduces reliance on external supervision: the judge is needed only to train the rubric generator, and the resulting self-generated signal outperforms using the judge directly. Additionally, a leaf-coverage reward provides a direct signal for decomposition quality, with the largest gains on tasks requiring coordination among interdependent subtasks. Beyond training, the learned rubric serves as an inference-time selector for tree search, further improving task success without additional training.
Several limitations remain. We evaluate only Qwen3-4B on two synthetic benchmarks, so generalization to larger models and real-world agent tasks remains untested. Because the policy both writes and applies its own rubrics, self-evaluation could be gamed by scores that drift from genuine task success; we mitigate this by training rubric generation only against verified outcomes—a label-free dispersion reward instead degrades performance (Section
4.2
)—but robustness under sparser or noisier verification, and the residual dependence on verified outcomes to anchor rubric training (Table
2
), remain open. Finally, the leaf-coverage reward treats all leaf nodes equally, and subtask-level importance weights may improve decomposition training.
Looking ahead, the rubric mechanism suggests learning rubrics that generalize across tasks, using the rubric to guide exploration during training, and extending self-evaluation to settings where even the root outcome is not exactly verifiable. Framing recursive-agent training as three coupled capabilities offers a useful foundation for this work.
AI use statement
In this work, we used generative AI tools in a limited capacity for grammar correction and polishing of author-written text, and for coding assistance and debugging. All research ideas, method design, experimental design, result analysis, figures, and tables were produced entirely by the authors. Every AI-suggested text edit was reviewed and accepted or rejected by the authors, and all AI-assisted code was reviewed and tested by the authors before use. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, code, and artifacts.
Ethics statement
This work trains language-model agents to decompose and solve tasks in simulated text environments. The benchmarks (TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync) are procedurally generated and do not involve human subjects, personal data, or real-world deployment. The self-evaluation mechanism enables agents to generate and score their own rubrics, which could in principle be misused to produce misleading self-assessments; we mitigate this by anchoring rubric training to externally verified outcomes and reporting all results against deterministic environment verification. We do not foresee significant negative societal impacts from this research.
Reproducibility statement
All hyperparameters, training schedules, and evaluation protocols are reported in Section
4
and Appendix
B
, including the alternating-update ratios, rollout group sizes, context lengths, and checkpoint steps for each method variant. The base model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507) is publicly available. Both benchmarks use deterministic environment verification for all reported success rates. We plan to release the training code and the TextWorld-Sync benchmark upon publication.

Appendix A
Recursive Execution and Supervision
Figure
2
illustrates the recursive execution structure shared by SERA and its baselines.
The root agent delegates subtasks to child instances of the same policy, which can delegate further or solve their assigned tasks directly.
Independent branches can run in parallel, while parents incorporate returned results into their own execution.
In SERA, each parent generates a subtask-specific rubric before the child runs and freezes it throughout that child’s execution.
After completion, the policy applies this rubric to the child’s trajectory and final environment state, producing its execution reward.
The rubric scorer and external verifier serve different purposes in this framework.
RAO uses externally supplied subtask outcomes directly as execution rewards; SERA uses them to train rubric generation on counterfactual rollouts.
These outcomes come from a program verifier on TextCraft-Synth and an external LLM judge on TextWorld-Sync.
SERA’s ordinary subtask execution instead receives the policy’s own rubric scores, while the root retains its environment-verified outcome.
The leaf-coverage reward separately credits delegation using the completed tree and root outcome, without additional subtask labels.
Thus, the three signals train execution, decomposition, and evaluation through distinct updates, as specified in Section
3
.

Here, D denotes decomposition training with the leaf-coverage reward, and RT denotes rubric-generation training with the verified-outcome ranking reward.

Each optimizer step activates one objective on the shared policy, rather than summing the three raw rewards.
For rubric-based execution, the policy both generates subtask-specific criteria and scores completed trajectories against them.
Generating or applying a rubric does not itself constitute RT; RT explicitly optimizes the rubric-generation action using verified counterfactual outcomes.

Appendix C
TextWorld-Sync Dataset Construction
TextWorld-Sync extends the CookingWorld environment in TextWorldExpress
(
Jansen and Côté, 2023
)
to test recursive delegation under shared-state constraints.
Its design separates local subtask completion from joint task success, complementing the independently verifiable crafting subtasks in TextCraft-Synth.
C.1
Shared World and Agent-Local Contexts
The standard TextWorldExpress interface exposes one mutable game through a single avatar.
We retain the CookingWorld dynamics and introduce a coordinator that lets recursive agents interact with one shared world.
Objects, containers, inventory, tools, doors, recipe progress, and task score are shared across agents.
Each agent maintains its own logical location, dialogue history, observation stream, and step budget.
Model calls may run concurrently, but environment reads and state transitions are serialized under a lock and committed atomically.
Consequently, an item acquired by one agent becomes unavailable to others, while their locations and histories remain separate.
This distinction permits concurrent planning while preserving consistent state updates and exposing dependencies between agents’ actions.
C.2
Procedural Tasks and Coordination Structures
An original CookingWorld instance specifies one recipe, its required ingredients, and a target meal.
TextWorldExpress procedurally samples recipes, layouts, object placements, and difficulty parameters.
We extend this generator to sample multiple disjoint recipes per seed, assign ingredients to dishes, and introduce one of seven coordination structures.
The complete instance is recorded in a fixed manifest and reconstructed at runtime by a multi-dish adapter.
Independent dish branches can be delegated in parallel, subject to the instance’s resource and dependency constraints.
Table
8
summarizes the seven task families and the coordination decisions they require.
They range from independent branches to shared-resource conflicts and nested dependencies, providing different conditions for evaluating decomposition quality.
The deterministic root evaluator reads structured environment state and requires every ingredient to be collected and correctly processed, and every dish prepared and consumed.
Completing an individual dish yields partial progress but does not terminate the root task.
This root-level check does not provide labels for arbitrary policy-generated subtasks; SERA therefore uses an external judge for rubric-training labels on this benchmark.
Table 8:
Coordination structures in TextWorld-Sync. The seven task families vary branch dependencies, workload allocation, resource constraints, and recursion. Every family uses a shared world and requires completion of all dishes for root-task success.
Task family
Structure and coordination requirement
Fork–join
Independent dish branches converge on shared preparation and consumption, requiring their results to be coordinated.
Critical path
One branch has a longer workload; launching it early reduces delays before the branches can join.
Load balanced
Branch workloads differ, requiring work to be distributed across agents.
Resource constrained
Inventory capacity, available tools, or a shared step budget limit concurrent work.
Dependency gate
A branch can proceed only after a prerequisite, such as opening a door, has been satisfied.
Conflict
Branches compete for a unique shared tool, such as a knife or stove, requiring coordinated access.
Hierarchical
Dish-level tasks contain ingredient-level subtasks, supporting delegation across multiple recursion depths.
C.3
Dataset Splits and Difficulty Levels
Tasks are assigned to Easy, Medium, Hard, or Extreme according to the number and scale of their constraints.
The fixed TextWorld-Sync split contains 1,500 training tasks, 200 validation tasks, and 1,400 test tasks.
Training comprises 900 Medium, 150 Hard, and 450 Extreme tasks; validation and test contain 50 and 350 tasks per difficulty, respectively.
For comparison, TextCraft-Synth training uses the fixed subset of 852 Medium tasks, with evaluation on 632 tasks spanning all four levels.
Thus, TextCraft-Synth tests transfer from Medium training tasks across recipe depths, whereas TextWorld-Sync training covers several levels of coordination difficulty.

article.headline: SERA：递归智能体学会自评子任务
article.lede: SERA 让同一策略在委派前写评分标准，并用验证结果训练评分生成，在两个文本环境中超过递归智能体基线 RAO。
article.problem: 递归语言模型智能体把任务拆成子任务并交给同一策略的子实例，最终结果可验证，但中间子任务没有真值。现有方法用验证器或裁判逐节点打分，既昂贵又粗粒度，还没有直接评价任务分解质量。
article.method: SERA 在父智能体委派前生成一组带权重的自然语言评分标准，并在子轨迹产生前冻结；子任务完成后由同一策略按标准打分，作为连续执行奖励。评分生成则用反事实 rollout 的已验证成败做排序训练，另设叶子覆盖率奖励直接训练分解，三个目标在共享策略上交替更新。训练好的评分标准还在推理时用于树搜索的候选选择。
article.results: 在 TextCraft-Synth 上，SERA 平均成功率 74.31%，比 RAO 高 5.38 个百分点；在 TextWorld-Sync 上平均 65.07%，高 13.14 个百分点。推理时用学习到的评分标准做树搜索，在 TextWorld-Sync 再提升 2.43 个百分点。外部 LLM 裁判调用从 147.80K 降到 35.79K，输入 token 从 633.80M 降到 125.32M。
article.why_it_matters: 把评估能力训练进同一策略，不只是加一个外部裁判，而是让评判子任务的能力反过来改善求解，并把学到的评分标准复用为推理时选择器。它也为递归智能体减少对外部监督的依赖提供了一条可操作的路径。
article.limitations: 论文只在 Qwen3-4B 和两个合成文本基准上验证，向更大模型和真实任务的外推尚未测试；自评可能被偏离真实成功的分数钻空子，且评分训练仍依赖已验证结果锚定。叶子覆盖率奖励对所有叶子等权，子任务重要性加权尚未处理。
article.figure_caption_zh: 基于评分标准的递归智能体优化：共享策略的根智能体递归委派子任务，每个完成的子智能体轨迹可获得评分标准奖励以及程序或 LLM 裁判奖励。

email_papers.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
email_papers.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

Abstract
Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control.
Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface.
In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction.
To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding.
Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored.
Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

1
A curated list of related work is available at
https://github.com/Jize-W/Awesome-World-Model-Interpretability
.
Keywords:
Machine Learning, ICML
1
Introduction
Learning models that can understand and predict the physical world is a long-standing goal of artificial intelligence
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Hafner et al., 2025
;
Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018
)
.
In particular, the emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs)
(
Assran et al., 2023
;
Bardes et al., 2024
;
Bardes et al., 2023
;
Ghaemi et al., 2026
;
Skenderi et al., 2025
)
offer a promising approach by predicting in representation space rather than reconstructing observations at the pixel level.
Recent notable developments such as V-JEPA 2
(
Assran et al., 2025
;
Maes et al., 2026
)
further extend this idea toward world modeling, where learned latent representations support the prediction of future states and, when conditioned on actions, can be used for planning and control. JEPA-based models have also expanded beyond general-purpose visual representation learning to embodied control and robotics
(
Sun et al., 2026
;
Yan et al., 2026
)
, 3D scene understanding
(
McVay et al., 2025
;
Hu et al., 2024
;
Zhu et al., 2026
)
, medical analysis
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Radhachandran et al., 2026
;
Shah et al., 2025
)
, scientific discovery
(
Larey et al., 2026
;
ElSheikh et al., 2026
;
Bardhan et al., 2025
)
, and other domains
(
He et al., 2026
;
Hassan et al., 2026
)
. As JEPAs take on broader roles, their latent spaces increasingly serve as internal states for representing and predicting how the world evolves.
This encouraging shift, on the other hand, also raises a largely overlooked question:
what world has a JEPA learned inside its latent space?
This question is challenging, because unlike generative world models that produce human-observable predictions, JEPAs intrinsically predict in an abstract representation space without a naturally interpretable interface.
When a prediction fails, it is therefore difficult to determine whether the failure arises from the represented state, learned dynamics, missing interactions, or errors accumulated over time. More broadly, predictive performance alone cannot establish whether a model has learned meaningful world structure or relies on shortcuts that succeed within its training distribution
(
Kang et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
Figure 1
:
Evolution and positioning of interpretability for latent-space world models. Despite rapid advances in latent-space world modeling and a rich XAI toolbox, direct interpretation of learned world models remains sparse. Existing efforts largely focus on latent-content probing or isolated analysis and intervention techniques, leaving systematic understanding of latent worlds underexplored.
Currently, few existing approaches to representation interpretability provide a natural starting point for addressing this problem. They can reveal what semantic or physical information is recoverable from learned representations, such as objects, motion, and actions
(
Yuan and Søgaard, 2025
;
Tehenan et al., 2025
;
Spies et al., 2025
)
. However, decodability alone does not establish how this information participates in the model’s internal world. Recovering velocity, for example, does not show how it relates to other variables, shapes latent dynamics, or causally contributes to prediction.
As such, interpreting a latent world model therefore requires moving beyond what its representations encode toward how they function together as a predictive system.
To instantiate this point, Figure
1
situates the gap within the broader landscape of world modeling and interpretability. Although general XAI and mechanistic interpretability offer a rich toolbox
(
Sundararajan et al., 2017
;
Wachter et al., 2017
;
Alain and Bengio, 2017
;
Kim et al., 2018
;
Huben et al., 2024
;
Olah et al., 2020
;
Meng et al., 2022
;
Turner et al., 2023
)
, this toolbox has rarely been applied to learned world models as the primary object of interpretation. Existing XAI studies involving world representations largely pursue different objectives.
Some introduce explicit world structure as a modeling mechanism: TDB
(
Dedieu et al., 2024
)
uses discrete bottlenecks to extract cognitive maps, OOCDM
(
Yu et al., 2024
)
builds object-oriented causal dynamics models, and C-JEPA
(
Nam et al., 2026
)
introduces object-centric latent structure.
Others use world models as an interpretability lens, asking whether Transformers or LLMs develop structured internal representations that resemble world models
(
Rohekar et al., 2025
;
Spies et al., 2025
;
Tehenan et al., 2025
)
. In both cases, the learned world model itself is not the primary object of interpretation. Direct interpretability of learned world models remains scarce. Existing efforts primarily probe what information is encoded in latent representations
(
Assran et al., 2025
;
Ming, 2026
)
or explore individual analysis and intervention techniques
(
Challagundla et al., 2026
;
Hong et al., 2026
)
. Consequently, how latent variables are organized, evolve, and causally support prediction remains largely unexplored.
Our position is therefore:
as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction.
Towards this shift, we envision a four-stage blueprint:
Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act
.
Specifically, Ground connects latent factors to variables in the external world. Structure studies how these factors relate and evolve through the model’s learned dynamics. Verify tests whether the identified factors and structures are causally involved in prediction through controlled interventions. Finally, Act uses this understanding to diagnose failures and improve model behavior. Together, these stages shift the interpretability from identifying information that can be extracted from representations to understanding the internal mechanisms through which a latent world model represents, predicts, and acts upon the world.
In sum, our contribution is to establish a clear formulation of latent-world interpretability for predictive world models and provide a systematic blueprint for studying it. We organize existing efforts through this lens, identify the key gaps that remain, and outline how closing these gaps could enable more informative diagnosis, evaluation, and improvement of predictive world models. Finally, we discuss alternative views and identify priorities for advancing this emerging research agenda.

Decodability establishes that information about a world variable is accessible from a latent state, but not how it is organized or used by the predictive dynamics. This distinction matters for world models, where latent states are transformed over time to predict how the world evolves.

5
Implications: What Understanding Latent Worlds Enables
In this section, we aim to shift the object of interpretation from representations to latent worlds, changing how world models can be analyzed and evaluated.
If the internal variables, relations, and dynamics of a JEPA can be grounded and causally verified, they can help explain model successes and failures, assess when predictions should be trusted, and guide improvements in model behavior.
To achieve this goal, we highlight four implications below.
5.1
Diagnosing where prediction failures arise
A prediction error alone reveals little about what went wrong inside a world model. Consider a robot pushing a cup near the edge of a table. If the model predicts that the cup will remain on the table but it instead falls, several internal failures could produce the same observed error. The latent state may fail to represent that the cup is near the edge (
state representation
); the predictor may represent the state correctly but fail to capture the dynamics of losing support (
dynamics
); it may fail to model the interaction among the robot, cup, and table (
interaction
); or initially correct predictions may drift during multi-step prediction (
rollout
).
Latent world understanding could make these failure modes distinguishable. Grounded factors can reveal whether the relevant state information is present, while recovered relations and transitions can expose where the predicted evolution departs from the expected dynamics. Causal analysis can further identify which internal mechanisms contribute to the failure. Thus, these capabilities could turn interpretability into a tool for localizing errors within the predictive process.
5.2
Distinguishing learned world models from shortcuts
Strong predictive performance does not necessarily imply that a model has captured the underlying structure of the world. Similar performance may arise from meaningful physical structure or from correlated cues such as background texture and camera motion. Latent world interpretability provides a way to distinguish these possibilities by examining whether verified internal mechanisms remain predictively relevant as such correlations change.
A model whose predictions consistently depend on stable world relevant factors across objects, scenes, and environments provides stronger evidence of having captured transferable world structure. Conversely, if prediction depends strongly on factors tied to incidental properties of the training distribution, the apparent world modeling capability may be more fragile than performance suggests. This distinction could provide a more informative basis for assessing what kind of world knowledge a JEPA has actually acquired.
5.3
Explaining generalization and its limits
Understanding latent worlds may also help explain why some predictive models generalize across environments while others fail under distribution shift. Rather than treating generalization only as an empirical property measured on downstream benchmarks, latent world analysis allows us to examine which parts of the internal model remain stable as the environment changes.
For example, latent factors that remain stable across changes in object appearance while varying systematically with geometry or dynamics may support transfer across visually different environments
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
. Conversely, factors that change strongly with background, camera viewpoint, or other task-irrelevant properties may reveal likely sources of out-of-distribution failure
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2024
)
. Studying these invariances and dependencies could connect the internal organization of a latent world to the conditions under which its predictions remain reliable
(
Poudel et al., 2024
)
.
Takeaway 4: Similar predictive performance can hide fundamentally different internal worlds.
Latent-world analysis can distinguish where failures arise, whether predictions rely on transferable world structure or shortcuts, and which internal mechanisms remain stable under distribution shift.
5.4
From post-hoc explanation to decision-bounded interpretation
The consequences of latent world understanding become particularly important when model predictions are used for planning and control. In this setting, an inaccurate internal world can affect not only what the model predicts, but also which actions an agent chooses. Interpretability could provide an additional basis for assessing predictions before they are used for decision making, for example by identifying whether relevant state variables are represented reliably or whether the predicted dynamics are consistent with previously verified mechanisms.
This perspective also broadens the role of interpretability in safety. Rather than explaining failures only after an action has been taken, latent world analysis could help assess predictions before they are used for action. For agents that use JEPA predictions for planning and control, interpretability could reveal whether a prediction depends on internal variables and dynamics that have been reliably identified and verified, or on patterns known to be unstable under similar conditions. Such information could provide a signal for deciding when a model’s prediction should be trusted.
6
Alternative Views and Limitations
We consider several alternative views that challenge our position and help clarify its scope.
One possible view is that decoding may sometimes be sufficient. This is indeed the case for many interpretability questions. If the goal is to determine whether a JEPA representation contains information about object identity, motion, geometry, or another property, a well-designed probe may provide all the evidence that is needed. The need for deeper analysis arises when the question concerns the internal predictive world: how represented information is organized, how it participates in prediction, or whether the model causally relies on it. These questions require evidence beyond decodability. Our blueprint is intended for precisely this setting, where representation-level interpretation is a useful starting point but not the end of the analysis.
A deeper concern is whether human-defined variables provide the right ontology for interpreting a latent world. A JEPA need not decompose its internal computation into familiar concepts such as position, velocity, or contact
(
Chawla et al., 2026
)
. Its representations may instead be distributed, nonlinear, relational, or task-dependent, and some predictive factors may have no simple human-interpretable counterpart. Grounding should therefore not presuppose a one-to-one correspondence between human concepts and individual neurons or latent directions. Instead, such concepts can serve as reference points for discovering testable correspondences involving subspaces, nonlinear structures, or distributed representations. Cases in which the model’s internal organization departs from human-defined variables may themselves reveal how it represents the world differently from our chosen description.
Another concern is that interventions in latent space may not always be valid. We agree that simply changing a latent factor is not sufficient to establish a causal relationship. A latent representation may encode multiple properties together, so changing a factor associated with velocity, for example, could unintentionally change other properties as well. The modified representation may also no longer correspond to a plausible state of the world. In either case, a change in prediction would be difficult to attribute to the intended intervention. An important challenge for Verify is therefore to develop interventions that change the target factor while preserving other relevant information and keeping the resulting latent state plausible. Determining how to construct and validate such interventions is an important direction for future research.
More broadly, interpretability may not be necessary for building reliable world models. Robust prediction and control can also be pursued through behavioral evaluation, uncertainty estimation, robustness training, and out-of-distribution testing without examining internal representations. Latent world interpretability should not replace these approaches. Its value is complementary: behavioral evaluation can reveal whether and under what conditions a model fails, while internal analysis may help identify the mechanisms behind those failures and distinguish models that achieve similar performance through different internal strategies. This additional evidence may be particularly useful when predictive models are used for planning and control, where prediction failures can directly affect subsequent decisions and actions.
Taken together, these considerations highlight important challenges of latent world interpretability. They also clarify where the proposed blueprint applies and where its assumptions and methods require further validation.
Takeaway 5: Going beyond decoding does not mean abandoning decoding or behavioral evaluation.
Decoding remains sufficient for representation-level questions, while latent-world understanding is needed for claims about predictive mechanisms. Such claims require valid interventions and should complement, rather than replace, behavioral evaluation.
7
Call to Action
In aggregate, the aforementioned discussions indicate that realizing latent-world interpretability inevitably requires redirecting research efforts beyond isolated applications of existing interpretability tools toward a systematic research program centered on the variables, structures, dynamics, and causal mechanisms of learned worlds. To help shape future research, we highlight four priorities toward this goal.
Build controlled testbeds and evaluation criteria.
A first priority is to develop settings in which latent world interpretations can be tested against known properties of the world. Environments with known objects, physical variables, interactions, and dynamics provide a basis for evaluating whether recovered latent structure reflects the underlying system. Evaluation should go beyond decoding accuracy to test whether interpretations remain stable across contexts, whether recovered relations and dynamics are consistent with observed behavior, and whether causal claims hold under controlled changes. Such testbeds will not capture the full complexity of real-world prediction, but they can provide a foundation for evaluating latent world interpretations systematically.
Study how latent worlds emerge and differ across models.
Latent world interpretability should examine how internal predictive structure develops through learning. The organization learned by a JEPA may depend on its architecture, training objective, data, model scale, and stage of training
(
Richens et al., 2025
)
. Comparing models along these dimensions could reveal when world-relevant factors and dynamics begin to emerge, whether similar structures arise across models, and which design choices lead to more stable or reusable internal structure. This would extend interpretability to studying how latent worlds form and evolve.
Connect interpretation to model behavior and design.
Interpretations should be tested against meaningful differences in prediction, generalization, failure modes, and downstream planning or control. Such connections can also inform model design. If particular internal structures are consistently associated with more reliable prediction or better generalization, they may provide useful evidence for comparing architectures, training objectives, or other design choices.
Interpretability could thereby serve not only to analyze trained models, but also to understand which design choices lead to better predictive world models.
Scale latent world analysis to realistic settings.
Methods developed in controlled environments must eventually be tested on natural video, long-horizon prediction, and embodied agents operating in complex environments. Doing so will require tools for extracting and comparing internal states, tracing predictive computation over time, performing controlled interventions, and analyzing rollouts across model families.
Shared infrastructure and evaluation protocols could make these analyses more reproducible and make it easier to compare findings across models and studies.
8
Conclusion
This Perspective aims to establish latent-world understanding as a central goal for interpreting predictive world models. We note that decodability is not understanding: accessible information does not reveal how it is organized, evolves, or causally supports prediction. Building on this observation, we envision the Ground–Structure–Verify–Act blueprint as a path toward this goal, and as a framework for shaping future research on latent-world interpretability. We call for future interpretability efforts to move beyond isolated representation-level analyses toward systematically understanding, validating, and acting on the internal worlds learned by predictive models.

article.headline: JEPA 可解释性：从解码表征到理解潜在世界
article.lede: 观点文章提出 Ground–Structure–Verify–Act 四阶段蓝图，主张 JEPA 可解释性应从「能解码什
article.problem: JEPA 直接在抽象表征空间里做预测，天生没有面向人类的可解释接口；当一个预测出错时，很难判断问题出在状态表征、学到的动力学、缺失的交互，还是多步 rollout 中累积的漂移。现有的表征可解释性方法（线性或非线性探针、概念探针、聚类、稀疏自编码器等）只能说明某个世界变量可以从潜在状态中解码出来，却不能说明这个变量如何与其他变量关联、如何塑造潜在动力学，以及预测器是否真的依赖它。
article.method: 作者把 JEPA 形式化为编码器 E 与预测器 P 组成的潜在预测世界模型，并区分「表征可及性」与「世界模型理解」：前者关心能从潜在状态中恢复什么信息，后者关心这些信息如何组织、演化并因果地参与预测。据此提出四阶段蓝图：Ground 把潜在因子或子空间对应到可解释的世界变量；Structure 恢复这些因子之间的关系与演化（动作条件下还包括动作如何影响演化）；Verify 通过受控的潜空间干预检验这些机制是否真的被预测器因果依赖；Act 则用已验证的机制诊断失败并通过潜空间引导、激活编辑、重训练等方式改进模型。作者进一步把 V-JEPA 2 probing、AIM probing、WorldModelLens、WAM Steering 等少量工作映射到这一框架上。
article.results: 这是一篇观点文章，论文未给出具体数字，也没有报告任何实验。其文献梳理显示：表 1 仅列出 4 项与潜在世界可解释性直接相关的工作，其中 JEPA 内部的直接证据主要停留在 Ground 阶段（如 V-JEPA 2 的探针显示冻结表征含有外观、运动与动作信息），唯一在 Act 阶段被标为完整覆盖的是非 JEPA 设定的 World Action Models 工作。作者还以机器人操作、3D 定位、医疗、科学发现 4 个应用域说明潜在世界随领域而异，并提出 4 项研究优先级（可控测试床与评价标准、潜在世界如何随训练涌现、把解释与模型行为和设计挂钩、把分析扩展到真实视频与具身智能体）。
article.why_it_matters: 如果能把预测失败定位到状态、动力学、交互或 rollout 中的某一环，并区分模型依赖的是可迁移的世界结构还是训练分布内的捷径，可解释性就能在规划与控制之前提供可信度信号，而不只是事后解释。
article.limitations: 作者自己承认：人定义的位置、速度、接触等概念未必是 JEPA 内部使用的本体，其表征可能是分布式、非线性或任务相关的；潜空间干预也未必合法，改动一个因子常会连带改变其他属性，甚至得到不对应任何真实世界状态的潜状态。此外论文明确表示，可解释性并非构建可靠世界模型的必要条件，应与行为评估、不确定性估计和分布外测试互补；而且作为没有实验的观点文章，Structure、Verify、Act 三个阶段在 JEPA 上基本尚无实证支撑。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从解码表征到理解潜在世界：Ground 将潜在因子对应到可解释的世界变量，Structure 恢复它们的关系与学到的动力学，Verify 通过受控潜空间干预检验其因果作用，Act 再据此诊断失败并定向改进模型行为。

figure.caption: From decoding representations to understanding latent worlds. Standard probing and decoding methods identify information recoverable from JEPA representations but do not reveal how that information is organized, used by the predictor, or relied upon in future predictions. Our proposed blueprint progresses through four stages: Ground connects latent factors to interpretable world variables; Structure recovers their relations and learned dynamics; Verify tests their causal relevance through controlled latent interventions; and Act uses verified mechanisms to diagnose failures and improve model behavior through targeted interventions.

email_papers.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
email_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose RSIFlow, a Recursive Self-Improvement framework that integrates adaptive workflow orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.
