Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose
RSIFlow
, a
R
ecursive
S
elf-
I
mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work
flow
orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.
Figure 1:
Motivation of RSIFlow.
(A) Two coupled challenges in RSI.
(B) The execution loop of RSIFlow.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to tackle complex tasks in coding, tool use, and multi-hop question answering
(
Yang et al., 2024
;
Schick et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2023
)
. To continuously enhance the development of agents’ capabilities in task domains, existing methods have adopted complementary approaches, including evolving execution harnesses
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, optimizing model parameters
(
Luo et al., 2025
)
, and refining executable artifacts
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
. These routes can be organized into self-improvement workflows that propose and evaluate changes using task feedback. Beyond executing such workflows, recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to strengthen not only task-solving capabilities but also the mechanisms that generate subsequent improvements
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Duan et al., 2026
)
.
Research on agent self-improvement spans three increasingly broad scopes of optimization. Component-level approaches optimize a predefined part of the system, such as the model or the harness (execution workflows)
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. System-level approaches coordinate updates across components, including joint model–harness optimization and feedback-driven selection of update targets
(
Chen et al., 2026d
;
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
. Meta-level approaches make improvement procedures editable through operator scheduling, program modification, and recursive skill evolution
(
Tan et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
. These developments expand both what can be modified and how modifications are organized. However, broader editability alone does not establish how effectively a workflow addresses the agent’s current bottlenecks, or whether the ability to organize that workflow improves with experience. This motivates a central question:
how can RSI systems adapt self-improvement workflows to evolving bottlenecks while learning to organize these workflows more effectively?
We formulate this challenge as
dynamic workflow adaptation
in RSI, where adapting bottlenecks and evolving workflow orchestration must be considered together. As illustrated in Fig.
1
, self-improvement workflows must adapt to bottlenecks that vary with task requirements and the agent’s capability state. Even within a fixed domain, successful updates can reshape these bottlenecks and alter the effectiveness of subsequent workflow orchestration. Meanwhile, workflow orchestration is itself a capability that can improve through experience. Feedback from workflow execution supports the accumulation and refinement of reusable knowledge for diagnosis, workflow selection, and execution. These processes form a feedback loop: task-level updates reshape improvement requirements, while workflow experience refines the orchestration capability that guides subsequent updates.
To address this challenge, we propose
RSIFlow
, a framework that couples
adaptive workflow orchestration
with
meta-agent capability evolution
. We instantiate three self-improvement workflows targeting the
Harness
,
Model
, and
Artifacts
. A meta-agent uses execution trajectories and environmental feedback to diagnose the task agent’s bottlenecks, select a workflow, and orchestrate candidate generation and validation. It then distills orchestration outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles to revise its own harness, including execution procedures and skill invocation. This experience-driven self-revision closes a recursive feedback loop in which workflow orchestration outcomes refine the orchestration mechanism that guides subsequent improvements.
Our main contributions are:
•
We formulate
dynamic workflow adaptation
as a key challenge in RSI, highlighting the coupling between evolving performance bottlenecks and continual refinement of workflow orchestration.
•
We propose
RSIFlow
, which adaptively organizes self-improvement workflows and uses their observed outcomes to evolve the meta-agent’s own harness, including its execution procedures and reusable skills.
•
We evaluate
RSIFlow
across six benchmarks and two backbones, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of the 12 benchmark–backbone settings. Ablations support the benefits of both adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution.
2
Related Work
Component-Specific Self-Improvement.
Many approaches to agent self-improvement optimize a single predefined component. STaR
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
)
improves model parameters by repeatedly fine-tuning on self-generated rationales that yield correct answers. AFlow
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
searches code-represented workflows, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
refines prompt-level harness specifications using pairwise feedback over revision histories. Related approaches include DSPy
(
Khattab et al., 2024
)
for language-model pipeline optimization, GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
for reflective prompt evolution, and ADAS
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
for meta-agent-guided search over agent programs. In contrast, AlphaEvolve
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
evolves candidate programs through execution-based evaluation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agent’s improvement procedure. Self-Refine
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
iteratively revises outputs using self-feedback, while Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent attempts and Voyager
(
Wang et al., 2024
)
accumulates reusable executable skills. Co-Harness
(
Chen et al., 2026d
)
and HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
connect external structure and internal capability by alternating harness refinement with model optimization. Their coupled updates address model–harness compatibility, but the prescribed update order leaves open how to adapt workflow orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks.
Figure 2:
Overview of RSIFlow.
(A)
Definition of task domains and agent workflows.
(B)
The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback.
(C)
The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows.
(D)
Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness.
The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop.
Adaptive and Recursive Self-Improvement.
Beyond prescribed alternation, SIA
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
uses trajectory and performance feedback to choose between harness and weight updates, while its selection policy relies on a frozen language-model prior. HASE
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
integrates task solving and harness editing into one action space and trains the policy with GRPO. A complementary direction makes the improver itself editable: Hyperagents
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
co-evolves task-agent and meta-agent programs and demonstrates transferable improvement strategies, whereas MetaSkill-Evolve
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
recursively updates task skills and their improvement procedures on different timescales. Building on these complementary directions, RSIFlow couples bottleneck-aware workflow orchestration with feedback-driven Meta-Harness evolution.

Ablation Study
Table

evaluates adaptive workflow orchestration and Meta-Agent evolution over five rounds. Compared with Vanilla, RSIFlow improves Code, Tool Use, and SearchQA by 19.04%, 3.92%, and 18.20% , respectively, increasing the three-domain average by 13.72 %. While fixed-component workflows exhibit domain-specific strengths, adaptive orchestration achieves the highest scores across all three domains, outperforming the fixed workflow by 4.13% - 8.81% on average. Overall, RSIFlow exceeds the average of all four ablated variants by 6.17 %. Disabling Meta-Agent evolution reduces average performance by 5.74 % , highlighting the importance of distilling historical feedback into reusable skills and principles. These results demonstrate that adaptive component orchestration enables balanced cross-domain improvements, while experience-driven Meta-Harness evolution further strengthens workflow effectiveness.

Rollout-budget and performance efficiency.
Fig.
3
compares performance under varying rollout budgets on all six benchmarks. RSIFlow generally lies on or near the empirical
Pareto frontier and achieves the highest observed score on each
benchmark. This advantage is consistent with its adaptive component
selection and Task–Meta co-evolution: RSIFlow reuses rollout

concentrate the rollout budget on informed workflow orchestration. Overall, RSIFlow offers a stronger performance–budget trade-off than the evaluated baselines.

We evaluate RSIFlow with three Meta-Agent backbones over five evolution rounds on HumanEval+. As shown in Fig.

From Round 3 to Round 5, it improves by 13.08%, compared with 6.15% and 4.17% for the other two backbones, suggesting that stronger Meta-Agents may better leverage accumulated intervention feedback. 5
Conclusion
We presented
RSIFlow
, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling adaptive workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution. Using accumulated execution feedback, the Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows. It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes into reusable skills and principles to evolve its Meta-Harness. Across six benchmarks and two backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses show a favorable performance–budget trade-off. These results demonstrate that continual Meta-Agent evolution enhances system effectiveness alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.
Limitations
RSIFlow is primarily evaluated using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as Task-Agent backbones. This setting is particularly relevant to resource-constrained agent deployments, where adaptive workflow orchestration enables targeted modifications to identified bottleneck components, while Meta-Agent evolution further improves bottleneck diagnosis and orchestration capabilities. However, whether these benefits remain significant with larger backbone models and at cluster scale remains unexplored. Future work will extend the evaluation to larger-scale settings to assess the scalability of RSIFlow.
RSIFlow couples the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent, evolving the Meta-Harness through reusable skills and general principles to improve workflow orchestration without updating the Meta-Agent’s model parameters. However, this process introduces additional computational overhead, while adopting a lower-cost Meta-Agent may compromise evolution gains. Moreover, the stability of experience-driven Meta-Harness updates remains to be fully investigated. Future work will explore counterfactual analysis to identify Meta-Agent deficiencies, apply targeted local modifications, and investigate Meta-Agent parameter optimization to improve evolution efficiency and stability.

Appendix A
Experimental Setup
We evaluate self-improvement across code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. This section describes the six benchmarks, the update mechanisms of the baselines, and the experimental configurations. Appendix
B
gives the algorithms for the three intervention routes.
A.1
Training and Reporting Data
Our evolution pool contains 3,000 distinct training tasks,
partitioned into five task-disjoint batches of 600 tasks each.
Each round uses 200 code-generation tasks, 200 tool-use tasks,
and 200 multi-hop questions. The fixed reporting set contains
744 tasks. Table
4
gives the
dataset-level allocation.
Code generation.
TACO
Li et al. (2023)
contains algorithmic programming problems that
require implementing a program from a natural-language
specification and satisfying its input/output contract.
We use 1,000 training problems from the TACO portion of the
DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset
.
The selected tasks include standard-input/output and
function-based interfaces, with correctness assessed by
executing the submitted program against task-specific tests.
They provide execution trajectories and feedback for
improving program construction, interface handling, and
algorithmic reasoning. The allocation contributes 200 tasks
per evolution round; HumanEval+ and MBPP+ are reserved for
reporting evaluation.
Tool use.
EnvScaler
Song et al. (2026)
provides executable, stateful environments
in which agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls.
Each task specifies a user goal and an initial environment
state; the agent must choose tools, construct arguments, and
adapt its actions to returned observations. Task-specific
validation checks assess whether the resulting state satisfies
the goal.
We allocate 1,000 scenarios to training, comprising 824 from
the source dataset’s
train
split and 176 from its
heldout
split. Both source partitions are assigned to
the training role in our study; tool-use reporting uses
BFCL-v3 and ACEBench. Each evolution round contains 200
EnvScaler scenarios. Different training tasks may share an
environment, so the round-disjoint allocation refers to task
instances rather than environment families.
Multi-hop question answering.
HotpotQA
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
contains
questions that require combining evidence across Wikipedia
passages, including bridge and comparison questions.
2WikiMultiHopQA
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
requires following multi-hop relations across entities and
combining the retrieved facts into an answer. We select 500
questions from the official training split of each dataset.
The Task-Agent retrieves evidence through the search interface
and produces an answer, providing trajectories for improving
evidence retrieval and multi-step reasoning. Each round uses
100 HotpotQA and 100 2WikiMultiHopQA training questions.
Reporting uses a separate fixed set of 100 questions from
each dataset’s official development split.

A.2
Benchmark Descriptions
The reporting set contains 744 tasks: 342 code-generation tasks, 202 tool-use tasks, and 200 multi-hop questions. Each method is evaluated on the same task IDs with the same benchmark-specific scorer. Table
5
summarizes the task counts and reported metrics.
Code generation.
HumanEval+
asks the agent to implement a Python function from its signature and natural-language specification. Its 164 tasks test functional correctness, including edge cases exposed by the augmented EvalPlus tests
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
MBPP+
asks for short Python programs from natural-language descriptions and illustrative tests, covering basic algorithms, data structures, and program construction. We use a frozen 178-task subset of MBPP+ v0.2.0.
For both benchmarks, a task succeeds when the final submitted program passes the base and augmented test suites. We report system pass@1: one final submission per task after the allowed agent execution. HumanEval+ uses v0.1.10, and both benchmarks use EvalPlus revision
26d6d00
with the recorded parser and process-isolation adapters.
Tool use.
BFCL-v3
evaluates function selection and argument construction in single-call, multiple-call, parallel-call, relevance, and multi-turn settings
(
Patil et al., 2025
)
. These settings cover complementary aspects of tool use: selecting an appropriate function, supplying the required arguments, coordinating multiple calls, and determining whether an available tool is relevant to the request. The multi-turn tasks also test whether the agent maintains context across stateful tool interactions, connecting individual call decisions to the evolving interaction history. Our subset contains 152 tasks across 17 categories; native category-specific checks determine correctness, and the aggregate is weighted by the number of tasks. This weighting reflects the composition of the evaluated subset, with categories containing more tasks contributing proportionally more to the reported aggregate.
ACEBench
evaluates API use under Normal, Special, and Agent settings, including ordinary function calls, incomplete or ambiguous instructions, and multi-step interactions
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
. Together, these settings examine how agents translate user requests into API actions under different instruction and interaction conditions. We use 50 English tasks, which produce 57 native scoring records. We report the native weighted score and separately retain complete-task success; these quantities use different denominators. The distinction matters because one task can contribute more than one native scoring record. Record-level scoring describes the evaluator’s individual scoring units, whereas complete-task success summarizes outcomes at the original task level. We therefore specify both task and scoring-record counts when describing this evaluation.
Multi-hop question answering.
HotpotQA
requires combining evidence from multiple Wikipedia passages to answer bridge or comparison questions
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
. We use 100 development questions with the v1 fullwiki protocol.
2WikiMultiHopQA
requires composing facts about multiple entities along multi-hop reasoning chains
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
; we use 100 development questions and the original v1 evaluator.
These tasks test whether agents can connect dispersed evidence and resolve questions requiring relational reasoning.
For both benchmarks, the agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and submits an answer. The main metric is normalized answer-token F1, with exact match (EM) retained separately. The evaluator revisions are
3635853
for HotpotQA and
13800e5
for 2WikiMultiHopQA.

A.3
Training–Evaluation Separation
We separate training-time evolution from evaluation on the
744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon
n
n
, we first complete
n
n
rounds on training tasks and then
evaluate the resulting system on the reporting set. Reporting
tasks are excluded from Task-model fine-tuning. Reporting-set
scores and item-level evaluation feedback are never used for
workflow selection, candidate acceptance, skill maintenance,
Meta-Harness revision, or manual selection of system versions.
Evaluations at different horizons measure the corresponding
training-derived states; their results are not fed back into
subsequent evolution.
The gain-based acceptance
rule in the evolution algorithm applies only to training-time
batches. The batch-level Artifacts procedure, including its
two-attempt allowance and fallback to the parent, is not run on
the reporting set. During reporting, the skill library and
Meta-Harness remain fixed across tasks. Permitted environment
feedback includes execution-interface signals such as
context-length limit errors and output-length or format
violations; it does not provide access to the reporting
evaluator for optimization or output selection. Reference
answers and hidden-test correctness signals are likewise
excluded from generation and output selection. All compared
methods receive the same environment feedback, tool permissions,
and per-task execution budgets.
We additionally checked the frozen training and reporting
manifests for overlap in task identifiers, recorded normalized
prompt hashes, and recorded task-group identifiers, finding no
matches between the two sets. This check establishes separation
under these matching criteria; it does not assess semantic
paraphrases or contamination in the backbone models’
pretraining data. Equal per-task execution budgets likewise do
not imply equal total evolution cost.

The loop has two coupled outputs: an accepted Task state and an updated improvement mechanism. Every candidate starts from the same round parent, so rejected edits do not accumulate. Failed implementation attempts and non-improving evaluations still enter the experience record. On a new task batch, task-bound outputs are generated anew; reusable knowledge is carried by the Meta-Harness and accepted changes to the Task model or Harness.
B.2
Workflow Orchestration
The Meta workflow connects six operations: evidence collection, diagnosis, skill retrieval, component intervention, paired evaluation, and skill integration. Diagnosis returns a bottleneck hypothesis with trajectory references; retrieval returns applicable procedures and counterexamples; intervention returns a candidate and its change record; evaluation returns paired outcomes; integration returns the next active skill set and the Action changes needed to use it.
A decision record binds the selected component to its expected behavioral effect and preservation constraints before construction. The Model branch receives eligible trajectories and a training configuration; the Harness branch receives a localized modification brief and interface contract; the Artifacts branch receives the Task’s own output and permitted feedback. Evaluation determines Task acceptance, while the entire record informs Meta evolution. An accepted Task change and a revised Meta procedure are thus separate decisions within the same loop.

B.4
Harness Updates
Harness intervention changes how the agent executes tasks. Meta localizes a recurring execution defect, refines a modification brief, generates a complete implementation, and validates it. The functional components are Action, Skill, and Planning; concrete modules may implement context organization, action handling, memory retrieval, or verification. Localization identifies the mechanism to change, rather than merely listing files. Executable checks establish that a candidate can run. Acceptance additionally requires a positive paired task gain. An output-contract check can ensure that a coding task receives source code, whereas a receipt-grounded completion check can ensure that a tool operation has actually succeeded. These are changes to reusable execution behavior.

D.3
Component-Specific Skills and a General Principle
The cards in Appendix
F.3
present three component-specific procedures
and one general selection principle. The Harness and Model cards
summarize stored procedures and their observed feedback.
The Artifacts card formulates feedback-guided revision of the
Task-Agent’s own output under a limited budget. The final card
synthesizes how failure scope and intervention cost guide
component selection.
Applicability conditions determine when a procedure can be reused.
On a new task, Meta retrieves relevant revision guidance and
uses it to guide the Task-Agent in revising that task’s own output from its feedback.
The Artifacts procedure and general principle express
methodological guidance rather than additional measured
intervention outcomes.
Harness skills: repair a reusable execution rule.
The submission-contract skill applies when the required deliverable is source code but the agent returns prose or execution output. Its reusable content is the condition under which a complete-source check should be invoked and the execution behavior that enforces it. Reuse therefore changes how subsequent tasks are handled by the Harness. A valid submission can still contain an algorithmic error, so satisfying the output contract resolves an interface failure without establishing semantic correctness. This distinction explains why later feedback can motivate a different intervention route.
Model skills: construct an eligible learning signal.
The replay skill describes how verified successful Task-Agent calls become training examples. Checkpoint provenance, task identity, native success, and target validity determine whether a call provides suitable evidence for the update. Reusing this skill means applying the same data-selection and training procedure to the current parent and available trajectories. R4 supplements M1 because it provides another observed response to that procedure. The added evidence informs when replay is useful; it does not imply that increasing replay volume always improves every task domain.
Artifacts skills: revise the current deliverable.
The output-revision skill targets a defect that permitted feedback localizes within the Task-Agent’s current submission. Its steps operate through the existing interface: inspect the feedback, edit the relevant output, test the revision, and resubmit within budget. The reusable element is this conditional repair procedure, including the circumstances in which further retries are unlikely to help. A later task supplies its own program or answer and its own feedback. Thus, the skill can guide a new revision without transferring the earlier answer or changing the Task-Harness.
General principles: connect diagnosis to intervention scope.
A general principle connects these procedures through a shared decision criterion. The same failed coding task may require a submission check, learning from successful trajectories, or a local program edit. The relevant distinction is where the failure occurs and which available intervention can address it under the remaining budget. A bounded output repair is appropriate when the feedback identifies an actionable defect; a recurring execution problem motivates a Harness change, while a persistent capability gap with eligible training data motivates a Model update. The principle guides this comparison while component-specific skills supply the concrete procedure.

Appendix E
Extended Related Work
Agent System Design and Adaptation.
Recent work on LLM agents explores approaches to adapting execution structures, maintaining persistent memory, and coordinating information acquisition. HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
jointly evolves execution harnesses and reasoning policies through failure-guided harness modification and harness-conditioned policy alignment. For persistent memory, All-Mem
(
Lv et al., 2026a
)
separates online retrieval from offline topology consolidation, preserving evidence while supporting retrieval under bounded computational budgets. Typed links enable budgeted expansion from anchors to archived evidence. For breadth-oriented information gathering, moreover, A-MapReduce
(
Chen et al., 2026c
)
decomposes wide-search objectives into parallel retrieval tasks and aggregates results, using experiential memory to refine task allocation and recomposition. These approaches improve how agents organize execution and retain or acquire information, with emphases on system compatibility, memory maintenance, and scalability.
Structured Supervision and Credit Assignment.
A complementary line of research studies the structure and granularity of supervision for agent learning and language model post-training. GEAR
(
Lv et al., 2026b
)
models prerequisite and activation dependencies among rubric criteria with a probabilistic graphical framework, suppressing unsupported criterion contributions when constructing scalar rewards. The resulting reward captures criterion dependencies at the response level. For long-horizon agent distillation, AlignOPSD
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
aligns privileged supervision with functionally corresponding decisions and distributes outcome-based credit across variable-duration decision spans and their constituent turns. TRCA
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
derives step-level supervision from action-induced state transitions using Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity rubrics. Its foundational reward evaluates local transition quality, while its breakthrough reward recognizes newly satisfied task conditions, providing fine-grained learning signals without requiring successful reference trajectories or learned process evaluators, even when terminal success feedback is sparse.

article.headline: RSIFlow：让元智能体自进化地编排自改进流程
article.lede: 北航等提出 RSIFlow，让元智能体依据执行反馈诊断任务智能体的瓶颈、选择改进流程，并把编排经验写回自身的元框架。
article.problem: 现有智能体自改进方法多沿模型参数、执行框架（harness）或可执行产物三条路线优化，递归自改进（RSI）进一步把改进机制本身也纳入优化范围。但性能瓶颈会随任务要求和智能体能力状态而变化，一次成功的更新就可能改变后续瓶颈，因此「如何让改进流程适配当前瓶颈、同时让编排能力随经验变强」仍未被解决。作者把这一耦合问题定义为动态工作流适配。
article.method: RSIFlow 把系统状态写成任务智能体与元智能体的联合状态：任务智能体含模型参数、执行框架与任务产物，元智能体则固定基础模型参数、只演化其元框架（Action、Skill、Planning）。每轮元智能体读取执行轨迹与环境反馈，诊断瓶颈后从 Model、Harness、Artifacts 三类改进流程中择一，在与父代相同的训练批次上评估候选，接受首个有效且增益为正的候选。随后它把成功与失败的经验蒸馏为组件级技能和跨组件原则，经 Add、Supplement、Revise、Merge 四种证据驱动操作维护技能库，并据此改写元框架的动作接口与调用流程，形成递归闭环。
article.results: 在 6 个基准、Qwen3-4B 与 Qwen3-8B 两个骨干上，RSIFlow 在 12 个基准—骨干组合中的 11 个取得最优；总体分数为 51.21%（4B）与 59.86%（8B），分别比最强基线高 6.06% 与 3.86%，逐指标平均领先 3.11%。单点最大提升出现在 HumanEval+，4B 上 pass@1 提升 14.02%；MBPP+ 跨骨干平均提升 3.91%；2Wiki 的 F1 跨骨干平均提升 5.20%，HotpotQA 在 8B 上提升 6.38%。消融显示，相对 Vanilla，Code、Tool Use、SearchQA 分别提升 19.04%、3.92%、18.20%，三域平均提升 13.72%；关掉元智能体演化会使平均性能下降 5.74%。五轮案例分析给出 Harness–Harness–Model–Model–Artifacts 路径，分数从 32.23% 升至 51.21%（总体 +18.98%），其中 R3、R4 分别使用 3,798 与 5,397 次 replay 调用。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「选哪条改进路线」和「如何把路线选得更好」放进同一个反馈回路，为智能体自改进提供了一个可复用的编排层，而不只是又一个固定的训练或提示搜索流程。

email_papers.title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
email_papers.abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation?
Existing OR benchmarks commonly begin with self-contained problem descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, leaving the work of translating original business materials into professionally validated solutions underrepresented.
We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios drawn from paid OR engagements totaling $3.68 million in project value.
It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification.
To evaluate information acquisition throughout optimization, we further introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise.
Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction.
Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero credit to infeasible deliveries.
Across 11 frontier LLMs evaluated with coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1.
Client information acquisition extends beyond initial clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages exhibiting higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions.
Trajectory analysis identifies failures spanning formulation and implementation, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks.
These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.

Introduction
Operations research (OR) supports high-value decisions across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and many other domains. Deploying an OR system, however, requires experts to transform incomplete business materials into an executable decision process through requirement elicitation, problem formulation, solution strategy selection, and solver implementation. Gurobi’s
State of Mathematical Optimization Report 2024
reports that 82% of survey respondents hold a master’s or doctoral degree
(
Gurobi Optimization, 2024
)
. We ask whether large language model (LLM) agents can carry out this work.

Trajectory Analysis Methodology

(S4), before the self-check passes (S5), and before final submission
(S6). We also record whether the agent asks again after solving feedback when
another decision opportunity remains.
For scientific inquiry, we annotate research opportunities: consequential
uncertainties visible to the agent and potentially reducible through
investigation. For each opportunity, we identify a testable hypothesis
(H), a mechanistic explanation (C), an executed diagnostic experiment
(A), evidence interpretation (E), and an evidence-grounded update (U).
A complete HCAEU chain links these behaviors within the same issue and
branch: H and C precede A, the experimental result informs E, and E
leads to U. We report chain completion and, among opportunities with
a complete chain, stage quality based on a three-level rubric.

We use Harbor 0.18.0 as the execution framework. The harness versions used in our experiments are Claude Code 2.1.278 and Codex 0.155.1. The interaction policy imposes a hard maximum of 500 rounds. 3. Boundaries for interpreting rules and deriving conclusions
A definitive judgment about a rule, calculation convention, or feasibility must be explicitly supported by the available evidence or follow directly from rules explicitly stated in it. You may derive conclusions, but you may not guess the business rules, field meanings, parameter mappings, or other premises required for the derivation.
When explaining or summarizing a rule, retain the objects, stages, conditions, scope, and quantifiers that affect the conclusion, such as “only,” “the last time,” and “within the same stage.” If shortening a statement would broaden what is allowed or prohibited, retain the full wording.
Distinguish business meaning from execution mechanisms. You may explain the business consequences of an explicit rule, but you may not infer that the system uses a particular calculation, comparison, validation, or execution method. Do not turn “this condition already guarantees the result” into “the system additionally performs the corresponding check.” A specific mechanism requires explicit evidence.
Distinguish the scope of an individual rule from overall feasibility. “This rule does not restrict a situation” does not mean “this arrangement is feasible overall.” If overall feasibility also depends on unknown rules or conditions, state only what the current rule establishes. Do not present a specific arrangement as definitively feasible.
When identically named fields, similar concepts, or similar processes occur for different objects, stages, or calculation conventions, do not assume they follow the same rules. Do not transfer clipping, updating, filtering, restrictions, or other processing from one context to another without evidence, in either direction.
For events that cross time boundaries, answer using the explicitly stated timestamps, boundaries, and attribution rules. State conditional conclusions that can be established directly; do not avoid answering merely because an event crosses a boundary.

article.headline: LLM运筹智能体：可行性88.39%，质量逊专家
article.lede: 新基准OR-License用31个真实运筹项目评估LLM智能体，最强配置可行性88.39%、DAQ 0.87，仍低于专家
article.problem: 现有运筹基准通常从自包含的问题描述或预定义优化任务开始，较少覆盖把原始商业材料转化为经专业验证方案的过程。论文要问：LLM智能体能否不经专家预先重构，直接从客户原始材料给出专家级运筹方案？
article.method: 作者构建OR-License端到端基准，含来自10个工业场景、付费运筹项目总值368万美元的31个实例，并在去标识化后保留原始需求、输入数据、交付格式和信息边界。配套ORSim作为受控客户模拟器，只披露业务事实而不提供运筹专业答案；隐藏评估检验可行性，并将目标质量与客户已接受的原始专家解比较，DAQ对不可行交付记零。
article.results: 在11个前沿LLM中，部分模型的条件目标质量超过专家参考，但没有模型在部署调整质量DAQ上匹配专家；最强的主Claude Code配置达到88.39%严格可行性和0.87的DAQ，专家参考为1。可评估任务上，不同模型的任务均衡研究链完成率为24%到45%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评估从解现成优化题推进到处理真实客户材料、信息缺口和交付可行性，更贴近运筹智能体的实际部署。
article.limitations: 基准只有31个实例、10个场景，规模仍小；信息获取由ORSim模拟，论文未给出真实客户部署中的量化验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 评估框架：专家从真实运筹项目中整理任务与参考解，智能体可在求解中查询，最终提交接受可行性与相对专家解质量的隐藏评估。

page_papers.title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization
page_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment. Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and evolving only one component is suboptimal---a harness tuned for one checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed harness. In light of this, we propose Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness proposer. Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step). The policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the policy's evolving failure modes. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings. Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. Self-HPO also improves reliability (Pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (Pass@k) over the base agent. Additionally, we show that with a stronger external model (e.g., Opus 4.8) as the harness proposer, the same framework yields a further performance boost.

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment.
Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and evolving only one component is suboptimal—a harness tuned for one checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed harness.
In light of this, we propose
Self-HPO
, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness proposer.
Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step).
The policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the policy’s evolving failure modes.
Across three coding benchmarks,
Self-HPO
consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B’s average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings.
Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains.

1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents have made rapid progress on complex, multi-step tasks such as software engineering
(
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2024
)
, web navigation
(
Zhou et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2024
;
Wei et al., 2025c
)
, and computer use
(
Xie et al., 2024
;
Agashe et al., 2025
)
.
Such an agent consists of two components: the policy model and its harness, which is the external scaffold that decides what the model observes, how its actions are executed, what feedback it receives, and when an episode terminates
(
Yao et al., 2023
;
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2024
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
.
Typically, the policy model defines the agent’s capability boundary, while the harness determines how these capabilities are elicited, hence the same model may succeed or fail on one problem depending on its harness
(
Le et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
.
There have been two main lines of research on improving such agents.
Harness optimization holds the policy fixed and searches over prompts, workflows, or agent code
(
Hu et al., 2024
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
, whereas policy optimization holds the harness fixed and updates the model from successful trajectories or verifiable rewards
(
Shao et al., 2024
;
Guo et al., 2025
;
Wei et al., 2025a
)
.
However, harness-only optimization cannot improve the underlying model, while policy-only training can learn only from the trajectories that its fixed harness elicits.
Although recent works begin to optimize both components
(
Kim et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026a
)
, they rely on an external harness proposer and face the challenge of a moving optimization target as the policy and its failure modes evolve, leaving self-driven evolution for coding agents underexplored.
In this work, we introduce
Self-HPO
, a framework for recursive self-improvement driven by the agent’s own policy.
As illustrated in Figure
1
,
Self-HPO
alternates harness optimization (H-step) with policy optimization under the optimized harness (P-step).
Harness optimization exposes and compensates for the weaknesses of the current policy, while policy optimization internalizes the elicited behaviors into the model and shifts the failures that the next harness should target.
Specifically, in the H-step, the current policy analyzes its failed trajectories and proposes harness revisions targeting its own failure modes, and selects the updated harness based on search-set performance (§
2.2
).
In the P-step, the policy is updated using reinforcement learning under the optimized harness (§
2.3
).
In the next H-step, the updated policy serves as the harness proposer, with hard tasks identified from the preceding P-step as the search set to keep harness search aligned with the policy’s evolving failure modes.

(

Across three coding benchmarks,
Self-HPO
consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only optimization, with the average resolve rate improving at every optimization step, as demonstrated in Figure
1
.
On SWE-Bench Verified
(
Chowdhury et al., 2024
)
, it improves the base resolve rate from 61.0% to 69.5%, with transferable gains on the out-of-distribution SWE-Bench Multilingual
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
and SWE-Bench Pro
(
Deng et al., 2025
)
.
Ablations further show that evolving the harness search set with hard tasks identified during policy learning yields better performance than reusing a fixed set.
We also extend
Self-HPO
to the external-model setup where Opus 4.8 is used as an external harness proposer, which further raises the resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified to 71.6%.
The main contributions of this work are as follows:
•
We propose
Self-HPO
, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, where the agent uses its own policy as the harness proposer and adapts harness search to the policy’s evolving failure modes.
•
We demonstrate that
Self-HPO
consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only baselines across three coding benchmarks, improving the average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings.
•
Our study shows that both optimized components of
Self-HPO
retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. We also find that
Self-HPO
not only improves reliability (pass@1) but also expands the capability frontier (pass@
k
k

3.5
Case Studies
Harness evolution adds targeted controls around the existing agent loop.
Figure
5
contrasts the seed harness with the harness obtained after HPO’s second H-step.
The optimized harness retains the underlying model-query and command-execution loop, but intervenes before budget exhaustion and at submission.
First, it warns the model as the step or time limit approaches and prompts a best-effort submission before the episode ends with an empty result.
Second, a one-time empty-patch guard asks the model to include newly created files via
git add -N
.
Third, it delays the first submission that passes the empty-patch guard to prompt a check of API names and signatures against the repository and tests.
Finally, a fallback uses the sandbox’s Git diff when the submitted patch fails the apply check.
These changes target distinct ways in which useful repository edits can fail to become a valid submission.
They combine explicit runtime checks, such as detecting an empty patch, with behavioral guidance, such as requesting an interface check.
Harness optimization can therefore change execution and termination logic, in addition to prompts.

gives a detailed diff against the seed harness together with the injected messages, and Appendix

5
Conclusion
We introduced Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization.
The evolving policy proposes its own harness revisions, learns through RL under the selected harness, and supplies hard tasks for the next round of harness search.
Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only baselines, improving the average resolve rate from
57.8
%
57.8\%
to
64.8
%
64.8\%
.
Analyses further show that harness and policy improvements are complementary and that Self-HPO improves reliability (pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (pass@
k
k
) over the base agent.

For subsequent H-steps, the search set consists of hard tasks from

These task IDs are reused to generate fresh failure evidence with the updated policy at the next H-step.
Harness optimization.
Self-HPO uses the current policy checkpoint as both task solver and harness proposer.
The proposer examines the experience of evaluated harnesses and their trajectories, including failed trajectories, and revises the current best harness.
HPO instead uses Opus 4.8 to propose revisions, while retaining the same alternating H-step–P-step structure.

The Self-Harness and Meta-Harness baselines use the same search budget.

echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch.txt

article.headline: 编码智能体让脚手架与策略交替自进化
article.lede: 微软研究提出 Self-HPO，让编码智能体用自身策略提出脚手架修改，并与强化学习交替迭代。
article.problem: LLM 编码智能体的性能同时取决于策略模型和连接环境的脚手架（harness）。只优化脚手架无法提升底层模型，只训练策略又只能学习固定脚手架诱发的轨迹；已有联合优化多依赖外部提议者，且策略变化后搜索目标会漂移。
article.method: Self-HPO 每一轮先固定策略，让当前策略分析自身失败轨迹并提出新的脚手架候选，在搜索集上选出最佳脚手架（H-step）。随后固定该脚手架，用 GRPO 加 BAR 的强化学习更新策略（P-step），并把本轮从未解决的任务作为下一轮搜索集。更新后的策略又成为下一轮的脚手架提议者。
article.results: 在 SWE-Bench Verified 上，Self-HPO 将 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 的 resolve rate 从 61.0% 提升到 69.5%；三个基准平均从 57.8% 到 64.8%，比 RLVR 高 2.9 个百分点。SWE-Bench Multilingual 和 SWE-Bench Pro 分别达到 59.7% 和 65.2%；改用 Opus 4.8 做外部提议者时，SWE-Bench Verified 达到 71.6%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把脚手架优化从一次性搜索变成与策略共同演化的闭环，为编码智能体的递归自我改进提供了不依赖外部提议者的路径。交叉评估还显示，H2 与 P2 联合带来 8.5 点提升，超过各自单独收益之和 6.9 点。
article.limitations: 论文只在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 与 mini-SWE-agent 上验证，训练和脚手架搜索仅用 Python 任务。提升也不均匀：Resolved 组 pass@1 下降 2.2 个百分点，案例中的 PR 意图提醒还出现误报。
article.figure_caption_zh: Self-HPO 总览：冻结策略在搜索集上分析失败并提出新脚手架，更新脚手架后策略通过强化学习演化，更新后的策略成为下一轮提议者，未解决任务构成下一轮搜索集。

figure.caption: {Overview of Self-HPO.} {Top ( ):} The frozen policy analyzes the agent's failures on the search set and proposes new harness candidates. {Bottom ( ):} With the updated harness, the policy evolves through reinforcement learning. The updated policy becomes the next harness proposer, while tasks never resolved during this form the next search set.

page_papers.title: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents
page_papers.abstract: Recursive language-model agents decompose tasks and delegate subtasks to child instances of the same policy, forming a tree of work. Training them, however, is hard: the final outcome is verifiable, but the self-invented intermediate subtasks are numerous and carry no ground truth. Existing methods score each node with a verifier or judge, which is costly at scale and blind to decomposition quality. We argue that a recursive agent must learn three coupled capabilities within one set of weights: decomposing problems into subtasks, solving them, and evaluating the outcomes, each requiring its own training signal. SERA (Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents) turns evaluation into a learned capability of the policy itself. Before delegating, the parent writes a rubric of weighted success criteria for each child subtask; a ranking objective against verified outcomes then trains rubric generation so that the criteria track genuine subtask success. In addition, a complementary leaf-coverage signal provides direct credit for task decomposition. Our central finding is that training the policy to generate aligned rubrics is what drives the gains: because the same weights both evaluate and execute, learning to judge subtasks sharpens the agent's ability to solve them. Notably, external supervision is also reduced: the judge is consulted only to train the rubric generator, while solving is trained against the agent's own rubric scores, which outperform direct use of the judge. Beyond training, the learned rubric doubles as an inference-time selector for tree search. On TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync, SERA improves over strong recursive-agent baselines by 5.38 and 13.14 points on average, and rubric-guided tree search at inference adds a further 2.43 points on TextWorld-Sync.
page_papers.content:
Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents

Abstract
Recursive language-model agents decompose tasks and delegate subtasks to child instances of the same policy, forming a tree of work. Training them, however, is hard: the final outcome is verifiable, but the self-invented intermediate subtasks are numerous and carry no ground truth. Existing methods score each node with a verifier or judge, which is costly at scale and blind to decomposition quality. We argue that a recursive agent must learn three coupled capabilities within one set of weights: decomposing problems into subtasks, solving them, and evaluating the outcomes, each requiring its own training signal. SERA (Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents) turns evaluation into a learned capability of the policy itself. Before delegating, the parent writes a rubric of weighted success criteria for each child subtask; a ranking objective against verified outcomes then trains rubric generation so that the criteria track genuine subtask success. In addition, a complementary leaf-coverage signal provides direct credit for task decomposition. Our central finding is that
training
the policy to generate aligned rubrics is what drives the gains: because the same weights both evaluate and execute, learning to judge subtasks sharpens the agent’s ability to solve them. Notably, external supervision is also reduced: the judge is consulted only to train the rubric generator, while solving is trained against the agent’s own rubric scores, which outperform direct use of the judge. Beyond training, the learned rubric doubles as an inference-time selector for tree search. On TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync, SERA improves over strong recursive-agent baselines by
5.38
5.38
and
13.14
13.14
points on average, and rubric-guided tree search at inference adds a further
2.43
2.43
points on TextWorld-Sync.

Introduction
Language-model agents are deployed on tasks that cannot be solved in a pass: multi-hop research questions require coordinating evidence across retrieval steps; repository-scale code changes involve interdependent edits. A natural response is to decompose the problem and delegate each piece to a child agent
(
Prasad et al., 2024
;
Schroeder et al., 2025
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
, turning one query into a tree of work where each child handles a focused subproblem in a fresh context. When the children are instances of the
same
policy, the system is
recursive
(
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
: a single set of weights drives every node. This is the design behind frontier coding and research agents
(
Anthropic, 2025
;
OpenAI, 2025
;
Tie et al., 2026
)
, and it composes across depth: a policy trained at shallow recursion generalises to deeper trees at inference
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
, making recursion a distinct axis of test-time scaling alongside longer chains of thought and wider sampling.
Training recursive agents is hard because supervision is scarce and unevenly distributed across the tree. The final outcome is typically verifiable (a research answer can be checked, code can be tested), but the intermediate subtasks the agent invents rarely admit a ground-truth check. The natural remedy is to score each node by its own success instead of broadcasting the root reward, using a verifier or an LLM judge (e.g.,
Gandhi et al., 2026
). This localises credit, but the resulting signal has three limitations. It is
coarse
: a binary per-node signal cannot separate a clean solution from a barely adequate one, or flag weak work inside a tree that still succeeds. It is
expensive
: a reliable signal at every node needs a verifier or judge call throughout the tree, which scales poorly. And it is
silent about decomposition
: rewarding whether subtasks were solved says nothing about whether they were the
right
subtasks to create, though that choice often decides whether the tree succeeds.
The root issue is structural: a recursive agent is not doing one thing but three. The same shared weights must
decompose
hard problems into tractable pieces,
solve
the subtasks that result, and
evaluate
whether delegated work was actually accomplished. Every child is a fresh instance of the parent, so all three functions live in a single policy. Training the agent well means giving each capability its own signal without the three interfering on shared parameters.
A self-invented subtask has no ground-truth check, so the agent must judge for itself whether it succeeded. We make this self-evaluation concrete with a
rubric
: when the parent delegates a subtask, it commits a short set of weighted natural-language success criteria for the child before the child runs, so they cannot be fitted to the trajectory they will later score. Applying the rubric to the child’s output yields a continuous, subtask-specific score in place of the coarse per-node signal.
However, a rubric helps only when its criteria align with subtask success. An untrained policy writes misaligned criteria, and using its scores as rewards helps little, inconsistently across tasks (§
4
). We therefore train rubric generation, but the signal for that training cannot be the task reward itself: since rubric generation and solving share weights, rewarding the rubric through task reward would let the two co-adapt, inflating rubric scores together without improvement. Instead, the signal comes from an external check: we score subtask rollouts with a verifier or judge and train the rubric to rank verified successes above failures. Importantly, the judge is used only here, never to reward nodes directly as common approaches do; the rubric provides the dense per-node signal itself, so external supervision is lighter overall. Grounded this way, shared weights become an asset: learning to judge subtasks reshapes how the policy solves them, which is our central empirical finding (§
4
).
A capability,
subtask decomposition
, is the choice of how to split a task into subproblems to delegate. We assign it a reward. In a solved tree, a delegation is credited by the fraction of the task’s leaf-level work its subtree covers, so a delegation that shoulders a large, well-scoped share of the solution scores high, while trivial hand-offs score near zero and delegations in failed trees score zero. This rewards the agent for using delegation to carry structural load, something no execution signal captures. The reward adds little on shallow, near-independent subtasks but helps when subtasks are interdependent, as in tasks with dependency chains, shared state, or coordination (§
4
).
Finally, since the learned rubric captures genuine subtask quality, it is useful beyond training. At inference we search the tree depth-first and select among candidate resolutions by rubric score, propagating the best upward. This further improves final task success without additional training (§
4.3
). The evaluation capability thus pays off as a reusable inference-time selector, a further scaling axis for recursive agents. We call the method
SERA
(Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents). Our contributions are as follows:
1.
A framing of recursive-agent training as learning three coupled capabilities (decomposing, solving, and evaluating subtasks) in a single shared policy, with evidence that each requires its own training signal (§
3
).
2.
A learned self-evaluation mechanism: policy-generated rubrics trained by a ranking objective against verified outcomes. We show that training rubric generation is what improves execution, that it reduces external supervision while outperforming direct use of the judge (§
3
).
3.
A leaf-coverage decomposition reward that credits a delegation by how much of the verified task it covers, with gains concentrated when subtasks are interdependent (§
3
).
4.
State-of-the-art results on TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync (§
4
), and the learned rubric as an inference-time selector for tree search, with further gains (§
4.3
).

Related Work
Recursive and multi-agent training.
Recursive and multi-agent scaffolds decompose tasks and route subproblems to child agents, scaling language-model agents at inference time
(
Prasad et al., 2024
;
Schroeder et al., 2025
)
, but most treat recursion as a fixed scaffold around a frozen model. Recent work instead trains agents to delegate, though largely at depth 1 with fixed or restricted workers: parallel delegation with reinforcement learning
(
Team et al., 2026b
)
and jointly trained organizer–worker systems
(
Sun et al., 2025
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
. Recursive Agent Optimization (RAO) is the closest prior work, combining recursion beyond depth 1, asynchronous subagent execution, and end-to-end RL training of both root agents and subagents
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
. We adopt this setting and use RAO as our primary baseline, but depart from it in the signal each node receives: RAO scores nodes with a binary success label from a verifier or judge and says nothing about decomposition quality, whereas SERA gives each node a trained continuous rubric and credits decomposition directly.
Dense rewards and process supervision for agents.
A large body of work densifies sparse outcome rewards with step- or process-level supervision, from process reward models
(
Lightman et al., 2024
)
to agentic variants that assign credit to intermediate actions
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
; these operate on flat, linear trajectories with the intermediate signal supplied by a separate critic or an additive decomposition of the return. Classical hierarchical RL such as options
(
Dietterich, 2000
)
and goal-conditioned hierarchies
(
Nachum et al., 2018
)
assigns credit across levels but assumes a fixed set of subtask types or hierarchy depth. In contrast, SERA operates on a dynamically generated tree where the hierarchy, the subtasks, and the evaluator are all produced by a single policy and vary from rollout to rollout.
Rubric-based reinforcement learning.
A separate question from where credit is assigned is what form the per-node signal takes. Rubrics extend RL beyond exactly verifiable domains by scoring outputs against generated criteria
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
. Because static rubrics saturate as the policy improves, recent work co-trains the rubric generator with the policy through per-step return decomposition
(
Tian et al., 2026
)
, alternating generator–judge optimization
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, or adversarial co-evolution
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
, with RubricEM the closest in domain family
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
. All assume flat or fixed-stage computation with a rubric model separate from the policy. SERA instead applies learned rubric generation to recursive, policy-invented subtasks whose topology varies across rollouts, uses the policy itself as the evaluator, and trains rubrics with a ranking objective anchored to verified outcomes. We find that the label-free discriminativeness signal favored in prior rubric learning degrades performance in a tree, where score spread reflects subtask-difficulty variation more than rubric quality (§
4.2
); relatedly, work documenting reward hacking under learned reward signals
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
motivates our verified-outcome anchoring.

Leaf-coverage reward for decomposition
Execution credit evaluates what an agent does after a decision, but it does not directly evaluate whether the decision to delegate was structurally useful. We therefore assign a separate reward to each delegation event. 3.6
Alternating optimization schedule
SERA jointly optimizes three objectives on shared parameters. Combining all three gradients in a single update risks instability, since the objectives can interfere and their scales differ. We instead alternate: each optimizer step activates exactly one objective, and the updates cycle in the fixed ratio
n
exec

The leaf-coverage and rubric-generation stages are lighter, each requiring only a small number of periodic updates to improve decomposition and refine the rubric that supplies the dense execution signal. Alternation keeps the credit sources well separated, and the ratio can be adjusted per domain without changing the method. The same learned rubric is then reused at inference time to rank candidate node resolutions during the bottom-up tree-search procedure described in Section

4
Experiments
Benchmarks.
We evaluate on two benchmarks that differ in a property central to our method: whether intermediate subtasks can be verified independently.
TextCraft-Synth
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
is a procedural crafting environment requiring hierarchical planning, tool use, and recursive delegation, in which the agent crafts a target item by looking up recipes and delegating sub-crafts to child agents. Crucially, each subtask has a deterministic program verifier returning a binary pass/fail outcome, so SERA’s rubric training requires no external judge here. Tasks span four difficulty levels defined by recipe depth; we train on Medium and evaluate across all levels to test generalization.
TextWorld-Sync
is our multi-agent extension of TextWorldExpress
(
Jansen and Côté, 2023
)
, a shared-state text environment for evaluating coordination under constraints, with seven task families spanning dependency chains, resource conflicts, load balancing, and hierarchical decomposition. Unlike TextCraft, subtask outcomes are not independently verifiable; rubric training instead uses an LLM judge that provides binary success/failure labels for counterfactual rollouts, making this the benchmark that tests SERA’s ability to amortize a sparse external signal. On both benchmarks the verified outcome
y

3

Conclusion
We presented SERA, a method for training recursive language-model agents that casts training as three coupled capabilities: decomposing tasks into subtasks, solving them, and evaluating their outcomes. Each capability receives its own training signal, and the three are optimized by alternating updates on a single shared policy.
The central finding is that training the policy to generate its own evaluation rubrics, through a ranking objective anchored to verified outcomes, is what drives the largest performance gains. Since evaluation and execution share weights, learning to judge subtask quality directly improves how the agent solves them. This trained rubric also reduces reliance on external supervision: the judge is needed only to train the rubric generator, and the resulting self-generated signal outperforms using the judge directly. Additionally, a leaf-coverage reward provides a direct signal for decomposition quality, with the largest gains on tasks requiring coordination among interdependent subtasks. Beyond training, the learned rubric serves as an inference-time selector for tree search, further improving task success without additional training.
Several limitations remain. We evaluate only Qwen3-4B on two synthetic benchmarks, so generalization to larger models and real-world agent tasks remains untested. Because the policy both writes and applies its own rubrics, self-evaluation could be gamed by scores that drift from genuine task success; we mitigate this by training rubric generation only against verified outcomes—a label-free dispersion reward instead degrades performance (Section
4.2
)—but robustness under sparser or noisier verification, and the residual dependence on verified outcomes to anchor rubric training (Table
2
), remain open. Finally, the leaf-coverage reward treats all leaf nodes equally, and subtask-level importance weights may improve decomposition training.
Looking ahead, the rubric mechanism suggests learning rubrics that generalize across tasks, using the rubric to guide exploration during training, and extending self-evaluation to settings where even the root outcome is not exactly verifiable. Framing recursive-agent training as three coupled capabilities offers a useful foundation for this work.
AI use statement
In this work, we used generative AI tools in a limited capacity for grammar correction and polishing of author-written text, and for coding assistance and debugging. All research ideas, method design, experimental design, result analysis, figures, and tables were produced entirely by the authors. Every AI-suggested text edit was reviewed and accepted or rejected by the authors, and all AI-assisted code was reviewed and tested by the authors before use. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, code, and artifacts.
Ethics statement
This work trains language-model agents to decompose and solve tasks in simulated text environments. The benchmarks (TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync) are procedurally generated and do not involve human subjects, personal data, or real-world deployment. The self-evaluation mechanism enables agents to generate and score their own rubrics, which could in principle be misused to produce misleading self-assessments; we mitigate this by anchoring rubric training to externally verified outcomes and reporting all results against deterministic environment verification. We do not foresee significant negative societal impacts from this research.
Reproducibility statement
All hyperparameters, training schedules, and evaluation protocols are reported in Section
4
and Appendix

Both benchmarks use deterministic environment verification for all reported success rates. We plan to release the training code and the TextWorld-Sync benchmark upon publication.

Appendix A
Recursive Execution and Supervision
Figure
2
illustrates the recursive execution structure shared by SERA and its baselines.
The root agent delegates subtasks to child instances of the same policy, which can delegate further or solve their assigned tasks directly.
Independent branches can run in parallel, while parents incorporate returned results into their own execution.
In SERA, each parent generates a subtask-specific rubric before the child runs and freezes it throughout that child’s execution.
After completion, the policy applies this rubric to the child’s trajectory and final environment state, producing its execution reward.
The rubric scorer and external verifier serve different purposes in this framework.
RAO uses externally supplied subtask outcomes directly as execution rewards; SERA uses them to train rubric generation on counterfactual rollouts.
These outcomes come from a program verifier on TextCraft-Synth and an external LLM judge on TextWorld-Sync.
SERA’s ordinary subtask execution instead receives the policy’s own rubric scores, while the root retains its environment-verified outcome.
The leaf-coverage reward separately credits delegation using the completed tree and root outcome, without additional subtask labels.
Thus, the three signals train execution, decomposition, and evaluation through distinct updates, as specified in Section
3
.

Appendix C
TextWorld-Sync Dataset Construction
TextWorld-Sync extends the CookingWorld environment in TextWorldExpress
(
Jansen and Côté, 2023
)
to test recursive delegation under shared-state constraints.
Its design separates local subtask completion from joint task success, complementing the independently verifiable crafting subtasks in TextCraft-Synth.
C.1
Shared World and Agent-Local Contexts
The standard TextWorldExpress interface exposes one mutable game through a single avatar.
We retain the CookingWorld dynamics and introduce a coordinator that lets recursive agents interact with one shared world.
Objects, containers, inventory, tools, doors, recipe progress, and task score are shared across agents.
Each agent maintains its own logical location, dialogue history, observation stream, and step budget.
Model calls may run concurrently, but environment reads and state transitions are serialized under a lock and committed atomically.
Consequently, an item acquired by one agent becomes unavailable to others, while their locations and histories remain separate.
This distinction permits concurrent planning while preserving consistent state updates and exposing dependencies between agents’ actions.
C.2
Procedural Tasks and Coordination Structures
An original CookingWorld instance specifies one recipe, its required ingredients, and a target meal.
TextWorldExpress procedurally samples recipes, layouts, object placements, and difficulty parameters.
We extend this generator to sample multiple disjoint recipes per seed, assign ingredients to dishes, and introduce one of seven coordination structures.
The complete instance is recorded in a fixed manifest and reconstructed at runtime by a multi-dish adapter.
Independent dish branches can be delegated in parallel, subject to the instance’s resource and dependency constraints.
Table
8
summarizes the seven task families and the coordination decisions they require.
They range from independent branches to shared-resource conflicts and nested dependencies, providing different conditions for evaluating decomposition quality.
The deterministic root evaluator reads structured environment state and requires every ingredient to be collected and correctly processed, and every dish prepared and consumed.
Completing an individual dish yields partial progress but does not terminate the root task.
This root-level check does not provide labels for arbitrary policy-generated subtasks; SERA therefore uses an external judge for rubric-training labels on this benchmark.
Table 8:
Coordination structures in TextWorld-Sync. The seven task families vary branch dependencies, workload allocation, resource constraints, and recursion. Every family uses a shared world and requires completion of all dishes for root-task success.
Task family
Structure and coordination requirement
Fork–join

Resource constrained

Conflict

Hierarchical
Dish-level tasks contain ingredient-level subtasks, supporting delegation across multiple recursion depths.
C.3
Dataset Splits and Difficulty Levels
Tasks are assigned to Easy, Medium, Hard, or Extreme according to the number and scale of their constraints.
The fixed TextWorld-Sync split contains 1,500 training tasks, 200 validation tasks, and 1,400 test tasks.
Training comprises 900 Medium, 150 Hard, and 450 Extreme tasks; validation and test contain 50 and 350 tasks per difficulty, respectively.
For comparison, TextCraft-Synth training uses the fixed subset of 852 Medium tasks, with evaluation on 632 tasks spanning all four levels.
Thus, TextCraft-Synth tests transfer from Medium training tasks across recipe depths, whereas TextWorld-Sync training covers several levels of coordination difficulty.

article.headline: SERA：递归智能体学会自评子任务
article.lede: SERA 让同一策略在委派前写评分标准，并用验证结果训练评分生成，在两个文本环境中超过递归智能体基线 RAO。
article.problem: 递归语言模型智能体把任务拆成子任务并交给同一策略的子实例，最终结果可验证，但中间子任务没有真值。现有方法用验证器或裁判逐节点打分，既昂贵又粗粒度，还没有直接评价任务分解质量。
article.method: SERA 在父智能体委派前生成一组带权重的自然语言评分标准，并在子轨迹产生前冻结；子任务完成后由同一策略按标准打分，作为连续执行奖励。评分生成则用反事实 rollout 的已验证成败做排序训练，另设叶子覆盖率奖励直接训练分解，三个目标在共享策略上交替更新。训练好的评分标准还在推理时用于树搜索的候选选择。
article.results: 在 TextCraft-Synth 上，SERA 平均成功率 74.31%，比 RAO 高 5.38 个百分点；在 TextWorld-Sync 上平均 65.07%，高 13.14 个百分点。推理时用学习到的评分标准做树搜索，在 TextWorld-Sync 再提升 2.43 个百分点。外部 LLM 裁判调用从 147.80K 降到 35.79K，输入 token 从 633.80M 降到 125.32M。
article.why_it_matters: 把评估能力训练进同一策略，不只是加一个外部裁判，而是让评判子任务的能力反过来改善求解，并把学到的评分标准复用为推理时选择器。它也为递归智能体减少对外部监督的依赖提供了一条可操作的路径。
article.limitations: 论文只在 Qwen3-4B 和两个合成文本基准上验证，向更大模型和真实任务的外推尚未测试；自评可能被偏离真实成功的分数钻空子，且评分训练仍依赖已验证结果锚定。叶子覆盖率奖励对所有叶子等权，子任务重要性加权尚未处理。
article.figure_caption_zh: 基于评分标准的递归智能体优化：共享策略的根智能体递归委派子任务，每个完成的子智能体轨迹可获得评分标准奖励以及程序或 LLM 裁判奖励。

page_papers.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
page_papers.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

Abstract
Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control.
Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface.
In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction.
To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding.
Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored.
Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.
