Introduction
Learning models that can understand and predict the physical world is a long-standing goal of artificial intelligence
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Hafner et al., 2025
;
Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018
)
.
In particular, the emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs)
(
Assran et al., 2023
;
Bardes et al., 2024
;
Bardes et al., 2023
;
Ghaemi et al., 2026
;
Skenderi et al., 2025
)
offer a promising approach by predicting in representation space rather than reconstructing observations at the pixel level.
Recent notable developments such as V-JEPA 2
(
Assran et al., 2025
;
Maes et al., 2026
)
further extend this idea toward world modeling, where learned latent representations support the prediction of future states and, when conditioned on actions, can be used for planning and control. JEPA-based models have also expanded beyond general-purpose visual representation learning to embodied control and robotics
(
Sun et al., 2026
;
Yan et al., 2026
)
, 3D scene understanding
(
McVay et al., 2025
;
Hu et al., 2024
;
Zhu et al., 2026
)
, medical analysis
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Radhachandran et al., 2026
;
Shah et al., 2025
)
, scientific discovery
(
Larey et al., 2026
;
ElSheikh et al., 2026
;
Bardhan et al., 2025
)
, and other domains
(
He et al., 2026
;
Hassan et al., 2026
)
. As JEPAs take on broader roles, their latent spaces increasingly serve as internal states for representing and predicting how the world evolves.
This encouraging shift, on the other hand, also raises a largely overlooked question:
what world has a JEPA learned inside its latent space?
This question is challenging, because unlike generative world models that produce human-observable predictions, JEPAs intrinsically predict in an abstract representation space without a naturally interpretable interface.
When a prediction fails, it is therefore difficult to determine whether the failure arises from the represented state, learned dynamics, missing interactions, or errors accumulated over time. More broadly, predictive performance alone cannot establish whether a model has learned meaningful world structure or relies on shortcuts that succeed within its training distribution
(
Kang et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
Figure 1
:
Evolution and positioning of interpretability for latent-space world models. Despite rapid advances in latent-space world modeling and a rich XAI toolbox, direct interpretation of learned world models remains sparse. Existing efforts largely focus on latent-content probing or isolated analysis and intervention techniques, leaving systematic understanding of latent worlds underexplored.
Currently, few existing approaches to representation interpretability provide a natural starting point for addressing this problem. They can reveal what semantic or physical information is recoverable from learned representations, such as objects, motion, and actions
(
Yuan and Søgaard, 2025
;
Tehenan et al., 2025
;
Spies et al., 2025
)
. However, decodability alone does not establish how this information participates in the model’s internal world. Recovering velocity, for example, does not show how it relates to other variables, shapes latent dynamics, or causally contributes to prediction.
As such, interpreting a latent world model therefore requires moving beyond what its representations encode toward how they function together as a predictive system.
To instantiate this point, Figure
1
situates the gap within the broader landscape of world modeling and interpretability. Although general XAI and mechanistic interpretability offer a rich toolbox
(
Sundararajan et al., 2017
;
Wachter et al., 2017
;
Alain and Bengio, 2017
;
Kim et al., 2018
;
Huben et al., 2024
;
Olah et al., 2020
;
Meng et al., 2022
;
Turner et al., 2023
)
, this toolbox has rarely been applied to learned world models as the primary object of interpretation. Existing XAI studies involving world representations largely pursue different objectives.
Some introduce explicit world structure as a modeling mechanism: TDB
(
Dedieu et al., 2024
)
uses discrete bottlenecks to extract cognitive maps, OOCDM
(
Yu et al., 2024
)
builds object-oriented causal dynamics models, and C-JEPA
(
Nam et al., 2026
)
introduces object-centric latent structure.
Others use world models as an interpretability lens, asking whether Transformers or LLMs develop structured internal representations that resemble world models
(
Rohekar et al., 2025
;
Spies et al., 2025
;
Tehenan et al., 2025
)
. In both cases, the learned world model itself is not the primary object of interpretation. Direct interpretability of learned world models remains scarce. Existing efforts primarily probe what information is encoded in latent representations
(
Assran et al., 2025
;
Ming, 2026
)
or explore individual analysis and intervention techniques
(
Challagundla et al., 2026
;
Hong et al., 2026
)
. Consequently, how latent variables are organized, evolve, and causally support prediction remains largely unexplored.
Our position is therefore:
as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction.
Towards this shift, we envision a four-stage blueprint:
Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act
.
Specifically, Ground connects latent factors to variables in the external world. Structure studies how these factors relate and evolve through the model’s learned dynamics. Verify tests whether the identified factors and structures are causally involved in prediction through controlled interventions. Finally, Act uses this understanding to diagnose failures and improve model behavior. Together, these stages shift the interpretability from identifying information that can be extracted from representations to understanding the internal mechanisms through which a latent world model represents, predicts, and acts upon the world.
In sum, our contribution is to establish a clear formulation of latent-world interpretability for predictive world models and provide a systematic blueprint for studying it. We organize existing efforts through this lens, identify the key gaps that remain, and outline how closing these gaps could enable more informative diagnosis, evaluation, and improvement of predictive world models. Finally, we discuss alternative views and identify priorities for advancing this emerging research agenda.

5
Implications: What Understanding Latent Worlds Enables
In this section, we aim to shift the object of interpretation from representations to latent worlds, changing how world models can be analyzed and evaluated.
If the internal variables, relations, and dynamics of a JEPA can be grounded and causally verified, they can help explain model successes and failures, assess when predictions should be trusted, and guide improvements in model behavior.
To achieve this goal, we highlight four implications below.
5.1
Diagnosing where prediction failures arise
A prediction error alone reveals little about what went wrong inside a world model. Consider a robot pushing a cup near the edge of a table. If the model predicts that the cup will remain on the table but it instead falls, several internal failures could produce the same observed error. The latent state may fail to represent that the cup is near the edge (
state representation
); the predictor may represent the state correctly but fail to capture the dynamics of losing support (
dynamics
); it may fail to model the interaction among the robot, cup, and table (
interaction
); or initially correct predictions may drift during multi-step prediction (
rollout
).
Latent world understanding could make these failure modes distinguishable. Grounded factors can reveal whether the relevant state information is present, while recovered relations and transitions can expose where the predicted evolution departs from the expected dynamics. Causal analysis can further identify which internal mechanisms contribute to the failure. Thus, these capabilities could turn interpretability into a tool for localizing errors within the predictive process.
5.2
Distinguishing learned world models from shortcuts
Strong predictive performance does not necessarily imply that a model has captured the underlying structure of the world. Similar performance may arise from meaningful physical structure or from correlated cues such as background texture and camera motion. Latent world interpretability provides a way to distinguish these possibilities by examining whether verified internal mechanisms remain predictively relevant as such correlations change.
A model whose predictions consistently depend on stable world relevant factors across objects, scenes, and environments provides stronger evidence of having captured transferable world structure. Conversely, if prediction depends strongly on factors tied to incidental properties of the training distribution, the apparent world modeling capability may be more fragile than performance suggests. This distinction could provide a more informative basis for assessing what kind of world knowledge a JEPA has actually acquired.
5.3
Explaining generalization and its limits
Understanding latent worlds may also help explain why some predictive models generalize across environments while others fail under distribution shift. Rather than treating generalization only as an empirical property measured on downstream benchmarks, latent world analysis allows us to examine which parts of the internal model remain stable as the environment changes.
For example, latent factors that remain stable across changes in object appearance while varying systematically with geometry or dynamics may support transfer across visually different environments
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
. Conversely, factors that change strongly with background, camera viewpoint, or other task-irrelevant properties may reveal likely sources of out-of-distribution failure
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2024
)
. Studying these invariances and dependencies could connect the internal organization of a latent world to the conditions under which its predictions remain reliable
(
Poudel et al., 2024
)
.
Takeaway 4: Similar predictive performance can hide fundamentally different internal worlds.
Latent-world analysis can distinguish where failures arise, whether predictions rely on transferable world structure or shortcuts, and which internal mechanisms remain stable under distribution shift.
5.4
From post-hoc explanation to decision-bounded interpretation
The consequences of latent world understanding become particularly important when model predictions are used for planning and control. In this setting, an inaccurate internal world can affect not only what the model predicts, but also which actions an agent chooses. Interpretability could provide an additional basis for assessing predictions before they are used for decision making, for example by identifying whether relevant state variables are represented reliably or whether the predicted dynamics are consistent with previously verified mechanisms.
This perspective also broadens the role of interpretability in safety. Rather than explaining failures only after an action has been taken, latent world analysis could help assess predictions before they are used for action. For agents that use JEPA predictions for planning and control, interpretability could reveal whether a prediction depends on internal variables and dynamics that have been reliably identified and verified, or on patterns known to be unstable under similar conditions. Such information could provide a signal for deciding when a model’s prediction should be trusted.
6
Alternative Views and Limitations
We consider several alternative views that challenge our position and help clarify its scope.
One possible view is that decoding may sometimes be sufficient. This is indeed the case for many interpretability questions. If the goal is to determine whether a JEPA representation contains information about object identity, motion, geometry, or another property, a well-designed probe may provide all the evidence that is needed. The need for deeper analysis arises when the question concerns the internal predictive world: how represented information is organized, how it participates in prediction, or whether the model causally relies on it. These questions require evidence beyond decodability. Our blueprint is intended for precisely this setting, where representation-level interpretation is a useful starting point but not the end of the analysis.
A deeper concern is whether human-defined variables provide the right ontology for interpreting a latent world. A JEPA need not decompose its internal computation into familiar concepts such as position, velocity, or contact
(
Chawla et al., 2026
)
. Its representations may instead be distributed, nonlinear, relational, or task-dependent, and some predictive factors may have no simple human-interpretable counterpart. Grounding should therefore not presuppose a one-to-one correspondence between human concepts and individual neurons or latent directions. Instead, such concepts can serve as reference points for discovering testable correspondences involving subspaces, nonlinear structures, or distributed representations. Cases in which the model’s internal organization departs from human-defined variables may themselves reveal how it represents the world differently from our chosen description.
Another concern is that interventions in latent space may not always be valid. We agree that simply changing a latent factor is not sufficient to establish a causal relationship. A latent representation may encode multiple properties together, so changing a factor associated with velocity, for example, could unintentionally change other properties as well. The modified representation may also no longer correspond to a plausible state of the world. In either case, a change in prediction would be difficult to attribute to the intended intervention. An important challenge for Verify is therefore to develop interventions that change the target factor while preserving other relevant information and keeping the resulting latent state plausible. Determining how to construct and validate such interventions is an important direction for future research.
More broadly, interpretability may not be necessary for building reliable world models. Robust prediction and control can also be pursued through behavioral evaluation, uncertainty estimation, robustness training, and out-of-distribution testing without examining internal representations. Latent world interpretability should not replace these approaches. Its value is complementary: behavioral evaluation can reveal whether and under what conditions a model fails, while internal analysis may help identify the mechanisms behind those failures and distinguish models that achieve similar performance through different internal strategies. This additional evidence may be particularly useful when predictive models are used for planning and control, where prediction failures can directly affect subsequent decisions and actions.
Taken together, these considerations highlight important challenges of latent world interpretability. They also clarify where the proposed blueprint applies and where its assumptions and methods require further validation.
Takeaway 5: Going beyond decoding does not mean abandoning decoding or behavioral evaluation.
Decoding remains sufficient for representation-level questions, while latent-world understanding is needed for claims about predictive mechanisms. Such claims require valid interventions and should complement, rather than replace, behavioral evaluation.
7
Call to Action
In aggregate, the aforementioned discussions indicate that realizing latent-world interpretability inevitably requires redirecting research efforts beyond isolated applications of existing interpretability tools toward a systematic research program centered on the variables, structures, dynamics, and causal mechanisms of learned worlds. To help shape future research, we highlight four priorities toward this goal.
Build controlled testbeds and evaluation criteria.
A first priority is to develop settings in which latent world interpretations can be tested against known properties of the world. Environments with known objects, physical variables, interactions, and dynamics provide a basis for evaluating whether recovered latent structure reflects the underlying system. Evaluation should go beyond decoding accuracy to test whether interpretations remain stable across contexts, whether recovered relations and dynamics are consistent with observed behavior, and whether causal claims hold under controlled changes. Such testbeds will not capture the full complexity of real-world prediction, but they can provide a foundation for evaluating latent world interpretations systematically.
Study how latent worlds emerge and differ across models.
Latent world interpretability should examine how internal predictive structure develops through learning. The organization learned by a JEPA may depend on its architecture, training objective, data, model scale, and stage of training
(
Richens et al., 2025
)
. Comparing models along these dimensions could reveal when world-relevant factors and dynamics begin to emerge, whether similar structures arise across models, and which design choices lead to more stable or reusable internal structure. This would extend interpretability to studying how latent worlds form and evolve.
Connect interpretation to model behavior and design.
Interpretations should be tested against meaningful differences in prediction, generalization, failure modes, and downstream planning or control. Such connections can also inform model design. If particular internal structures are consistently associated with more reliable prediction or better generalization, they may provide useful evidence for comparing architectures, training objectives, or other design choices.
Interpretability could thereby serve not only to analyze trained models, but also to understand which design choices lead to better predictive world models.
Scale latent world analysis to realistic settings.
Methods developed in controlled environments must eventually be tested on natural video, long-horizon prediction, and embodied agents operating in complex environments. Doing so will require tools for extracting and comparing internal states, tracing predictive computation over time, performing controlled interventions, and analyzing rollouts across model families.
Shared infrastructure and evaluation protocols could make these analyses more reproducible and make it easier to compare findings across models and studies.
8
Conclusion
This Perspective aims to establish latent-world understanding as a central goal for interpreting predictive world models. We note that decodability is not understanding: accessible information does not reveal how it is organized, evolves, or causally supports prediction. Building on this observation, we envision the Ground–Structure–Verify–Act blueprint as a path toward this goal, and as a framework for shaping future research on latent-world interpretability. We call for future interpretability efforts to move beyond isolated representation-level analyses toward systematically understanding, validating, and acting on the internal worlds learned by predictive models.

article.headline: JEPA 可解释性：从解码表征到理解潜在世界
article.lede: 观点文章提出 Ground–Structure–Verify–Act 四阶段蓝图，主张 JEPA 可解释性应从「能解码什
article.problem: JEPA 直接在抽象表征空间里做预测，天生没有面向人类的可解释接口；当一个预测出错时，很难判断问题出在状态表征、学到的动力学、缺失的交互，还是多步 rollout 中累积的漂移。现有的表征可解释性方法（线性或非线性探针、概念探针、聚类、稀疏自编码器等）只能说明某个世界变量可以从潜在状态中解码出来，却不能说明这个变量如何与其他变量关联、如何塑造潜在动力学，以及预测器是否真的依赖它。
article.method: 作者把 JEPA 形式化为编码器 E 与预测器 P 组成的潜在预测世界模型，并区分「表征可及性」与「世界模型理解」：前者关心能从潜在状态中恢复什么信息，后者关心这些信息如何组织、演化并因果地参与预测。据此提出四阶段蓝图：Ground 把潜在因子或子空间对应到可解释的世界变量；Structure 恢复这些因子之间的关系与演化（动作条件下还包括动作如何影响演化）；Verify 通过受控的潜空间干预检验这些机制是否真的被预测器因果依赖；Act 则用已验证的机制诊断失败并通过潜空间引导、激活编辑、重训练等方式改进模型。作者进一步把 V-JEPA 2 probing、AIM probing、WorldModelLens、WAM Steering 等少量工作映射到这一框架上。
article.results: 这是一篇观点文章，论文未给出具体数字，也没有报告任何实验。其文献梳理显示：表 1 仅列出 4 项与潜在世界可解释性直接相关的工作，其中 JEPA 内部的直接证据主要停留在 Ground 阶段（如 V-JEPA 2 的探针显示冻结表征含有外观、运动与动作信息），唯一在 Act 阶段被标为完整覆盖的是非 JEPA 设定的 World Action Models 工作。作者还以机器人操作、3D 定位、医疗、科学发现 4 个应用域说明潜在世界随领域而异，并提出 4 项研究优先级（可控测试床与评价标准、潜在世界如何随训练涌现、把解释与模型行为和设计挂钩、把分析扩展到真实视频与具身智能体）。
article.why_it_matters: 如果能把预测失败定位到状态、动力学、交互或 rollout 中的某一环，并区分模型依赖的是可迁移的世界结构还是训练分布内的捷径，可解释性就能在规划与控制之前提供可信度信号，而不只是事后解释。
article.limitations: 作者自己承认：人定义的位置、速度、接触等概念未必是 JEPA 内部使用的本体，其表征可能是分布式、非线性或任务相关的；潜空间干预也未必合法，改动一个因子常会连带改变其他属性，甚至得到不对应任何真实世界状态的潜状态。此外论文明确表示，可解释性并非构建可靠世界模型的必要条件，应与行为评估、不确定性估计和分布外测试互补；而且作为没有实验的观点文章，Structure、Verify、Act 三个阶段在 JEPA 上基本尚无实证支撑。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从解码表征到理解潜在世界：Ground 将潜在因子对应到可解释的世界变量，Structure 恢复它们的关系与学到的动力学，Verify 通过受控潜空间干预检验其因果作用，Act 再据此诊断失败并定向改进模型行为。

figure.caption: From decoding representations to understanding latent worlds. Standard probing and decoding methods identify information recoverable from JEPA representations but do not reveal how that information is organized, used by the predictor, or relied upon in future predictions. Our proposed blueprint progresses through four stages: Ground connects latent factors to interpretable world variables; Structure recovers their relations and learned dynamics; Verify tests their causal relevance through controlled latent interventions; and Act uses verified mechanisms to diagnose failures and improve model behavior through targeted interventions.

page_papers.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
page_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose RSIFlow, a Recursive Self-Improvement framework that integrates adaptive workflow orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose
RSIFlow
, a

RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

Motivation of RSIFlow.
(A) Two coupled challenges in RSI.
(B) The execution loop of RSIFlow.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to tackle complex tasks in coding, tool use, and multi-hop question answering
(
Yang et al., 2024
;
Schick et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2023
)
. To continuously enhance the development of agents’ capabilities in task domains, existing methods have adopted complementary approaches, including evolving execution harnesses
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, optimizing model parameters
(
Luo et al., 2025
)
, and refining executable artifacts
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
. These routes can be organized into self-improvement workflows that propose and evaluate changes using task feedback. Beyond executing such workflows, recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to strengthen not only task-solving capabilities but also the mechanisms that generate subsequent improvements
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Duan et al., 2026
)
.
Research on agent self-improvement spans three increasingly broad scopes of optimization. Component-level approaches optimize a predefined part of the system, such as the model or the harness (execution workflows)
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. System-level approaches coordinate updates across components, including joint model–harness optimization and feedback-driven selection of update targets
(
Chen et al., 2026d
;
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
. Meta-level approaches make improvement procedures editable through operator scheduling, program modification, and recursive skill evolution
(
Tan et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
. These developments expand both what can be modified and how modifications are organized. However, broader editability alone does not establish how effectively a workflow addresses the agent’s current bottlenecks, or whether the ability to organize that workflow improves with experience. This motivates a central question:
how can RSI systems adapt self-improvement workflows to evolving bottlenecks while learning to organize these workflows more effectively?
We formulate this challenge as
dynamic workflow adaptation
in RSI, where adapting bottlenecks and evolving workflow orchestration must be considered together. As illustrated in Fig.
1
, self-improvement workflows must adapt to bottlenecks that vary with task requirements and the agent’s capability state. Even within a fixed domain, successful updates can reshape these bottlenecks and alter the effectiveness of subsequent workflow orchestration. Meanwhile, workflow orchestration is itself a capability that can improve through experience. Feedback from workflow execution supports the accumulation and refinement of reusable knowledge for diagnosis, workflow selection, and execution. These processes form a feedback loop: task-level updates reshape improvement requirements, while workflow experience refines the orchestration capability that guides subsequent updates.
To address this challenge, we propose
RSIFlow
, a framework that couples
adaptive workflow orchestration
with
meta-agent capability evolution
. We instantiate three self-improvement workflows targeting the
Harness
,
Model
, and
Artifacts
. A meta-agent uses execution trajectories and environmental feedback to diagnose the task agent’s bottlenecks, select a workflow, and orchestrate candidate generation and validation. It then distills orchestration outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles to revise its own harness, including execution procedures and skill invocation. This experience-driven self-revision closes a recursive feedback loop in which workflow orchestration outcomes refine the orchestration mechanism that guides subsequent improvements.
Our main contributions are:
•
We formulate
dynamic workflow adaptation
as a key challenge in RSI, highlighting the coupling between evolving performance bottlenecks and continual refinement of workflow orchestration.
•
We propose
RSIFlow
, which adaptively organizes self-improvement workflows and uses their observed outcomes to evolve the meta-agent’s own harness, including its execution procedures and reusable skills.
•
We evaluate
RSIFlow
across six benchmarks and two backbones, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of the 12 benchmark–backbone settings. Ablations support the benefits of both adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution.
2
Related Work
Component-Specific Self-Improvement.
Many approaches to agent self-improvement optimize a single predefined component. STaR
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
)
improves model parameters by repeatedly fine-tuning on self-generated rationales that yield correct answers. AFlow
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
searches code-represented workflows, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
refines prompt-level harness specifications using pairwise feedback over revision histories. Related approaches include DSPy
(
Khattab et al., 2024
)
for language-model pipeline optimization, GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
for reflective prompt evolution, and ADAS
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
for meta-agent-guided search over agent programs. In contrast, AlphaEvolve
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
evolves candidate programs through execution-based evaluation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agent’s improvement procedure. Self-Refine
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
iteratively revises outputs using self-feedback, while Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent attempts and Voyager
(
Wang et al., 2024
)
accumulates reusable executable skills. Co-Harness
(
Chen et al., 2026d
)
and HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
connect external structure and internal capability by alternating harness refinement with model optimization. Their coupled updates address model–harness compatibility, but the prescribed update order leaves open how to adapt workflow orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks.
Figure 2:
Overview of RSIFlow.
(A)
Definition of task domains and agent workflows.
(B)
The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback.
(C)
The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows.
(D)
Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness.
The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop.
Adaptive and Recursive Self-Improvement.
Beyond prescribed alternation, SIA
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
uses trajectory and performance feedback to choose between harness and weight updates, while its selection policy relies on a frozen language-model prior. HASE
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
integrates task solving and harness editing into one action space and trains the policy with GRPO. A complementary direction makes the improver itself editable: Hyperagents
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
co-evolves task-agent and meta-agent programs and demonstrates transferable improvement strategies, whereas MetaSkill-Evolve
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
recursively updates task skills and their improvement procedures on different timescales. Building on these complementary directions, RSIFlow couples bottleneck-aware workflow orchestration with feedback-driven Meta-Harness evolution.

Ablation Study
Table

evaluates adaptive workflow orchestration and Meta-Agent evolution over five rounds. Compared with Vanilla, RSIFlow improves Code, Tool Use, and SearchQA by 19.04%, 3.92%, and 18.20% , respectively, increasing the three-domain average by 13.72 %. While fixed-component workflows exhibit domain-specific strengths, adaptive orchestration achieves the highest scores across all three domains, outperforming the fixed workflow by 4.13% - 8.81% on average. Overall, RSIFlow exceeds the average of all four ablated variants by 6.17 %. Disabling Meta-Agent evolution reduces average performance by 5.74 % , highlighting the importance of distilling historical feedback into reusable skills and principles. These results demonstrate that adaptive component orchestration enables balanced cross-domain improvements, while experience-driven Meta-Harness evolution further strengthens workflow effectiveness.

Rollout-budget and performance efficiency.
Fig.
3
compares performance under varying rollout budgets on all six benchmarks. RSIFlow generally lies on or near the empirical
Pareto frontier and achieves the highest observed score on each
benchmark. This advantage is consistent with its adaptive component
selection and Task–Meta co-evolution: RSIFlow reuses rollout
evidence to guide targeted updates to the Task-Agent’s Model,
Harness, or Artifacts, rather than relying solely on additional
exploration under a fixed harness. The co-evolving Meta-Agent
further distills workflow outcomes into reusable skills and
refines its improvement procedure, allowing accumulated experience
to guide subsequent updates. Together, these mechanisms help
concentrate the rollout budget on informed workflow orchestration. Overall, RSIFlow offers a stronger performance–budget trade-off than the evaluated baselines.
Meta-agent backbone sensitivity.
We evaluate RSIFlow with three Meta-Agent backbones over five evolution rounds on HumanEval+. As shown in Fig.
4
, all three models achieve overall performance improvements, with gains of 11.48%, 5.09%, and 24.41% for Claude-Sonnet-5, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and GPT-5.6-Sol, respectively. GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest final performance of 68.29%, albeit with greater API token consumption. From Round 3 to Round 5, it improves by 13.08%, compared with 6.15% and 4.17% for the other two backbones, suggesting that stronger Meta-Agents may better leverage accumulated intervention feedback. These results demonstrate that RSIFlow supports different Meta-Agent backbones, while the Meta-Agent’s underlying capabilities influence the cumulative effectiveness of recursive self-improvement.
Meta-evolution necessity analysis.
Table 3 compares different Meta versions improving the same initial Task-Agent, with scores averaged over two benchmarks per domain. Meta0 improves SearchQA by 10.10%, reaching 44.62% through harness updates. Although Meta4 also selects the harness, it further outperforms Meta0 by 20.56% and 9.51% on Code and SearchQA, respectively. Meta3 achieves the highest Tool Use score of 31.83% through artifact updates. These results indicate that the evolution of meta-agent capabilities not only enables better adaptive workflow orchestration but also enhances the performance of workflow orchestration across different task domains. 5
Conclusion
We presented
RSIFlow
, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling adaptive workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution. Using accumulated execution feedback, the Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows. It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes into reusable skills and principles to evolve its Meta-Harness. Across six benchmarks and two backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses show a favorable performance–budget trade-off. These results demonstrate that continual Meta-Agent evolution enhances system effectiveness alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.
Limitations
RSIFlow is primarily evaluated using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as Task-Agent backbones. This setting is particularly relevant to resource-constrained agent deployments, where adaptive workflow orchestration enables targeted modifications to identified bottleneck components, while Meta-Agent evolution further improves bottleneck diagnosis and orchestration capabilities. However, whether these benefits remain significant with larger backbone models and at cluster scale remains unexplored. Future work will extend the evaluation to larger-scale settings to assess the scalability of RSIFlow.
RSIFlow couples the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent, evolving the Meta-Harness through reusable skills and general principles to improve workflow orchestration without updating the Meta-Agent’s model parameters. However, this process introduces additional computational overhead, while adopting a lower-cost Meta-Agent may compromise evolution gains. Moreover, the stability of experience-driven Meta-Harness updates remains to be fully investigated. Future work will explore counterfactual analysis to identify Meta-Agent deficiencies, apply targeted local modifications, and investigate Meta-Agent parameter optimization to improve evolution efficiency and stability.

Appendix A
Experimental Setup
We evaluate self-improvement across code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. This section describes the six benchmarks, the update mechanisms of the baselines, and the experimental configurations. Appendix
B
gives the algorithms for the three intervention routes.
A.1
Training and Reporting Data
Our evolution pool contains 3,000 distinct training tasks,
partitioned into five task-disjoint batches of 600 tasks each.
Each round uses 200 code-generation tasks, 200 tool-use tasks,
and 200 multi-hop questions. The fixed reporting set contains
744 tasks. Table
4
gives the
dataset-level allocation.
Code generation.
TACO
Li et al. (2023)
contains algorithmic programming problems that
require implementing a program from a natural-language
specification and satisfying its input/output contract.
We use 1,000 training problems from the TACO portion of the
DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset
.
The selected tasks include standard-input/output and
function-based interfaces, with correctness assessed by
executing the submitted program against task-specific tests.
They provide execution trajectories and feedback for
improving program construction, interface handling, and
algorithmic reasoning. The allocation contributes 200 tasks
per evolution round; HumanEval+ and MBPP+ are reserved for
reporting evaluation.
Tool use.
EnvScaler
Song et al. (2026)
provides executable, stateful environments
in which agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls.
Each task specifies a user goal and an initial environment
state; the agent must choose tools, construct arguments, and
adapt its actions to returned observations. Task-specific
validation checks assess whether the resulting state satisfies
the goal.
We allocate 1,000 scenarios to training, comprising 824 from
the source dataset’s
train
split and 176 from its
heldout
split. Both source partitions are assigned to
the training role in our study; tool-use reporting uses
BFCL-v3 and ACEBench. Each evolution round contains 200
EnvScaler scenarios. Different training tasks may share an
environment, so the round-disjoint allocation refers to task
instances rather than environment families.

(

contains

The Task-Agent retrieves evidence through the search interface
and produces an answer, providing trajectories for improving

100 HotpotQA and 100 2WikiMultiHopQA training questions.
Reporting uses a separate fixed set of 100 questions from

A.2
Benchmark Descriptions
The reporting set contains 744 tasks: 342 code-generation tasks, 202 tool-use tasks, and 200 multi-hop questions. Each method is evaluated on the same task IDs with the same benchmark-specific scorer. Table
5
summarizes the task counts and reported metrics.
Code generation.
HumanEval+
asks the agent to implement a Python function from its signature and natural-language specification. Its 164 tasks test functional correctness, including edge cases exposed by the augmented EvalPlus tests
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
MBPP+
asks for short Python programs from natural-language descriptions and illustrative tests, covering basic algorithms, data structures, and program construction. We use a frozen 178-task subset of MBPP+ v0.2.0.
For both benchmarks, a task succeeds when the final submitted program passes the base and augmented test suites. We report system pass@1: one final submission per task after the allowed agent execution. HumanEval+ uses v0.1.10, and both benchmarks use EvalPlus revision
26d6d00
with the recorded parser and process-isolation adapters.
Tool use.
BFCL-v3
evaluates function selection and argument construction in single-call, multiple-call, parallel-call, relevance, and multi-turn settings
(
Patil et al., 2025
)
. These settings cover complementary aspects of tool use: selecting an appropriate function, supplying the required arguments, coordinating multiple calls, and determining whether an available tool is relevant to the request. The multi-turn tasks also test whether the agent maintains context across stateful tool interactions, connecting individual call decisions to the evolving interaction history. Our subset contains 152 tasks across 17 categories; native category-specific checks determine correctness, and the aggregate is weighted by the number of tasks. This weighting reflects the composition of the evaluated subset, with categories containing more tasks contributing proportionally more to the reported aggregate.
ACEBench
evaluates API use under Normal, Special, and Agent settings, including ordinary function calls, incomplete or ambiguous instructions, and multi-step interactions
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
. Together, these settings examine how agents translate user requests into API actions under different instruction and interaction conditions. We use 50 English tasks, which produce 57 native scoring records. We report the native weighted score and separately retain complete-task success; these quantities use different denominators. The distinction matters because one task can contribute more than one native scoring record. Record-level scoring describes the evaluator’s individual scoring units, whereas complete-task success summarizes outcomes at the original task level. We therefore specify both task and scoring-record counts when describing this evaluation.
Multi-hop question answering.
HotpotQA
requires combining evidence from multiple Wikipedia passages to answer bridge or comparison questions
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
. We use 100 development questions with the v1 fullwiki protocol.
2WikiMultiHopQA
requires composing facts about multiple entities along multi-hop reasoning chains
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
; we use 100 development questions and the original v1 evaluator.
These tasks test whether agents can connect dispersed evidence and resolve questions requiring relational reasoning.
For both benchmarks, the agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and submits an answer. The main metric is normalized answer-token F1, with exact match (EM) retained separately. The evaluator revisions are
3635853
for HotpotQA and
13800e5
for 2WikiMultiHopQA.

A.3
Training–Evaluation Separation
We separate training-time evolution from evaluation on the
744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon
n
n
, we first complete
n
n
rounds on training tasks and then
evaluate the resulting system on the reporting set. Reporting
tasks are excluded from Task-model fine-tuning. Reporting-set
scores and item-level evaluation feedback are never used for
workflow selection, candidate acceptance, skill maintenance,
Meta-Harness revision, or manual selection of system versions.
Evaluations at different horizons measure the corresponding
training-derived states; their results are not fed back into
subsequent evolution.
The gain-based acceptance
rule in the evolution algorithm applies only to training-time
batches. The batch-level Artifacts procedure, including its
two-attempt allowance and fallback to the parent, is not run on
the reporting set. During reporting, the skill library and
Meta-Harness remain fixed across tasks. Permitted environment
feedback includes execution-interface signals such as
context-length limit errors and output-length or format
violations; it does not provide access to the reporting
evaluator for optimization or output selection. Reference
answers and hidden-test correctness signals are likewise
excluded from generation and output selection. All compared
methods receive the same environment feedback, tool permissions,
and per-task execution budgets.
We additionally checked the frozen training and reporting
manifests for overlap in task identifiers, recorded normalized
prompt hashes, and recorded task-group identifiers, finding no
matches between the two sets. This check establishes separation
under these matching criteria; it does not assess semantic
paraphrases or contamination in the backbone models’
pretraining data. Equal per-task execution budgets likewise do
not imply equal total evolution cost.

A.4
Baseline Configurations
We compare seven baselines using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
. Within each backbone scale, the comparison protocol uses a common initial checkpoint and Task-Harness, task IDs, and evaluators. Table
6
summarizes editable Task components, weight training, Harness updates, adaptive component selection, and Meta-Agent evolution. These dimensions distinguish how each baseline allocates adaptation across model parameters, task components, and orchestration.
Model updates.
SFT
trains on successful Task-Agent trajectories while keeping the Harness fixed.
GRPO
samples groups of trajectories, scores their task outcomes, and updates the model using group-relative rewards
(
Shao et al., 2024
)
. Both methods improve the Task model without a component-selection mechanism.
Harness and joint updates.
AFlow
searches executable agent workflows through iterative proposal and evaluation
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
MermaidFlow
represents workflows as graphs and searches their structure
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
. These are the Harness-only configurations used in the main comparison.
HarnessForge
combines feedback-guided Harness modification with model training in a prescribed co-adaptation procedure
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
.
SIA
uses execution feedback to choose between Harness and model updates
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
.
Meta-Agent evolution.
HyperAgents
makes both the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent programs editable, allowing the improvement procedure itself to evolve
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
. Its code-editing mechanism differs from parameter training.
RSIFlow
selects among Model, Harness, and Artifacts interventions and updates its Meta-Harness through accumulated intervention skills. The comparison therefore separates access to multiple Task-update routes from the ability to revise the Meta-Agent that chooses and implements them.

B.1
Task–Meta Evolution Loop
Algorithm
A.5

The loop has two coupled outputs: an accepted Task state and an updated improvement mechanism. Every candidate starts from the same round parent, so rejected edits do not accumulate. Failed implementation attempts and non-improving evaluations still enter the experience record. On a new task batch, task-bound outputs are generated anew; reusable knowledge is carried by the Meta-Harness and accepted changes to the Task model or Harness.
B.2
Workflow Orchestration
The Meta workflow connects six operations: evidence collection, diagnosis, skill retrieval, component intervention, paired evaluation, and skill integration. Diagnosis returns a bottleneck hypothesis with trajectory references; retrieval returns applicable procedures and counterexamples; intervention returns a candidate and its change record; evaluation returns paired outcomes; integration returns the next active skill set and the Action changes needed to use it.
A decision record binds the selected component to its expected behavioral effect and preservation constraints before construction. The Model branch receives eligible trajectories and a training configuration; the Harness branch receives a localized modification brief and interface contract; the Artifacts branch receives the Task’s own output and permitted feedback. Evaluation determines Task acceptance, while the entire record informs Meta evolution. An accepted Task change and a revised Meta procedure are thus separate decisions within the same loop.
B.3

Preserving Artifacts in this branch refers to the intervention scope; the candidate model generates its own outputs during evaluation. B.4
Harness Updates
Harness intervention changes how the agent executes tasks. Meta localizes a recurring execution defect, refines a modification brief, generates a complete implementation, and validates it. The functional components are Action, Skill, and Planning; concrete modules may implement context organization, action handling, memory retrieval, or verification. Localization identifies the mechanism to change, rather than merely listing files. Executable checks establish that a candidate can run. Acceptance additionally requires a positive paired task gain. An output-contract check can ensure that a coding task receives source code, whereas a receipt-grounded completion check can ensure that a tool operation has actually succeeded. These are changes to reusable execution behavior.

D.3
Component-Specific Skills and a General Principle
The cards in Appendix
F.3
present three component-specific procedures
and one general selection principle. The Harness and Model cards
summarize stored procedures and their observed feedback.
The Artifacts card formulates feedback-guided revision of the
Task-Agent’s own output under a limited budget. The final card
synthesizes how failure scope and intervention cost guide

Applicability conditions determine when a procedure can be reused.
On a new task, Meta retrieves relevant revision guidance and
uses it to guide the Task-Agent in revising that task’s own output from its feedback.
The Artifacts procedure and general principle express
methodological guidance rather than additional measured
intervention outcomes.
Harness skills: repair a reusable execution rule.
The submission-contract skill applies when the required deliverable is source code but the agent returns prose or execution output. Its reusable content is the condition under which a complete-source check should be invoked and the execution behavior that enforces it. Reuse therefore changes how subsequent tasks are handled by the Harness. A valid submission can still contain an algorithmic error, so satisfying the output contract resolves an interface failure without establishing semantic correctness. This distinction explains why later feedback can motivate a different intervention route.
Model skills: construct an eligible learning signal.
The replay skill describes how verified successful Task-Agent calls become training examples. Checkpoint provenance, task identity, native success, and target validity determine whether a call provides suitable evidence for the update. Reusing this skill means applying the same data-selection and training procedure to the current parent and available trajectories. R4 supplements M1 because it provides another observed response to that procedure. The added evidence informs when replay is useful; it does not imply that increasing replay volume always improves every task domain.
Artifacts skills: revise the current deliverable.
The output-revision skill targets a defect that permitted feedback localizes within the Task-Agent’s current submission. Its steps operate through the existing interface: inspect the feedback, edit the relevant output, test the revision, and resubmit within budget. The reusable element is this conditional repair procedure, including the circumstances in which further retries are unlikely to help. A later task supplies its own program or answer and its own feedback. Thus, the skill can guide a new revision without transferring the earlier answer or changing the Task-Harness.
General principles: connect diagnosis to intervention scope.
A general principle connects these procedures through a shared decision criterion. The same failed coding task may require a submission check, learning from successful trajectories, or a local program edit. The relevant distinction is where the failure occurs and which available intervention can address it under the remaining budget. A bounded output repair is appropriate when the feedback identifies an actionable defect; a recurring execution problem motivates a Harness change, while a persistent capability gap with eligible training data motivates a Model update. The principle guides this comparison while component-specific skills supply the concrete procedure.

HHMMA illustrates knowledge development: H1 supplies a contract-checking criterion for H2 at R2; M1 accumulates training response evidence at R4; and R5 formulates a bounded output-repair procedure for local code defects. The case illustrates reuse within an evolving system; it does not isolate the causal contribution of an individual skill.
From a retrieved record to an executable intervention.
Retrieval provides Meta with a procedure; integration guides its use in the next attempt. For example, a receipt-grounded skill links an unsupported completion claim to the evidence needed for assessment. The Harness change implements this check; paired evaluation determines whether it improves task outcomes. This chain connects the stored lesson to an intervention whose effects can be examined.

Extended Related Work
Agent System Design and Adaptation.
Recent work on LLM agents explores approaches to adapting execution structures, maintaining persistent memory, and coordinating information acquisition. HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
jointly evolves execution harnesses and reasoning policies through failure-guided harness modification and harness-conditioned policy alignment. For persistent memory, All-Mem
(
Lv et al., 2026a
)
separates online retrieval from offline topology consolidation, preserving evidence while supporting retrieval under bounded computational budgets. Typed links enable budgeted expansion from anchors to archived evidence. For breadth-oriented information gathering, moreover, A-MapReduce
(
Chen et al., 2026c
)
decomposes wide-search objectives into parallel retrieval tasks and aggregates results, using experiential memory to refine task allocation and recomposition. These approaches improve how agents organize execution and retain or acquire information, with emphases on system compatibility, memory maintenance, and scalability.
Structured Supervision and Credit Assignment.
A complementary line of research studies the structure and granularity of supervision for agent learning and language model post-training. GEAR
(
Lv et al., 2026b
)
models prerequisite and activation dependencies among rubric criteria with a probabilistic graphical framework, suppressing unsupported criterion contributions when constructing scalar rewards. The resulting reward captures criterion dependencies at the response level. For long-horizon agent distillation, AlignOPSD
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
aligns privileged supervision with functionally corresponding decisions and distributes outcome-based credit across variable-duration decision spans and their constituent turns. TRCA
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
derives step-level supervision from action-induced state transitions using Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity rubrics. Its foundational reward evaluates local transition quality, while its breakthrough reward recognizes newly satisfied task conditions, providing fine-grained learning signals without requiring successful reference trajectories or learned process evaluators, even when terminal success feedback is sparse.

article.headline: RSIFlow：让元智能体自进化地编排自改进流程
article.lede: 北航等提出 RSIFlow，让元智能体依据执行反馈诊断任务智能体的瓶颈、选择改进流程，并把编排经验写回自身的元框架。
article.problem: 现有智能体自改进方法多沿模型参数、执行框架（harness）或可执行产物三条路线优化，递归自改进（RSI）进一步把改进机制本身也纳入优化范围。但性能瓶颈会随任务要求和智能体能力状态而变化，一次成功的更新就可能改变后续瓶颈，因此「如何让改进流程适配当前瓶颈、同时让编排能力随经验变强」仍未被解决。作者把这一耦合问题定义为动态工作流适配。
article.method: RSIFlow 把系统状态写成任务智能体与元智能体的联合状态：任务智能体含模型参数、执行框架与任务产物，元智能体则固定基础模型参数、只演化其元框架（Action、Skill、Planning）。每轮元智能体读取执行轨迹与环境反馈，诊断瓶颈后从 Model、Harness、Artifacts 三类改进流程中择一，在与父代相同的训练批次上评估候选，接受首个有效且增益为正的候选。随后它把成功与失败的经验蒸馏为组件级技能和跨组件原则，经 Add、Supplement、Revise、Merge 四种证据驱动操作维护技能库，并据此改写元框架的动作接口与调用流程，形成递归闭环。
article.results: 在 6 个基准、Qwen3-4B 与 Qwen3-8B 两个骨干上，RSIFlow 在 12 个基准—骨干组合中的 11 个取得最优；总体分数为 51.21%（4B）与 59.86%（8B），分别比最强基线高 6.06% 与 3.86%，逐指标平均领先 3.11%。单点最大提升出现在 HumanEval+，4B 上 pass@1 提升 14.02%；MBPP+ 跨骨干平均提升 3.91%；2Wiki 的 F1 跨骨干平均提升 5.20%，HotpotQA 在 8B 上提升 6.38%。消融显示，相对 Vanilla，Code、Tool Use、SearchQA 分别提升 19.04%、3.92%、18.20%，三域平均提升 13.72%；关掉元智能体演化会使平均性能下降 5.74%。五轮案例分析给出 Harness–Harness–Model–Model–Artifacts 路径，分数从 32.23% 升至 51.21%（总体 +18.98%），其中 R3、R4 分别使用 3,798 与 5,397 次 replay 调用。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「选哪条改进路线」和「如何把路线选得更好」放进同一个反馈回路，为智能体自改进提供了一个可复用的编排层，而不只是又一个固定的训练或提示搜索流程。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 Qwen3-4B 与 Qwen3-8B 两个任务骨干，作者自述在更大模型和集群规模上是否有同样收益尚未验证；元智能体演化带来额外算力开销，换成更便宜的元智能体可能削弱增益，且经验驱动的元框架更新稳定性仍待研究。案例研究也只是展示技能复用，作者明确表示未隔离单个技能的因果贡献。
article.figure_caption_zh: RSIFlow 总览：(A) 定义任务域与智能体工作流；(B) 任务智能体执行任务并收集轨迹与反馈；(C) 元智能体检索技能、自适应编排工作流；(D) 工作流结果被蒸馏为技能、原则与元框架，更新后的元框架指导后续编排，闭合递归自改进回路。

figure.caption: {Overview of RSIFlow.} {(A)} Definition of task domains and agent workflows. {(B)} The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback. {(C)} The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows. {(D)} Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness. The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop.

page_papers.title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
page_papers.abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation?
Existing OR benchmarks commonly begin with self-contained problem descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, leaving the work of translating original business materials into professionally validated solutions underrepresented.
We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios drawn from paid OR engagements totaling $3.68 million in project value.
It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification.
To evaluate information acquisition throughout optimization, we further introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise.
Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction.
Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero credit to infeasible deliveries.
Across 11 frontier LLMs evaluated with coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1.
Client information acquisition extends beyond initial clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages exhibiting higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions.
Trajectory analysis identifies failures spanning formulation and implementation, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks.
These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.

Introduction
Operations research (OR) supports high-value decisions across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and many other domains. Deploying an OR system, however, requires experts to transform incomplete business materials into an executable decision process through requirement elicitation, problem formulation, solution strategy selection, and solver implementation. Gurobi’s
State of Mathematical Optimization Report 2024
reports that 82% of survey respondents hold a master’s or doctoral degree
(

. We ask whether large language model (LLM) agents can carry out this work.

For scientific inquiry, we annotate research opportunities: consequential

article.headline: LLM运筹智能体：可行性88.39%，质量逊专家
article.lede: 新基准OR-License用31个真实运筹项目评估LLM智能体，最强配置可行性88.39%、DAQ 0.87，仍低于专家
article.problem: 现有运筹基准通常从自包含的问题描述或预定义优化任务开始，较少覆盖把原始商业材料转化为经专业验证方案的过程。论文要问：LLM智能体能否不经专家预先重构，直接从客户原始材料给出专家级运筹方案？
article.method: 作者构建OR-License端到端基准，含来自10个工业场景、付费运筹项目总值368万美元的31个实例，并在去标识化后保留原始需求、输入数据、交付格式和信息边界。配套ORSim作为受控客户模拟器，只披露业务事实而不提供运筹专业答案；隐藏评估检验可行性，并将目标质量与客户已接受的原始专家解比较，DAQ对不可行交付记零。
article.results: 在11个前沿LLM中，部分模型的条件目标质量超过专家参考，但没有模型在部署调整质量DAQ上匹配专家；最强的主Claude Code配置达到88.39%严格可行性和0.87的DAQ，专家参考为1。可评估任务上，不同模型的任务均衡研究链完成率为24%到45%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评估从解现成优化题推进到处理真实客户材料、信息缺口和交付可行性，更贴近运筹智能体的实际部署。
article.limitations: 基准只有31个实例、10个场景，规模仍小；信息获取由ORSim模拟，论文未给出真实客户部署中的量化验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 评估框架：专家从真实运筹项目中整理任务与参考解，智能体可在求解中查询，最终提交接受可行性与相对专家解质量的隐藏评估。

figure.caption: {The evaluation framework.} Experts curate tasks and reference solutions from real-world OR projects. Agents may query throughout problem solving. Final submissions undergo hidden evaluation of feasibility and expert-relative solution quality.

page_papers.title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
page_papers.abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

Abstract
Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable
visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2)
inconsistent
image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits.
To address these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion.
Specifically, we propose
Single-Turn
D
istribution
M
atching
D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation.
Additionally, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.
Figure 1
:
Overview of MT Forcing.
Top left: Our approach reduces artifacts after eight editing turns. Top right: turn-wise and eight-turn mean scores for SenseNova-U1.5 with and without MT Forcing. Bottom: qualitative comparisons illustrate the roles of Single-Turn DMD and Teacher-Forcing Guidance in improving visual quality and cross-turn consistency.
1  Introduction
Multi-turn image editing
[
112
,
40
,
28
,
92
,
61
]
aims to progressively modify an image through a sequence of user instructions.
With rapid advances in unified multimodal models (UMMs)
[
15
,
67
,
12
]
, this task has attracted growing attention from the research community.
Compared with conventional single-turn editing
[
3
,
68
,
30
,
36
,
57
,
10
,
100
]
, it enables users to continuously refine visual content as their creative intentions evolve, making it well suited to creative workflows requiring precise control over successive edits.
Since each edit builds on the results of prior turns, multi-turn image editing is inherently causal
[
86
,
62
]
, which naturally aligns with autoregressive (AR) diffusion
[
23
,
19
,
37
,
13
]
in UMMs.
Such a design enables later edits to draw on the accumulated interaction history while responding to new user instructions.
However, existing methods often exhibit drift after only a few editing turns (see Fig.
1
for examples), manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable
visual quality, with accumulating visual artifacts and progressive degradation of fine-grained textures and local structures; and 2)
inconsistent
image content, with unintended alterations to regions outside the requested edit and failures to retain prior edits that should remain unchanged. We attribute these failures to exposure bias
[
60
,
66
]
, arising from the mismatch between training and inference conditions.
During training, the model typically conditions on reference histories, whereas inference requires recursively conditioning on its own imperfect histories.
To overcome these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a training paradigm for UMMs based on AR diffusion that enables stable and consistent multi-turn image editing. First, we introduce Single-Turn
D
istribution
M
atching
D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
) to counteract visual-quality drift across editing turns.
Our design follows two observations: 1) a single editing turn typically introduces limited degradation
[
72
]
; and 2) editing models can execute multiple actions in one turn
[
73
]
(see Fig.
4
).
These observations motivate using single-turn editing quality as the reference for every turn of a multi-turn student.
Specifically, we reorganize all instructions up to the current turn into a
bundled prompt
that expresses their cumulative editing intent as a single edit to the source image.
Conditioned on this prompt and the source image, the teacher executes the accumulated edits in one turn, providing a quality reference without cross-turn error accumulation.
The student performs autoregressive self-rollouts during training
[
29
,
1
]
, conditioning each edit on its own imperfect outputs.
At each turn, a DMD loss
[
95
,
94
,
16
,
44
]
aligns the student’s rollout output distribution with the teacher’s single-turn output distribution for the same cumulative editing intent.
This trains the student to maintain visual quality under the histories encountered during inference, mitigating exposure bias and progressive visual degradation.
However, the bundled prompt specifies cumulative editing intent without fixing the visual details established in preceding student outputs (see Fig.
4
), so per-turn distribution matching alone does not guarantee cross-turn consistency.
To improve cross-turn consistency, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which trains the student with teacher forcing on consistent reference trajectories
[
27
,
31
,
99
]
.
We apply this teacher-forced supervision in two stages.
1)
Teacher-Forcing Warmup
: before Single-Turn DMD training, we perform supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to produce consistent edits conditioned on coherent reference histories.
2)
Teacher-Forcing Regularization
: during Single-Turn DMD training, we retain this supervision with a lower weight as a regularizer to preserve history-dependent behavior and cross-turn consistency during distillation
[
97
,
78
,
8
]
.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that MT Forcing achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following across successive editing turns.
To evaluate multi-turn image editing comprehensively, we build on MTEdit-Bench’s
[
6
]
assessment of instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality.
We additionally introduce
Pixel
\mathrm{Pixel}
, a metric based on image matching
[
24
]
that measures geometric alignment between successive editing outputs.
MT Forcing also achieves better alignment under this metric, providing additional evidence of improved content preservation across turns.
In summary, we 1) propose Single-Turn DMD to stabilize visual quality across editing turns by aligning student rollouts with a single-turn teacher;
2) introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance to preserve cross-turn content consistency through teacher-forced training on consistent reference trajectories; and 3) combine these complementary objectives into MT Forcing, which achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following in extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments.

Multi-Turn Image Editing
extends instruction-based image editing

,
26
,
46

to an interactive setting, where users progressively refine an image through a sequence of instructions.
A straightforward approach is to recursively apply a single-turn editor, conditioning each turn on the previous output and the current instruction
[

,
40
,
28
,
101
]
.
However, this formulation does not explicitly model the full interaction history, limiting its ability to retain earlier constraints and resolve context-dependent instructions

91
]
.
Recent approaches build on UMMs to incorporate previous instructions and generated images into a shared context for subsequent edits

,
92

Diffusion Distillation

Teacher-trajectory regression learns the teacher’s sampling dynamics through direct noise-to-image regression

or progressive step compression

Consistency-based methods constrain predictions along a diffusion trajectory to share a common endpoint

Continuous-time formulations improve scalability

Distribution-level methods supervise generated samples through adversarial objectives

DMD

Subsequent work improves distillation quality and scalability

Auxiliary student-score estimation can also be replaced by generator-derived surrogates

We use DMD2 to transfer single-turn editing quality to outputs under imperfect multi-turn histories.
Autoregressive Diffusion
generates visual content in a causal autoregressive manner.
For images, UMMs
[
12
,
67
,
15
,
14
,
82
,
83
,

,

For videos, a common strategy distills pretrained bidirectional diffusion models into few-step autoregressive generators, reducing latency and enabling streaming beyond the training clip length
[
96
,
29
]

CausVid
[

Diffusion Forcing
[
5

[

Other studies improve causal student initialization
[

,
108

and scalable few-step or one-step distillation

,

Long-horizon stability is further strengthened through streaming training and error control

As shown in Fig.

Sec.
3.1
defines the multi-turn editing problem and its training–inference mismatch.
Sec.
3.2

Sec.

presents Teacher-Forcing Guidance for cross-turn consistency.

5  Conclusion
We presented MT Forcing, which combines learning on self-generated histories with reference supervision for stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive UMMs.
Single-Turn DMD transfers single-turn editing quality to student rollouts using a teacher that realizes cumulative editing intent directly from the source image, avoiding recursive error accumulation in its supervision.
Teacher-Forcing Guidance complements marginal distribution matching with reference-conditioned supervision during warmup and distillation, encouraging the history–output dependencies needed for content preservation.
Experiments on SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 demonstrate improved instruction following, content consistency, and drift robustness on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench, with increasingly pronounced benefits at later turns.

article.headline: MT Forcing：用单轮教师稳定多轮图像编辑
article.lede: 研究者提出 MT Forcing，用单轮分布匹配蒸馏和教师强制引导，缓解多轮图像编辑的画质漂移与内容不一致。
article.problem: 多轮图像编辑要求模型按连续指令修改图像，但现有方法在几轮后出现两类漂移：视觉质量不稳定，伪影累积、细节退化；内容不一致，未要求区域被改动、先前编辑丢失。作者将原因归结为 exposure bias——训练时条件于参考历史，推理时却递归条件于自身不完美输出。
article.method: Single-Turn DMD 把截至当前轮的所有指令重组为一个 bundled prompt，让冻结的单轮教师直接从源图完成累计编辑，并用 DMD 损失把学生自回归 rollout 的每轮输出分布对齐到该教师分布，避免教师监督本身递归累积误差。Teacher-Forcing Guidance 则在参考轨迹上用 flow matching 监督依赖历史的转移，先做 warmup，蒸馏时再以较低权重作为正则项。整体目标为 L_DMD + λ_TF L_TF。
article.results: 在 MTEdit-Bench step-wise 子集（100 个 session、每个 8 条指令）上，SenseNova-U1 第 8 轮 IF/CC 分别提升 7.45 和 6.82；SenseNova-U1.5 第 8 轮 IF/CC 提升 4.65 和 4.46。SenseNova-U1.5 的 DRS 全程维持在 4.20–4.35，基线从 4.09 降到 3.03；八轮平均 Pixel 从 6.34 降到 0.74，降幅 88.4%。消融中完整方法取得 9.66 IF、8.40 CC、4.30 DRS、0.74 Pixel，优于仅 DMD 的 9.02/7.64/4.12/2.51、仅 Teacher-Forcing Guidance 的 9.10/7.83/3.92/2.74 和无组件基线 8.47/7.09/3.83/6.34。需注意 SenseNova-U1.5 在第 1–3 轮的 IF/CC 并非全部提升（第 1 轮 IF 9.90→9.74、CC 9.49→8.82），从第 4 轮起四项指标才全面优于基线。
article.why_it_matters: 多轮编辑是交互式视觉创作的关键形态，而训练-推理历史不匹配是自回归统一多模态模型的共性问题。MT Forcing 在缺少能联合生成完整编辑轨迹的双向教师时，给出了一套可操作的分布匹配加参考监督方案。
article.limitations: 实验仅在 MTEdit-Bench 的 step-wise 子集和 SenseNova-U1/U1.5 上验证，且主要是同一编辑器有无 MT Forcing 的对比，未与 MT-OPSD 等其他多轮方法横向比较；SenseNova-U1.5 早期轮次 IF/CC 还出现下降。单轮教师自身会产生跨轮内容不一致（论文图 4 的茶壶花纹变化），bundled prompt 由学生条件到教师条件的映射不可逆，λ_TF 取 1 或 0.5 时还会带来可见模糊，这些都需要额外权衡。
article.figure_caption_zh: MT Forcing 总览：单轮 DMD 将学生自回归 rollout 的每轮输出分布对齐到单轮教师，教师强制引导在参考轨迹上监督历史依赖转移，整体训练先做教师强制 warmup，再进行带教师强制正则的 DMD。

figure.caption: {Overview of MT Forcing.} (a)~Single-Turn DMD matches student rollout marginals to single-turn teacher distributions. (b)~Teacher-Forcing Guidance supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories via flow matching to encourage cross-turn consistency. (c)~Overall training: teacher-forcing warmup followed by DMD with teacher-forcing regularization.

page_papers.title: RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction
page_papers.abstract: An effective visual tokenizer must preserve image fidelity while producing latents that downstream diffusion models can learn efficiently. Prior work improves latent diffusability through semantic alignment or joint tokenizer--diffusion training. Revisiting REPA-E, a representative approach, we find that removing its diffusion objective and dedicated generative blocks while retaining semantic prediction from corrupted latents yields comparable downstream generation performance under a matched setting. This observation motivates a general principle of robust prediction: generation-relevant information should remain recoverable from corrupted latents. We instantiate this principle with two complementary objectives. RobustAlign predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents to preserve high-level structure, while RobustRecon reconstructs the clean image to retain fine-grained spatial and appearance information. Together, they form Robust Alignment and Reconstruction VAE (RoAR-VAE). Our analysis suggests that robust prediction improves diffusability by making useful information more accessible in high-variance latent directions, which diffusion models tend to learn earlier. Empirically, RoAR-VAE improves average generation benchmark performance by 2.19 points over the strongest baseline tokenizer under the same training budget, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy by 16.93 percentage points over FLUX.1-VAE. These results demonstrate that RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and downstream generative learnability.

RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction
Yang Yue Fangyun Wei Yitong Wang Jinjing Zhao
Henry Zheng  Dong Chen  Gao Huang
1
