page_papers.title: Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
page_papers.abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes. The source code is publicly available at https://mias.group/MaSS.
page_papers.content:
Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
Mengtan Zhang   Yuchuan Cui   Yu Ma   Zizhan Guo   Wei Ye   Rui FanTongji University
Abstract
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes.
The source code is publicly available at
https://mias.group/MaSS
.

1
Introduction
The fundamental advantage of self-supervised learning lies in its potential to leverage ubiquitous unlabeled data for scalable model training. However, most existing self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SSMDE) research
[
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
]
is predominantly confined to training models individually on single datasets or scenarios, leaving much of this potential unexplored. Recent efforts have attempted to directly train models with existing SSMDE methods on large-scale video sequences curated from online platforms
[
6
,
7
]
, as well as to incorporate vision foundation models (VFMs) as backbones
[
8
,
7
]
. Despite these advances, overall performance improvements remain limited. As demonstrated by our preliminary experiments (see Fig.
1
(b)), when existing methods are trained simultaneously on diverse monocular video data (
e.g.
, indoor, outdoor, dynamic, and adverse weather scenarios), they fail to benefit mutually from the increased diversity and do not exhibit improved generalization to out-of-distribution scenes. Instead, we observe a performance decline compared to models trained individually on a single dataset. This observation demonstrates that existing SSMDE methods have not yet achieved effective scalability to diverse data.
This study begins by investigating the challenges that arise when SSMDE is exposed to diverse data distributions during training. It is worth noting that the novel-view synthesis-based supervision inevitably introduces noisy and artifact-laden supervisory signals in scenarios involving occlusions, textureless regions, and illumination changes
[
9
,
10
]
. Even setting aside such noise, the gradients induced by self-supervised losses often fail to reflect depth errors faithfully
[
4
]
. As a result, the optimization process is inherently prone to local minima, leading to poor convergence stability
[
4
]
. Although these challenges frequently occur during self-supervised training, existing methods can still achieve reasonable accuracy on a single, homogeneous dataset
[
3
]
. This is largely because the network can exploit the structural bias inherent to that dataset, thereby compensating for weak supervision. The key evidence we find is that under the existing SSMDE framework, the coarsest, high-level feature of the depth encoder does not capture depth-related cues, such as the foreground–background relation and perspective geometry. Instead, it primarily reflects the dataset-specific structural biases. When training on diverse datasets, different data domains often require the model to learn inconsistent structural biases for their respective convergence, leading to the observed performance drop.
These findings motivate us to explicitly guide the network to learn a robust, generalized scene-structure representation for depth decoding. Based on this core idea, we develop the
MaSS
framework that
Ma
ke
S
elf-supervised depth learning
S
calable to diverse data. MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM through a bidirectional interaction architecture, drawing inspiration from
[
11
]
. In this design, the depth encoder focuses on extracting geometric cues that are difficult to recover from VFM features
[
8
]
. The interacted VFM features are then fed into two feature projectors to reconstruct complementary, collapse-free representations under explicit constraints and learning objectives. Specifically, one projector is adapted to learn a contextual representation informative for depth estimation, such as object-level spatial relationships, while retaining generalized semantics with the original VFM features as anchors. The other projector is then constrained to be decoupled from the contextual one, thereby reserving its representational capacity for scene structure.
To explicitly define this representation, we introduce a scene-structure discrimination objective via contrastive learning. This objective organizes the feature space based on scene layout similarity, which is measured by the histogram distribution of predicted depth. Driven by this objective, the second projector learns transferable structural representations that capture global scene layout and perspective geometry, rather than dataset-specific biases. Together, these two complementary representations enable more reliable depth predictions while reducing their reliance on dataset-specific biases.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that MaSS outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SoTA) self-supervised methods by a large margin (as presented in Fig.
1
(a)) and achieves accuracy comparable to certain supervised depth foundation models. Moreover, MaSS represents the first self-supervised approach to achieve clear performance gains from increasing the diversity of training data (Fig.
1
(b)), resulting in notable generalizability improvements particularly on out-of-distribution scenes (Fig.
1
(c)).
2
Related Works
To alleviate the reliance on extensive ground-truth data in monocular depth estimation (MDE), SSMDE from monocular video, first introduced in the study
[
12
]
, has attracted growing attention. Within this paradigm, improvements have focused on enhancing photometric supervision
[
1
]
, addressing scale inconsistency
[
13
]
, and incorporating additional visual cues to handle occlusions and dynamic scenes
[
14
,
3
,
15
,
16
,
4
]
.
Though significant progress has been made, these SSMDE methods are typically trained on single domains with limited-scale datasets and rely on task-specific network architectures
[
17
,
18
,
19
,
20
]
. The study
[
21
]
first demonstrates the feasibility of self-supervised depth learning from heterogeneous in-the-wild videos by jointly estimating depth, camera motion, object motion, and camera intrinsics. With the rise of VFMs
[
22
,
23
]
, increasing efforts have been devoted to developing depth foundation models (DFMs)
[
24
,
25
,
26
]
trained on large-scale annotated data, achieving strong performance and generalization.
Building upon this trend, recent studies
[
6
,
7
]
have taken initial steps toward scaling SSMDE training, while the others
[
9
,
27
,
5
]
demonstrate that developing DFMs in a self-supervised fashion requires not only harnessing the large pretrained models’ capacity, but also addressing challenges unique to self-supervised learning. Among them, cross-domain learning conflicts under mixed-domain training pose a fundamental yet underexplored obstacle to scalability, which this work primarily aims to address.
Three lines of research inform our approach. The first draws on pretrained knowledge to improve depth representations. For example, the study
[
28
]
uses a pretrained semantic network to guide the learning of geometric features. The studies
[
29
,
30
]
further emphasize preserving transferable pretrained representations during adaptation. The second focuses on organizing depth representations. The prior arts
[
31
,
32
,
33
,
27
]
have introduced contrastive objectives that structure the feature space according to weather variations, color or geometric consistency, historical predictions, and relationships guided by language. The third conditions depth prediction distributions on scene characteristics to account for domain shifts. For example, the study
[
34
]
conditions these distributions on scene categories. Drawing on these insights, MaSS explicitly decouples contextual and structural representations, preserves contextual relationships derived from VFMs, and adaptively organizes structural features according to similarities in scene layout. Depth prediction is then conditioned on the resulting structural representations to reduce learning conflicts across domains.
Figure 2:
Feature activation map comparison among a conventional self-supervised depth model, DINOv2, and the two representations learned by MaSS. (a) The conventional depth model tends to encode dataset-specific biases, whereas (b) DINOv2 lacks sufficient geometric cues. In contrast, MaSS decouples features into contextual and structural representations: (c) contextual ones capture fine-grained object details and foreground–background relations; (d) structural ones encode global scene layouts that are transferable across diverse datasets.
3
Methodology
SSMDE models are prone to learning dataset-specific inductive biases and struggle to generalize across varying depth distributions during both training and inference. For example, Fig.
1
(c) presents depth predictions on out-of-distribution indoor and outdoor scenes from two representative self-supervised depth models
[
3
,
4
]
, trained on the NYUv2
[
35
]
and KITTI
[
36
]
datasets, respectively. It can be observed that the model trained on driving scenes tends to predict depth with a vanishing point, while the model trained on small rooms fails to capture the more uniform depth distributions in large halls. To find the source of such inductive biases, we investigate the internal feature representations. As shown in Fig.
2
(a), the DepthNet encoder
[
4
]
trained on driving data produces feature activation maps with a consistent low-activation region. This pattern closely resembles the biased depth predictions in Fig.
1
(c) and fails to reflect variations aligned with the actual scene geometry. These results indicate that the dataset-specific inductive biases are already embedded in the intermediate representations. The above findings inspire us with a possible solution to make self-supervised learning scalable: explicitly guide the network to learn robust, generalized structural representations that are discriminative of scene layout before decoding depth.
Figure 3:
The overall architecture of the proposed MaSS framework.
MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM via a bidirectional interaction module. The interacted VFM features are fed into a pair of anchored–decoupled feature projectors, producing collapse-free contextual and structural representations. The structural projectors learn generalized representations from discriminating scene structures, making the self-supervised depth learning scalable.
3.1
MaSS Model
The first restriction of existing approaches towards this goal is from the model architecture design.
Although the pretrained VFM (
e.g.
, DINOv2
[
22
]
) exhibits strong generalization and is widely adopted as initialization for supervised depth foundation models
[
24
,
37
,
38
]
, its adaptation is unreliable under self-supervision due to noisy training signals
[
9
]
. Direct fine-tuning may deteriorate the pretrained representations
[
39
]
, yet keeping the VFM frozen leaves its semantic features containing less sufficient geometric cues for structural modeling
[
8
]
(as seen in Fig.
2
(b)). This dilemma motivates a bidirectional interaction architecture between a trainable traditional depth encoder and a frozen VFM encoder, drawing on the ViT-Adapter design
[
11

Another key observation is that different viewpoints of the same scene, or different scenes containing similar objects, may appear contextually alike yet differ substantially in spatial structure. Conversely, visually distinct scenes can share similar structural layouts.
Such misalignment suggests that entangling contextual and structural features within a single representation pathway may lead to representational conflict and collapse.

The second term decouples the structural features from contextual ones, encouraging them to focus solely on the complementary geometric cues that reflect scene layout and viewpoint variations, rather than redundant semantic content.
The above two architectural designs jointly establish a geometrically enriched and collapse-free structural pathway for representation learning, for which the corresponding learning objective is introduced in the following section.

Experiments
4.1
Experimental Setups
Implementation details.
The MaSS model utilizes the pre-trained DINOv2 ViT-B/14 architecture
[
22
]
as its VFM encoder and employs the depth encoder
[
19
]
.
The interaction module follows the design of ViT
-
Adapter
[
11
]
. During training, the DINOv2 encoder remains frozen while all other parameters are updated.
The MaSS model can be trained on a single RTX 4090 GPU with a batch size of 6, which takes approximately 2.5 days to complete.
Data augmentation strategy and optimizer settings adhere to the previous studies
[
1
,
19
,
4
]
without additional tuning.
The proposed scene-structure discrimination objective operates on the depth predictions to formulate supervision for representation learning.
Consequently, it is infeasible to train the depth model from scratch with this objective, as unreliable early predictions would adversely affect representation learning. Therefore, an additional initialization stage for one epoch is required to obtain reasonable depth estimates before applying this objective.
During training, we follow the prior work
[
3
]
to handle dynamic scenes and extreme conditions that may compromise training stability
[
45
,
5
]
.

While our models achieve strong results when trained on individual datasets, such settings do not reflect the scalability challenges posed by large-scale and diverse training data, which constitute the primary focus of this work.
To this end, we further conduct comparative experiments in a mixed-dataset training setting. 4.4
Ablation Study
Efficacy of each innovative component.
To verify that the three key components of MaSS for learning generalizable structural representations are all indispensable, we conduct ablation studies in Table
4
(a).
Removing (a1) the contrastive learning objective eliminates explicit supervision for structural representation learning, leading to a significant performance drop, particularly on zero-shot datasets.
Removing (a2) the specialized structural pathway for representation decoupling prevents the model from preserving contextual information while learning structure, resulting in consistent degradation across all datasets.
Removing (a3) the interaction architecture forces the model to learn structural representations directly from DINOv2 features, which lack sufficient geometric cues, and thus causes a substantial performance decline.
Superiority over alternative designs.
MaSS builds upon well-established components such as DINOv2
[
22
]
and ViT-Adapter
[
11
]
, making it important to verify that the superior performance stems from our design rather than from simply adopting these components. To this end, we compare MaSS with several plausible alternative configurations in Table
4
(b):
(b1) directly fine-tuning a DPT
[
59
]
head with a frozen pretrained DINOv2 backbone,
(b2) fully fine-tuning the entire DINOv2–DPT architecture, and
(b3) incorporating ViT-Adapter while fine-tuning both the adapter and the DPT head.
Results show that MaSS outperforms all these alternative designs by a large margin. This confirms our analysis that effective scaling of self-supervised depth learning requires explicitly modeling scene structure, rather than relying solely on stronger pretrained backbones.
Effect of VFM backbone.
As demonstrated in Table
4
(c), replacing the VFM backbone with a stronger self-supervised pretrained model (DINOv3
[
30
]
) leads to only marginal performance changes. This result corroborates our earlier analysis that pretrained VFMs in our framework mainly provide generalizable semantic priors and are not directly responsible for depth decoding.
This naturally raises a follow-up question: since pretrained depth or geometry foundation models encode rich geometric priors, can MaSS benefit from them, or even further enhance such models?

5
Conclusion
This study revisited self-supervised depth estimation from the perspective of large-scale, mix-domain training and prediction,
recognizing that the model’s tendency to capture dataset-specific structural bias is the key barrier.
MaSS addressed this by coupling a depth encoder with a pretrained VFM and explicitly decoupling the structural representations from the contextual ones to learn scene-generalized structural representations via contrastive learning.
MaSS achieved SoTA accuracy and remarkable out-of-distribution generalization, demonstrating improved scalability with larger and more diverse data.

Figure S1:
Quantitative analyses of the proposed scene-structure discrimination objective for structural representation learning.
A.1
Details of Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures
In the main paper, we define a structural discrepancy metric to determine positive and negative samples within a training batch, thereby formulating a scene-structure discrimination objective for learning structural representations. To illustrate how the metric functions and how the objective guides representation learning, we present several quantitative examples in Fig.
S1
.
The key observations from Fig.
S1
can be summarized as follows:
(1) Our method does not trivially treat each sample as the sole positive instance, nor does it degenerate into discriminating samples based on coarse scene categories (
e.g.
, indoor vs. outdoor).
As shown in Fig.
S1
(a), Sample ① is an outdoor scene but is not considered positive relative to other outdoor samples; this is because its structural layout—a narrow passage flanked by cars and buildings—differs from more open outdoor environments. Fig.
S1
(b) provides an inverse case, where a wide-open outdoor scene (Sample ①) is correctly distinguished from narrow outdoor passages. These observations are further supplemented by Sample ⑥ in Fig.
S1
(c).
Moreover, our method captures shared structural properties across scene categories. For instance, in Fig.
S1
(d), the outdoor scene in Sample ⑥ forms positive pairs with multiple indoor samples due to their similar structure. Similarly, in Fig.
S1
(e), the indoor library aisle (Sample ①) is identified as positive relative to outdoor samples ③, ⑤, and ⑥, which share the “narrow corridor” structure. Meanwhile, it remains negative to the room scene of Sample ②. These results demonstrate that our model prioritizes underlying structural similarity over nominal scene labels.
(2) The hyperparameters of the proposed structural discrepancy metric, together with the masking strategy, effectively identify meaningful contrastive relationships. As visualized in the Discrepancy Metric and Pos./Neg. Mask columns, the resulting similarity maps align well with the expected structural relationships described in the above analysis. Meanwhile, the threshold used in our implementation effectively determines the positive and negative sample pairs accordingly.
(3) Finally, within the MaSS framework, the specialized pathway effectively learns structural representations that are discriminative with respect to different scene structures. This is evidenced by the strong consistency between the feature similarities of the learned structural representations and the in-batch structural discrepancy relationships computed from the predicted depth maps.
A.2

We provide a quantitative analysis of the data distributions across all datasets used in this work to better illustrate how our approach improves the scalability of self-supervised depth learning and enhances model generalizability.
As shown in Fig.

Notably, while nuScenes shares a relatively similar depth distribution with KITTI, its RGB distribution differs significantly.
These observations help interpret the zero-shot evaluation results. For the zero-shot outdoor datasets (Waymo Open

This suggests that the limited generalization ability of previous methods is not primarily caused by differences in depth ranges. Instead, the performance degradation is largely attributed to appearance shifts, revealing the limited robustness of conventional encoder architectures with restricted pretraining. In contrast, our method learns robust and transferable contextual and structural representations from diverse appearance distributions, substantially improving generalization in depth estimation.
For the zero-shot indoor datasets (iBims-1

B.3
Generalizability Evaluation on In-the-Wild Data.
While the previously discussed OOD datasets demonstrate the strong generalization capability of our model, their diversity and domain shift relative to the training data remain limited. To further evaluate robustness, we collect a set of in-the-wild images from online repositories and mobile photography, covering a wide range of real-world challenges.
As illustrated in Fig.
S4
, the first three rows (a–c) present unstructured natural scenes. Notably, (a) and (c) contain specular reflections on water surfaces, while (b) includes dense vegetation with high-frequency textures.
Rows (d–f) exhibit complex geometries and structures that differ significantly from standard urban or indoor benchmarks, such as the detailed roof tiles in (e) and the repetitive grid structure in (f).
Row (g) includes power lines to evaluate the model’s ability to estimate thin structures.
Rows (h–j) further evaluate model robustness under extreme lighting and motion blur conditions. In particular, row (j) presents a challenging case with strong visual ambiguity at a road junction caused by shadows and lighting effects.
Qualitative comparisons are conducted among SC-DepthV3
[
3
]
(trained on NYUv2), SC-DepthV3
†
, Jasmine
[
9
]
(trained on KITTI), and MaSS
†
. As shown in Fig.
S4
, SC-DepthV3 performs unsatisfactorily on complex and unseen structures and tends to interpret scenes with an indoor bias. When trained under the mixed-dataset setting, SC-DepthV3
†
further deteriorates, suffering from severe structural confusion caused by the diverse training data. Jasmine represents one of the strongest self-supervised generative depth models. Although it produces detailed predictions and exhibits improved generalization due to diffusion priors, extreme RGB domain shifts can cause the diffusion process to become unstable and produce depth predictions with significant errors. In contrast, our method remains robust across these challenging in-the-wild scenes, producing depth predictions with both fine-grained details and consistent structural layouts.
Figure S4:
Qualitative monocular depth estimation results on in-the-wild, out-of-distribution data.
Figure S5:
Qualitative monocular reconstruction estimation results on in-the-wild, out-of-distribution data.
B.4
Geometric Fidelity Evaluation on In-the-Wild Data.
Since ground-truth depth is unavailable for these in-the-wild images, quantitative evaluation is infeasible. Instead, we assess the geometric correctness of the predicted depth through monocular 3D reconstruction.
We compare our method with two representative monocular reconstruction approaches, VGGT
[
38
]
and MoGe
[
62
]
. To evaluate geometric fidelity, we synthesize novel viewpoints with slight viewpoint changes relative to the original image. As shown in Fig.
S5
, VGGT produces relatively noisy depth maps on these in-the-wild scenes, leading to noticeable artifacts in the reconstructed geometry. MoGe represents one of the most robust monocular reconstruction foundation models, benefiting from strong geometric supervision during training, and achieves high-quality reconstructions in most cases, with only minor local inconsistencies observed in (b)-(d). Our method, benefiting from the inherent geometric constraints of self-supervised learning as well as effective scaling with diverse training data, achieves reconstruction results comparable to these prior approaches, with significantly less training data. These results highlight the potential of self-supervised methods for building versatile “DepthAnything”-style models from ubiquitous unlabeled data.
Appendix C
Discussion and Future Work
In addition to increasing the training data scale, as discussed in Sect.
4.5
, the scalability of SSMDE also depends on the availability of diverse and suitable training data.
Although self supervision enables learning from imagery collected in the wild, systematically curated datasets covering diverse scenes remain scarce. Existing methods therefore still rely heavily on commonly used datasets originally collected for supervised learning. Constraints imposed by data collection platforms (
e.g.
, vehicles, handheld devices, or UAVs), together with the high cost of sensor calibration and annotation, often limit these datasets to relatively homogeneous scenes, such as typical indoor rooms and common driving environments. This limited diversity may constrain the potential benefits of self-supervision. Such limited diversity may even reduce the potential advantages of self-supervised learning. Systematically curating large and diverse datasets from imagery collected in the wild is therefore a promising direction for advancing SSMDE and extending the benefits of self-supervision to other vision tasks.

article.headline: 解耦场景结构表征，让自监督深度估计跨域可扩展
article.lede: 同济大学提出 MaSS：把上下文与结构表征解耦，用深度直方图构造对比目标，首次让自监督深度模型从混合域训练中获益。
article.problem: 自监督单目深度估计理论上能随无标注数据扩展，但现有方法各自在单一数据集上训练，一旦混合室内、室外、动态与恶劣天气数据共同训练，性能反而不如单数据集训练。作者发现根源在于：自监督信号的噪声使模型倾向于编码数据集特定的结构偏置，深度编码器最粗层的高层特征反映的是数据集偏置而非前景背景关系与透视几何，不同域的偏置要求相互冲突，就造成跨域优化冲突。
article.method: MaSS 用双向交互模块（借鉴 ViT-Adapter）把可训练的传统深度编码器与冻结的 DINOv2 ViT-B/14 桥接，再由一对「锚定—解耦」投影器分别输出上下文表征与结构表征：前者以 VFM 的样本间语义关系为锚，后者被约束为与前者正交。结构分支用预测深度下采样 8 倍后的软直方图（20 个 bin）计算对称 KL 散度，作为场景布局相似度，并以此构造多正样本 InfoNCE 目标，正样本相似度阈值取 0.95、对比温度 0.1。两路特征金字塔拼接后送入深度解码器。
article.results: 在四个训练评测数据集单数据集训练下，MaSS 的 Abs Rel、δ1 分别为 KITTI 0.094/0.909、DDAD 0.128/0.845、NYUv2 0.109/0.868、nuScenes 0.139/0.851，均优于表中此前方法。混合域训练（MaSS†）进一步提升到 0.092/0.913、0.125/0.862、0.104/0.890、0.134/0.852，而对比方法混合训练后普遍下降。八个零样本数据集上，Waymo 0.123/0.867、DrivingStereo 0.100/0.905、Cityscapes 0.103/0.896、iBims-1 0.107/0.883、SUN-RGBD 0.127/0.893、7-Scenes 0.120/0.861、DIML 0.104/0.890、DIODE 0.289/0.736。模型 93.2M 参数、81.6G FLOPs、训练数据 150K；加入 50K TartanAir 样本扩到 200K 后，训练域 Abs Rel 平均变化 +1.5%、δ1 +0.2%，更具挑战的 DIML 与 DIODE 上 +4.3% 与 +3.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 这是首个报告自监督深度模型能随训练数据多样性增加而稳定获益的工作，且在 DIML、DIODE 等分布外场景上接近部分监督深度基础模型的水平，同时只用 150K 训练样本和单卡 RTX 4090、约 2.5 天即可完成训练。它提示「显式建模场景结构」比单纯换更强的预训练骨干更关键，在消融中换成 DINOv3 只带来边际变化。
article.limitations: 在标准室内数据集上仍明显落后于监督深度基础模型（iBims-1 上 DA V2 为 0.045，MaSS 为 0.107），作者归因于这些数据深度分布简单同质且已在监督模型训练集中。可扩展性证据也偏初步：200K 训练规模远小于 Depth Anything 系列的 62M 量级，且方法需先跑一个 epoch 初始化才能启用结构对比目标；另外部分与 DA V2、KBR 系列的对比受 Median 与逆深度域 LSQ* 对齐方式差异影响，直接比较并不完全对等。
article.figure_caption_zh: MaSS 框架总览：深度编码器与冻结的预训练 VFM 经双向交互模块交换信息，再由一对锚定—解耦投影器分别输出无塌缩的上下文表征与结构表征，结构分支通过判别场景结构学到可迁移的布局表示。

figure.caption: The overall architecture of the proposed MaSS framework. MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM via a bidirectional interaction module. The interacted VFM features are fed into a pair of anchored–decoupled feature projectors, producing collapse-free contextual and structural representations. The structural projectors learn generalized representations from discriminating scene structures, making the self-supervised depth learning scalable.

page_papers.title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
page_papers.abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.

Abstract
Edge–cloud collaboration offers a promising way to combine the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the substantially stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted frontier models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC
2
-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. EC
2
-Bench provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge–cloud collaboration. Our study reveals several key findings. First, edge–cloud collaboration provides an effective execution paradigm for long-horizon agents by achieving a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become smaller, while privacy exposure remains strongly dependent on the chosen strategy. Third, stronger edge capability changes the preferred collaboration mode, shifting from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities underlying such effective collaboration. These findings establish a systematic understanding of edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and provide insights for designing future edge models that can effectively collaborate with cloud models. All codes and resources are available at
https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench
.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
(
Achiam et al., 2023
)
, together with the emergence of agent harnesses such as Claude Code
(
Anthropic, 2025
)
and OpenClaw
(
OpenClaw, 2025
)
, have shifted LLM applications from isolated prompt–response interactions toward long-horizon, goal-directed agent execution
(
Wang et al., 2024a
)
. These agents tackle complex end-to-end workflows, including software development, data analysis, information seeking, and workplace automation, through iterative interaction with external environments and tool use
(
Yao et al., 2022
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Hu et al., 2024b
;
Shen et al., 2023
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2024b
)
.
Bringing such agents to edge devices, however, remains challenging because edge platforms are inherently constrained by limited computational resources and memory
(
Qu et al., 2025
)
. Consequently, practical on-device deployment often relies on relatively small LLMs (e.g., models with
≤
\leq
10B parameters), which can struggle with demanding reasoning, planning, and tool-use tasks
(
Choi et al., 2026
)
, making reliable long-horizon execution challenging
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
. To address this limitation, recent work has explored edge–cloud LLM collaboration, where lightweight edge models are complemented by cloud-hosted frontier LLMs when additional capability is required
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. This paradigm combines efficient edge-side execution with stronger cloud capabilities, but requires effective coordination of edge and cloud participation to realize these complementary benefits
(
Ding et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2024
;
Agrawal and Mayer,
)
.
Prior edge–cloud LLM systems largely treated collaboration as a one-shot coordination process for each query, typically through routing or escalation decisions
(
Pozi and Sato, 2025
;
Han et al., 2026
)
. In long-horizon agent execution, however, collaboration can become more interleaved, with edge and cloud models participating at different points along the trajectory as capability requirements change
(
Yi et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. Such interleaving introduces trajectory-level dependencies: cloud participation decisions can influence subsequent execution steps, accumulate resource costs over the trajectory, and determine how much potentially sensitive information leaves the local environment. Yet existing analysis still largely focuses on isolated routing or escalation decisions at the query level, leaving these trajectory-level effects underexplored
(
Hu et al., 2024a
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026a
;
Li et al., 2025
)
. To close this gap, in this paper, we conduct a systematic empirical study of edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agentic execution. Specifically, we organize our study around three research questions. We first ask:
does edge–cloud collaboration remain effective for realistic long-horizon agent execution?
(
RQ1
) We evaluate this question jointly in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. As edge models become more capable, more execution can be handled locally while cloud assistance is reserved for capability-demanding operations. We therefore ask:
how does increasing edge capability impact edge–cloud collaborative execution?
(
RQ2
); As increasing edge capability changes how computation is distributed between edge and cloud, collaboration strategies that are effective under one capability regime may not remain equally suitable under another. This motivates our final question:
how should edge–cloud collaboration evolve as edge capability advances?
(
RQ3
).
To provide a common empirical basis for this study, we introduce
EC
2
-Bench
(
E
dge–
C
loud
C
ollaborative Agent Benchmark), an evaluation framework that combines a diverse suite of real-world digital-workspace agent tasks with a unified execution and evaluation environment for edge–cloud collaboration.
EC
2
-Bench
characterizes each configuration along three dimensions: task performance
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
, resource usage
(
Fang et al., 2025
)
, and privacy exposure. We explicitly consider privacy because cloud participation may reveal sensitive workspace information encountered during agent execution, making privacy exposure an important dimension of evaluating such collaboration
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
. Using
EC
2
-Bench
, we systematically investigate edge–cloud collaboration across diverse agent tasks, collaboration strategies, and edge-capability regimes.
Our study yields three main findings. First, edge–cloud collaboration remains effective for long-horizon agents: partial cloud participation improves task performance over edge-only execution while requiring substantially less cloud resource usage and privacy exposure than cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become much smaller; however, their differences in privacy exposure remain substantial. Thus, privacy remains an important differentiator even when task performance converges. Third, the collaboration strategy that works best changes with edge capability. Weaker edge models benefit more from external routing and direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models benefit more from edge-controlled invocation and cloud advisory. Further analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decisions and instruction following are key edge-side abilities for stronger-edge collaboration modes. These findings highlight the value of optimizing future edge models for both standalone capability and effective cloud collaboration, enabling more capable edge agents.
2
Related Work
A growing body of work has investigated how edge and cloud LLMs can be coordinated to leverage their complementary capabilities and deployment characteristics, balancing overall task performance with local efficiency
(
Zhu and Yang, 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
. A substantial line of work focuses on one-shot coordination for individual queries, either by routing each query to an edge or cloud model or by cascading from the local model to the cloud when additional capability is needed
(
Chen et al., 2023
;
Ong et al., 2024
;
Miao and Fang,
)
. These approaches therefore center on improving the accuracy of routing and escalation decisions
(
Ding et al., 2024
)
. More recent work has extended edge–cloud collaboration to agent execution, where edge and cloud participation can be coordinated at different steps throughout a multi-step trajectory rather than determined once for the entire query, enabling finer-grained use of their complementary capabilities. Within this setting, recent approaches have explored different designs for coordinating edge–cloud collaboration, mainly along two dimensions. Some dynamically determine when the cloud model should participate, either through dedicated rule-based controllers or routers, or by allowing the edge agent itself to decide when to invoke the cloud
(
Shao et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Zeng et al., 2026b
)
. Beyond deciding when the cloud should participate, other approaches have explored complementary functional roles for edge and cloud models during execution, such as execution, planning, or providing guidance
(
Yi et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2026a
)
.
Existing work has begun to develop dedicated evaluation resources for edge–cloud LLM systems. LLMSwitchBench
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
evaluates edge–cloud routing for smart-home queries, while M4A1
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
extends device–cloud evaluation to multimodal, multitask, and multi-turn conversations, focusing on where individual inference requests should be executed. More general LLM routing benchmarks instead abstract away from the edge–cloud setting and evaluate routing systems over heterogeneous model pools, primarily focusing on routing quality and overall cost–performance trade-offs
(
Huang et al., 2025
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
. Despite this progress, existing evaluations pay more attention on routing decisions for individual queries, tasks, or turns, typically over standalone inference workloads such as knowledge, reasoning, coding, and instruction-following tasks. Our study instead treats edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution as the primary object of empirical analysis, aiming to systematically characterize its effectiveness and system-level behavior across different edge capability levels and collaboration designs.

Task Curation.
Starting from the collected candidate pool, we further adapt and curate the tasks to construct the final task suite. Specifically, we first adapt tasks from different source benchmarks to a common execution environment and evaluation interface, enabling all tasks to be executed under the same agent runtime and evaluated under consistent conditions while preserving their original objectives, workspace states, required interactions, and success criteria. We then apply a collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering procedure to retain tasks that are informative for studying edge–cloud collaboration. We evaluate each adapted task under edge-only and cloud-only execution to characterize task difficulty at the two execution endpoints. Tasks that are consistently solved by both endpoints are removed because they provide limited opportunity to differentiate agent execution paradigms, while tasks where neither endpoint achieves meaningful completion are excluded because they provide limited basis for evaluating collaborative execution. Following these steps, we further supplement the task suite with tasks from underrepresented scenarios to maintain broad workload coverage. The resulting task suite consists of 128 executable tasks.
To measure the potential exposure of sensitive information from local workspaces to the cloud during collaboration, we further incorporate sensitivity annotations into

2

We then use an LLM-based approach to identify appropriate locations, generate realistic synthetic sensitive information, and insert it into relevant workspace artifacts, while preserving the original task objective, required interactions, and evaluation criteria. This process results in fine-grained sensitivity annotations for 100 tasks, where each sensitivity unit corresponds to an atomic piece of sensitive information grounded in a workspace artifact.

Empirical Study
We now use
EC
2
-Bench
to systematically study edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. Our analysis follows the three research questions introduced in Section
1
, examining whether edge–cloud collaboration is effective, how improving edge capability affects collaborative execution, and how collaboration mechanisms evolve as edge models become stronger.
6.1
Effectiveness of Edge–Cloud Collaboration in Agent Execution (RQ1)
(a)

(b)

We first examine whether edge–cloud collaboration provides a useful execution regime between edge-only and cloud-only agents when task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure are considered jointly. As shown in Table
2
, the two execution extremes exhibit clear trade-offs. Cloud-only execution achieves the strongest task performance but incurs substantial cloud resource usage and privacy exposure, whereas edge-only execution avoids cloud usage and exposure at the cost of lower task performance. Collaborative execution occupies the space between these extremes, improving task performance over edge-only execution while substantially reducing cloud dependence relative to cloud-only execution. For example, with Qwen3.5-2B as the edge model, step-level routing improves task completion from 12.75 to 39.97 while using only 22.7% of the cloud-only cost. These results indicate that partial cloud participation can recover substantial capability without incurring the full cost of cloud-only execution.

We further examine whether these trade-offs reflect benefits beyond a proportional mixture of the two execution extremes. For each edge model, we use the linear interpolation between its edge-only and cloud-only endpoints as a reference, representing the performance expected from proportionally trading local and cloud execution
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
. As shown in Figures
2(a)
and
2(b)
, multiple collaborative configurations lie above the corresponding interpolation baselines in the cost–performance and privacy–performance spaces, achieving higher task performance at comparable cloud cost or privacy exposure. These results show that edge–cloud collaboration can provide gains beyond an interpolation between edge-only and cloud-only execution.
6.2
Impact of Improving Edge Capability on Collaborative Execution (RQ2)
As edge models continue to advance rapidly
(
Xiao et al., 2025
)
, we study how improving edge capability changes edge–cloud collaborative execution. To probe how collaboration may evolve beyond current lightweight edge models, we additionally include Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.7-Plus as prospective proxies for stronger future edge models. As shown in Table
2
, stronger edge models consistently improve collaborative execution and bring its performance closer to cloud-only execution. The best available collaborative configuration increases from 39.97% completion with Qwen3.5-2B to 76.84% with Qwen3.7-Plus, approaching the 82.70% completion of cloud-only execution.
We further examine how increasing edge capability changes the variation among collaboration strategies. Specifically, for each edge model, we measure the gap between the highest and lowest completion scores and privacy exposure values. As shown in Figures
3(a)
and
3(b)
, task performance becomes substantially less sensitive to the collaboration strategy as edge capability increases. The completion gap among the evaluated strategies narrows from 25.22% with Qwen3.5-2B to 3.67% with Qwen3.7-Plus. In contrast, privacy exposure does not exhibit the same convergence, with substantial differences persisting across collaboration strategies. Notably, with Qwen3.7-Plus, the strategies differ by only 3.67% in completion but by 66.23% in privacy exposure. These results show that stronger edge capability substantially compresses performance differences across collaboration strategies, while privacy exposure remains highly differentiated.
6.3
How Does Edge–Cloud Collaboration Evolve with Edge Capability? (RQ3)
Beyond improving collaborative performance, increasing edge capability may also change effective collaboration mechanisms. We examine this shift along two dimensions: who determines cloud participation and what role the cloud plays once invoked. As shown in Table
2
, both dimensions exhibit clear shifts with improving edge capability. In terms of participation control, externally routed strategies generally outperform edge-controlled strategies with weaker edge models. For example, with Qwen3.5-2B, Per-step Routing achieves 39.97% completion, compared with 15.86% for Edge-Ctrl. Delegation. As edge capability improves, however, this pattern reverses. A similar reversal appears in the role of the cloud: weaker edge models benefit more from direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models favor advisory support.

These shifts motivate further analysis of two edge-side abilities associated with this trend: cloud-assistance decision making and cloud-guidance utilization. Detailed experimental settings and additional analyses are provided in Appendix

Cloud-Assistance Decision Making.
The shift toward agent-controlled invocation motivates us to examine whether stronger edge models can make more effective cloud-assistance decisions. Since there is no explicit annotation indicating when cloud assistance is necessary, we compare Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation against a matched random-invocation baseline. Specifically, we preserve the same cloud-call rate as the agent-controlled strategy while randomly selecting invocation steps. As shown in Figure
4(a)
, edge-controlled delegation consistently outperforms random invocation. The gain is only 1.2% for Qwen3.5-2B, but reaches 3.0–4.4% for the more capable edge models. This pattern suggests that stronger edge models may make more effective cloud-invocation decisions.
Cloud Guidance Utilization.
We next examine whether instruction-following ability is associated with improved advisory collaboration. Starting from Qwen3.5-2B, we apply targeted instruction-following training and evaluate intermediate checkpoints under a fixed cloud-advisory setting. As shown in Figure
4(b)
and Appendix
A.10
, task completion under cloud advisory consistently improves as instruction-following ability develops during training, increasing from 24.8% before training to 28.8% after 600 steps. These results suggest that instruction-following ability is associated with improved utilization of cloud-provided guidance.
7
Conclusion
In this work, we study edge–cloud collaboration for long-horizon LLM agent execution, where cloud participation is interleaved throughout the execution trajectory. To enable systematic investigation of this problem, we introduce
EC
2
-Bench
, an evaluation framework that combines executable digital-workspace agent tasks with unified measurements of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Our findings show that edge–cloud collaboration can achieve a favorable balance between capability, cost, and privacy compared with purely edge-side or cloud-side execution. As edge models become stronger, collaborative execution increasingly approaches cloud-only performance, while privacy exposure remains highly dependent on how cloud participation is organized. We further find that stronger edge models benefit from agent-controlled cloud invocation and advisory interaction. Additional analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction-following are important abilities for edge–cloud collaboration, motivating future work to develop more capable edge agents by strengthening their ability to collaborate with cloud models.
AI Use Statement
Generative AI tools were used to assist with language polishing and improving the clarity of the manuscript. All research ideas, experimental design, implementation, analysis, and conclusions were developed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of the paper.
Ethics Statement
This work studies edge–cloud collaboration for LLM-powered agents and evaluates different collaboration strategies in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure.
EC
2
-Bench
is designed for research evaluation and responsible system development. We do not use real private user data to construct privacy-sensitive benchmark content. When additional sensitive information is required for evaluation, it is synthetically generated and does not correspond to real individuals, organizations, credentials, or financial records. Human annotation is used only to validate benchmark annotations and synthetic content; no annotator personal information is collected or analyzed. The privacy annotations in
EC
2
-Bench
are intended to support systematic evaluation of sensitive information exposed during edge–cloud collaboration and to facilitate the development of more privacy-aware agent systems.
Reproducibility Statement
We provide detailed descriptions of the benchmark construction, collaboration strategies, experimental setup, and evaluation procedures in the main paper and appendix. In particular, we document the task adaptation and filtering process, sensitivity annotation procedure and validation, implementations of the four edge–cloud collaboration strategies, model and inference configurations, and the metrics used to evaluate task performance, cloud resource usage, edge computation, and privacy exposure. We further report the experimental settings and implementation details for the analyses conducted in each research question. These details are provided to facilitate reproduction of the benchmark and the reported experimental results.

A.2
Detailed Comparison with Prior Benchmarks
We provide additional details on how
EC
2
-Bench
differs from representative benchmarks for LLM routing and edge–cloud collaboration. Overall, prior benchmarks primarily study model allocation over queries or conversational turns and evaluate task quality together with inference-related costs, whereas
EC
2
-Bench
extends the evaluation to long-horizon agent execution, broader collaboration mechanisms, and trajectory-level privacy exposure. We next compare these benchmarks along three aspects: evaluation scenario, collaboration mode, and evaluation dimension.
Evaluation Scenario.
Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate routing over conventional LLM queries or conversational interactions, while
EC
2
-Bench
focuses on long-horizon agent execution in interactive environments. RouterBench
(
Hu et al., 2024a
)
evaluates routing across a collection of general LLM tasks. LLMRouterBench
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
further broadens the task coverage to include software-engineering and tool-use benchmarks in addition to conventional reasoning, knowledge, and code-generation tasks. LLMSwitchBench
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
focuses on independent smart-home queries spanning binary, multiple-choice, and open-ended formats. M4A1
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
considers multi-modal and multi-task interactions within multi-turn conversations. In comparison,
EC
2
-Bench
evaluates collaboration over multi-step agent trajectories, where models repeatedly interact with tools, applications, and persistent workspace states.
Collaboration Modes.
Prior benchmarks predominantly study routing-based collaboration, whereas
EC
2
-Bench
additionally considers collaboration in which the edge agent itself controls cloud participation. RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, and LLMSwitchBench formulate model allocation primarily as query routing, where each input query is assigned to a selected model. M4A1 allows device–cloud placement to be reconsidered for different tasks throughout a multi-turn conversation.
EC
2
-Bench
includes both Query Routing and Per-Step Routing, and further considers two edge-controlled modes. Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation allows the edge agent to decide when to delegate the next execution step to the cloud, while Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory lets the edge agent request cloud guidance while retaining responsibility for subsequent action generation.
Evaluation Dimensions.
Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate task quality and inference-related efficiency, while
EC
2
-Bench
additionally quantifies privacy exposure over the complete execution trajectory. RouterBench focuses on task performance and economic cost, while LLMRouterBench evaluates performance-oriented and performance–cost routing and additionally provides latency-aware analysis. M4A1 jointly considers response quality, latency, and usage cost in device–cloud offloading. LLMSwitchBench incorporates privacy-sensitive queries and privacy-aware routing mechanisms, including local execution and masking before cloud inference, while its main routing evaluation reports task-quality metrics and inference cost. In
EC
2
-Bench
, privacy exposure is directly quantified by tracking which annotated sensitive information from the local workspace becomes visible to the cloud during execution. Resource usage is likewise measured over the complete trajectory, including cloud-side token consumption and monetary cost as well as edge-side computation.

2

We first collect candidate tasks from multiple Claw-style executable-workspace agent benchmarks and adapt them to the
EC
2

A.4
Task Adaptation Protocol
This section describes how tasks collected from heterogeneous executable-workspace benchmarks are adapted into standardized executable instances for
EC
2
-Bench
. The adaptation protocol consists of three components: standardizing task execution, standardizing task evaluation, and validating that the resulting instances preserve comparable task difficulty. We then illustrate the resulting task format and execution workflow with a representative
EC
2
-Bench
instance.
Standardization and Fidelity Check.
Inspired by the task format used in
Ding et al. (2026)
, we first standardize task execution by organizing each task into a unified configuration and workspace structure. Each task is converted into a unified configuration format specifying its prompt, workspace paths, tools, environment settings, and other execution requirements. Task-relevant files and resources are organized into a common workspace structure, while tool and skill settings are aligned across tasks so that instances from different sources can follow the same agent loop and logging mechanism. We next standardize task evaluation while preserving the original success criteria of each task. The original verification logic is converted into a set of task-specific evaluation checks compatible with
EC
2
-Bench
, including rule-based validation, file or application-state auditing, command-output inspection, and rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge verification when semantic judgment is required. The resulting check scores are aggregated into the task completion score defined in Section
4.2
.
To validate adaptation fidelity, we examine whether the adapted instances preserve comparable execution and evaluation outcomes. For each task, we execute both the original and adapted versions with Qwen3.5-9B and compare their average completion scores over three independent runs. Tasks whose absolute difference in average completion score exceeds 0.3 are discarded. This validation helps identify substantial behavioral or scoring shifts introduced during adaptation.

To illustrate the resulting standardized task format, Table

The example requires the agent to identify customers overdue for contact, inspect their previous email communications, and prepare tier-specific follow-up drafts using CRM and Gmail services.
Using this task as an example, the harness first parses the standardized task configuration to obtain the task instruction, workspace, required skills, environment settings, initialization commands, and evaluation checks. It then creates an isolated execution environment for the task, loads the task workspace and task-specific skills, and executes the warmup procedure to instantiate the required application state. In this example, the customer and inbox data are used to initialize local CRM and Gmail services, which expose the application interfaces subsequently used by the agent. The evaluation ground truth is kept separate from the execution environment and is not made available to the agent during this stage. The harness then configures the evaluated model, starts the OpenClaw runtime, and passes the task instruction to the agent. During execution, the agent iteratively interacts with the CRM and Gmail services through the provided skills, observes the resulting application states, and decides subsequent actions until the task terminates or reaches the time limit. The complete interaction history is recorded as the execution trajectory and retained for subsequent analysis. After execution terminates, the ground-truth evaluation data are injected into the evaluation environment, and the task-specific checks assess customer identification, email-style differentiation, and draft quality to compute the task completion score. For privacy evaluation, the annotated sensitivity units are matched against the cloud-visible contexts recorded during collaborative execution to determine privacy exposure. The harness additionally collects the execution transcript and model-usage statistics for resource evaluation.

This subsection describes how sensitivity-unit annotations are constructed in
EC
2
-Bench
. Since privacy-relevant information in digital workspaces can be distributed across heterogeneous files, application states, and other task artifacts, we adopt an LLM-based annotation process to identify and annotate sensitive information from two sources: information already present in the task environment and realistically synthesized sensitive content introduced into suitable task artifacts. Across the resulting task environments, more than 15,000 information units are represented in total, of which 3,385 are annotated as sensitive, spanning 100 tasks and 12 fine-grained privacy categories. Both sources are represented under a common annotation schema and privacy taxonomy, with annotation quality further validated through human evaluation. The resulting sensitivity-unit annotations are used to measure privacy exposure during collaborative execution. Privacy exposure quantifies the fraction of annotated sensitive information units that become visible to the cloud through cloud-visible contexts along the execution trajectory.
Identification of Pre-existing Sensitive Information.
For each task, we use an LLM to inspect the local workspace and identify privacy-relevant information. The workspace may contain files, application states, and other task artifacts accessible to the agent during execution. Each identified item is grounded in its source artifact or application record, and the corresponding sensitive content and source location are recorded as a sensitivity unit. This grounding establishes both that the information is available within the task environment and where it originates, providing a concrete reference for subsequent exposure evaluation. The resulting annotations are stored separately as task metadata.
Synthesis of Sensitive Information.
To broaden the coverage of sensitivity annotations across tasks and privacy categories, we additionally introduce synthetic sensitive content into suitable task artifacts. We only augment tasks for which such content can be incorporated without changing the task objective, required interaction, expected output, or success criteria. For each eligible task, an LLM-assisted pipeline selects an appropriate artifact and insertion location and generates synthetic sensitive content consistent with the surrounding format and semantics. Each inserted span is then recorded as a sensitivity unit using the same annotation schema as pre-existing sensitive information.
We further apply a separate LLM-based verification step to improve the realism of the synthesized content. The verifier examines whether each synthetic unit resembles plausible real-world sensitive information and replaces unrealistic or placeholder-like values with more realistic synthetic alternatives. Table
7
presents representative examples before and after verification.
Sensitivity-Unit Representation and Taxonomy.
All sensitivity units, whether identified from the original workspace or synthetically introduced, follow a common annotation schema that records the sensitive content, its source location, and its privacy category. The source location links each unit to the artifact or application record from which it originates, allowing its exposure to be traced during agent execution. We organize sensitivity units into two top-level domains—
Personal Sensitive Information
and
Organizational Confidential Information
—comprising 12 fine-grained categories in total. The personal-information categories build on prior privacy taxonomies
(
Ngong et al., 2026
;
Shen et al., 2025
)
, while the organizational categories are further informed by WIPO guidance on trade secrets
(
WIPO, 2024
)
. Table
6
summarizes the resulting taxonomy, annotation statistics, and task coverage.
We use GLM-5.3 for sensitivity identification and synthesis, while GPT-5.5 serves as an independent verifier for the synthesized content. We further conduct human evaluation to validate the accuracy of pre-existing sensitivity-unit identification and the realism and placement quality of synthetic sensitive content. Detailed protocols and results are provided in Appendix
A.7
.

Implementation Details
This section provides implementation details for reproducing the experiments in
EC
2
-Bench
, including the execution environment and the implementation of the evaluated edge–cloud collaboration strategies.
Experimental Environment.
All experiments are conducted using OpenClaw as the agent execution framework. The maximum context window is configured to 128K tokens, with each individual model interaction limited to 32K tokens. OpenClaw additionally employs an automatic context compression mechanism to manage context growth during long-horizon execution. The agent execution environment is hosted in E2B sandboxes with stable resource allocation to ensure consistent and reliable execution across experiments. All collaboration strategies share the same agent runtime, execution environment, and model deployment configuration. For all experiments, when cloud assistance is requested,
v
t
c
v_{t}^{c}
consists of the current task instruction and the execution history maintained by OpenClaw, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations. No additional redaction or privacy filtering is applied before cloud invocation.
Query Routing.
Query Routing makes a single routing decision before agent execution and assigns the entire task trajectory to either the edge model
M
e
M_{e}
or the cloud model
M
c
M_{c}
. We directly use the matrix-factorization-based router released with RouteLLM
(
Ong et al., 2024
)
. We calibrate the threshold on the validation set to obtain an approximately 15% cloud-participation rate at the step level and apply the same threshold during evaluation. This target cloud-participation rate is selected to keep the cloud usage of routing-based strategies comparable to that of edge-controlled strategies, enabling a more controlled comparison under similar cloud resource budgets.
Per-Step Routing.
Per-Step Routing revisits the edge–cloud decision at every agent interaction step. We adapt the uncertainty signal used by GlimpRouter
(
Zeng et al., 2026c
)
to agent execution. Before generating the action at each step, we obtain the edge model’s next reasoning-token distribution and compute its entropy as an uncertainty score. If the entropy exceeds a calibrated threshold, the current step is routed to
M
c
M_{c}
for action generation; otherwise, generation continues with
M
e
M_{e}
. The routing decision is repeated independently throughout the trajectory. We calibrate the routing threshold on the validation set such that approximately 15% of tasks are assigned to the cloud, aiming to maintain a cloud usage level comparable to other collaboration strategies, and apply the same threshold during evaluation.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation.
Unlike the two routing-based strategies above, Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation places the cloud-participation decision within the edge agent itself. The edge model is provided with a delegation tool backed by
M
c
M_{c}
and can invoke it at any point during execution. When invoked, the current conversation history, including previous actions, tool calls, and observations, is forwarded to the cloud model, which directly performs the next agent step. Control then returns to the edge model for subsequent execution. The delegation instruction encourages the edge agent to invoke the cloud before committing to a substantive approach, when it encounters difficulty or considers changing its approach, and before declaring the task complete. Thus, both the timing and frequency of cloud participation are determined dynamically by the edge agent rather than by an external router.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory uses the same agent-controlled invocation mechanism but assigns a different role to the cloud model. The edge model is provided with an advisory tool and autonomously decides when cloud guidance is needed during execution. Upon invocation, the current execution history, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations, is provided to
M
c
M_{c}
. The cloud model returns advisory information in natural language, such as plans, suggestions, or corrective feedback. The advice is appended to the edge model’s context, after which
M
e
M_{e}
generates the next action based on the task instruction, execution history, and received advice.

A.10
Understanding Edge-Side Abilities for Collaboration
To further understand the edge-side abilities associated with the observed shift toward edge-controlled collaboration, we conduct two controlled analyses focusing on cloud-assistance decision making and guidance following.
Cloud-Assistance Decision Making.
Directly evaluating the quality of cloud-invocation decisions is challenging because there is no explicit ground-truth annotation indicating when cloud assistance is necessary during agent execution. Therefore, we evaluate the effectiveness of edge-controlled invocation through a matched random baseline. For each edge model, we first execute the Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation strategy and record its cloud-call rate. We then construct a random-invocation baseline that preserves the same cloud-call rate but randomly selects the invocation steps throughout the trajectory. Both approaches therefore receive the same amount of cloud assistance, while differing only in whether the invocation timing is determined by the edge agent or randomly selected. We compare their task completion performance, where the performance gain over random invocation serves as an indicator of whether the edge agent can identify execution states where cloud assistance is beneficial.
Cloud Guidance Utilization.
To examine whether instruction-following ability is associated with effective advisory collaboration, we conduct a controlled instruction-following training experiment. Starting from Qwen3.5-2B, we apply targeted instruction-following RL training using the IF data provided by Ultradata
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
. The model is trained for 600 steps with GRPO, using a batch size of 32 per step and 8 rollouts per prompt.
To separate guidance utilization from cloud-invocation decisions, we evaluate all checkpoints under a fixed advisory setting, where cloud advisory calls are triggered at predetermined edge execution steps (e.g., every five steps) rather than dynamically selected by the edge model. We evaluate the model from two perspectives. First, we measure instruction-following ability using three instruction-following benchmarks (IFEval
(
Zhou et al., 2023
)
, IFBench
(
Pyatkin et al., 2026
)
, and Multi-IF
(
He et al., 2024
)
) to verify that the training improves the targeted capability. Second, we evaluate the resulting models on
EC
2
-Bench
under both advisory collaboration and edge-only execution. The edge-only setting serves as a control to examine whether improvements are accompanied by general gains in agent execution capability.
As shown in Figure
5
, instruction-following performance consistently improves throughout training, while edge-only task performance remains largely unchanged. In contrast, advisory collaboration performance increases with instruction-following training, improving from 24.8% at initialization to 28.8% after 600 training steps. These results suggest that instruction-following ability is particularly relevant to cloud guidance utilization, beyond general improvements in edge-only task execution.

article.headline: 长任务智能体的边缘云协作：128项任务系统评测
article.lede: 新基准EC2-Bench用128个可执行工作区任务，从完成度、云端开销与隐私暴露三方面，评测长周期智能体的边云协作。
article.problem: 现有边缘云协作研究多把协作当成单次查询的路由或升级决策，而长周期智能体执行中云端参与会在轨迹中反复穿插，产生轨迹级依赖：一次调用会影响后续步骤、累积资源开销，并决定多少敏感信息离开本地。这类轨迹级效应此前缺少系统评测，已有基准如RouterBench、LLMSwitchBench、M4A1也主要考察单查询或多轮对话的路由质量与成本。
article.method: 作者构建EC2-Bench，从六个可执行智能体基准中收集并统一到同一运行时与评测接口，再按'两端点都能解或都不能解则剔除'的难度过滤，得到128个任务，其中100个带有细粒度敏感性标注（共3385个敏感信息单元，分12类）。评测覆盖任务完成度与Pass^3、云端token与费用、边缘FLOPs，以及轨迹中暴露给云端的敏感单元比例；协作方式分四种：查询级路由、逐步路由、边缘自主委托云端执行、边缘自主请求云端建议，边缘模型取Qwen3.5-2B/9B/27B与Qwen3.7-Plus，云端主模型为GLM-5.3。
article.results: 云端单干（GLM-5.3）完成度82.70、云端费用56.42美元、隐私暴露87.01%；边缘单干Qwen3.5-2B仅12.75。以2B为边缘模型时，逐步路由把完成度从12.75提到39.97，云端费用仅为云端单干的22.7%。随边缘变强，最佳协作配置从39.97%（2B）升至76.84%（Qwen3.7-Plus），逼近云端单干的82.70%；各协作策略间的完成度差距从25.22%（2B）收窄到3.67%（Qwen3.7-Plus），但同期隐私暴露差距仍达66.23%。2B时逐步路由39.97%远高于边缘自主委托的15.86%，边缘变强后这一格局反转。边缘自主委托相对同等调用率的随机调用，2B仅高1.2%，更强边缘模型高3.0–4.4%；对2B做指令跟随训练后，固定云端建议设置下的完成度从24.8%升到28.8%（600步）。隐私暴露检测器对200个人工裁决样本的F1为96.9%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把边云协作从'单次路由准确率'推进到长周期智能体的轨迹级评测，指出边缘模型该优化的不只是单机能力，还有'何时叫云端'和'听懂云端建议'这两种协作能力。对端侧智能体的模型设计与部署策略来说，这是可复用的评测口径。
article.limitations: 主实验只用一个云端模型GLM-5.3（附录用DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash复验趋势一致），Qwen3.5-27B与Qwen3.7-Plus只是'未来边缘模型'的代理，并非真实端侧部署；边缘开销用参数估算FLOPs，未测真实时延与能耗；隐私暴露只在100个标注任务上由LLM裁判判定。任务集经过'两端点都能解/都不能解即剔除'的过滤，天然偏向能区分协作方式的场景，绝对完成度不宜外推到一般智能体负载。
article.figure_caption_zh: EC2-Bench中的长周期智能体边云协作概览：一个典型工作流、四种云端参与方式，以及关于协作有效性、边缘能力影响与协作方式随边缘变强如何演化的三个研究问题。

Generative Representation Learning
for Scalable Latent Tokenization
Alan Baade
†
†

Correspondence to
baade@stanford.edu
.

Stanford University

†
