Stanford University
Justin Johnson
Li Fei-Fei
Gordon Wetzstein
Affiliation:
University of Michigan
Abstract
We introduce an approach for self-supervised representation learning designed to be used as a tokenizer for generative modeling. Our objective supervises a representation loss by factorizing the pointwise mutual information of the data, which we estimate by taking information differences between conditional predictions from a learned generative model. We justify our algorithm theoretically and empirically, demonstrating that our generative approach to representation learning avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression in cases where commonly used methods like DINO and LeJEPA fail. Moreover, we show our representation learning technique is scalable; expending more compute leads to predictably better latent tokenization.
For the first time, we perform a careful analysis of the
combined
flop efficiency of tokenizer and generative model and demonstrate that our approach is a compute-optimal improvement over direct diffusion for pixel-space generation, obtaining an FID-50K of
2.18
with JiT-L. Applied to ImageNet and the text-to-image dataset GPIC, we show tokenizer encoder scaling laws for diffusability, where extrapolating our approach achieves representations in
𝟕
×
\mathbf{7\times}
fewer FLOPs than DINOv2 on ImageNet and
𝟖
×
\mathbf{8\times}
fewer FLOPs than WebSSL on GPIC. Code at
https://github.com/AlanBaade/repr
1
Introduction
Representation learning decides what information matters. Traditionally, that decision has been guided by downstream tasks: augmentation invariance, for example, encourages representations that preserve semantic content while discarding other latent variables.
Yet representations designed this way have become a foundation for generative modeling, serving as latent tokenizers for diffusion models. Methods such as RAE
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, for example, inherit encoders like DINOv2
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
, whose objectives were not designed to make generation easier. Moreover, these encoders can require orders of magnitude more data and compute to train than the generative models built on top of them. This leaves two basic questions unresolved:
what makes a representation good for generation, and is learning one actually more compute-efficient than modeling pixels directly?
In this paper, we seek to discover whether there is a representation learning algorithm that demonstrates tokenizer encoder scaling laws: As more compute and data is given to train the tokenizer, generative models trained on these representations converge faster, and the compute optimal balance between training a tokenizer and generative model places nonzero weight on tokenization. Although prior work has shown scaling laws for tokenization
(
Yao et al., 2025a
;
Hansen-Estruch et al., 2026
)
, these works couple tokenizer decoders, which are a part of the generative process that has been widely shown to improve with scale
(
Kaplan et al., 2020
)
, with tokenizer encoders that instead have been shown to
worsen
with scale
(
Siméoni et al., 2025
;
Hansen-Estruch et al., 2026
;
Yao et al., 2025b
)
, a phenomenon we discuss in depth.
Toward the goal of discovering scalable encoders, we identify three primary reasons for the failures of current recipes.
1) Feature suppression:
Standard representation learning techniques such as Contrastive Learning
(
Hadsell et al., 2006
;
van den Oord et al., 2018a
)
and LeJEPA
(
Balestriero and LeCun, 2025
)
can have their objectives saturated by a small number of bits, behavior commonly referred to as feature suppression
(
Geirhos et al., 2020
;
Chen et al., 2021a
)
. Although suppressed objectives may be ideal for tasks like ImageNet probing, where only a few semantic bits need highlighting, in generative modeling all latent variables in the data are sampled.
2) Causal Theoretical Grounding:
Representation learning algorithms like contrastive learning optimize a CLS token, but the tokenizer used by methods like RAE is instead “emergent” internal patch features that have demonstrated instability under scaling
(
Darcet et al., 2024
)
.
3) Architectural scalability:
Classic tokenizers such as VAEs
(
Kingma and Welling, 2022
)
and VQ-VAE
(
van den Oord et al., 2018b
)
bottleneck gradient descent through techniques like the reparameterization trick or straight-through gradient estimation and fail to learn semantics
(
Yao et al., 2025b
)
, resulting in the transition toward tokenizers based on representation learning such as DINOv2
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
.
To address these issues preventing scalable representations, we propose an approach to move representation learning away from discriminative tasks, such as contrastive learning, and toward generative approaches instead.
Specifically, we observe that Word Embeddings and Contrastive Learning implicitly factorize a pointwise mutual information (PMI) matrix of the data distribution
(
Levy and Goldberg, 2014
;
van den Oord et al., 2018a
;
Chen et al., 2023
)
. We propose to use a generative model to directly estimate a weighted PMI that our representation learner factorizes explicitly. By factorizing the PMI of the data, we directly inherit the long-studied theoretical properties of Contrastive Learning in our latent space.
By using a generative objective instead of a discriminative objective, our approach both uses no negative samples and is robust to feature suppression, enabling our approach to directly supervise tokenizer patch feature representations rather than relying on intermediate features in a network
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
or excessively destroying information when directly using contrastive representations
(
Ramesh, 2022
)
.
Our PMI estimation inherits scalability from existing generative models, we use continuous gradient descent and standard Transformer architectures, and our representation supervision loss is directly interpretable as Nats Squared.
We empirically demonstrate our approach for the task of image generation on both ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2009
)
and GPIC
(
Chandrasegaran et al., 2026
)
, a text-to-image dataset.
We isolate our gains solely to the diffusability of the encoder by training generative models with Latent Forcing
(
Baade et al., 2026
)
, demonstrating scaling directly on pixel generation while using no decoder, perceptual losses, adversarial losses, or external models. We further show that our approach is generalizable to different settings, such as unconditional generation, guided and unguided generation, and GAN+LPIPS decoding
(
Goodfellow et al., 2021
;
Zhang et al., 2018
)
. Our resulting approach provides a FLOP-wise performance improvement over JiT, obtaining an FID-50K of
2.18
2.18
with JiT-L.
In summary, we make the following contributions:
1.
We introduce Relative Prediction Representations (RePR), a theoretically grounded representation learning algorithm for discovering latent variables within a signal that correlate between different masked views of the data.
2.
We provide a practical implementation on real high-dimensional image data.
3.
A careful analysis of tokenizer encoder scaling laws and the
combined
FLOP efficiency of representation learning and generative modeling, improving JiT-L FID-50K on ImageNet to
2.18
2.18
with equal FLOPs and extrapolating to equivalent tokenizer quality
7
×
7\times
faster than DINOv2
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
on ImageNet and
8
×
8\times
WebSSL
(
Fan et al., 2025
)
on GPIC.
2
Related Work
Representation Learning.
Contrastive Learners
(
Chen et al., 2020
;
He et al., 2020
)
are a staple of representation learning that supervise a loss objective by encouraging high similarity between augmented views of the same scene and low similarity across different scenes. Empirically improving on contrastive-style objectives has seen great success in the widely-used DINO v1,v2,v3 series of models
(
Caron et al., 2021
;
Oquab et al., 2024
;
Siméoni et al., 2025
)
. A longstanding flaw of contrastive objectives is that they struggle with strongly conditioned views, where hard negative examples
(
Robinson et al., 2021
)
that prevent trivializing the objective are difficult to find. As a result, contrastive learning objectives often exhibit feature suppression
(
Chen et al., 2021a
)
, where contrastive representations only capture a subset of relevant variables in a scene, for example probing well to object class but losing scene structure. To combat issues of hard negatives and feature suppression, substantial effort has been devoted to designing hand-crafted augmentations intended to highlight signal for desired variables
(
Chen et al., 2020
)
. Representation learning has also seen success through predictive objectives, such as predicting masked-out pixels in an image as done in Context Encoders and MAE
(
Pathak et al., 2016
;
He et al., 2022
)
, or by replacing the pixel prediction target with
a neural network latent such as BYOL, Data2Vec, JEPA, and MAGE
(
Grill et al., 2020
;
Baevski et al., 2022
;
Assran et al., 2023
;
Bardes et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2022
)
.
Pointwise Mutual Information and Representations
The Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) of the data is closely tied to many representation learning algorithms.
The connection between factorizing the PMI and representation learning was first established by
Levy and Goldberg (2014)
for Word2Vec
(
Mikolov et al., 2013
)
and afterward extended to contrastive learning
(
van den Oord et al., 2018a
;
Chen et al., 2023
)
. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
(
Huh et al., 2024
)
proposes that large-scale neural networks emergently converge to similarly structured representations and suggests PMI factorization as a candidate for such a space. However, recent work
(
Koepke et al., 2026
)
has shown that at large scales, neural representations fail to match such structure. In this work, we directly supervise representations to match the PMI, rather than assuming emergence at scale.
Pixel and Latent Space Generative Modeling.
The current state-of-the-art for image generative modeling uses diffusion transformers
(
Peebles and Xie, 2023
)
, of which there are two main varieties: direct pixel diffusion and latent diffusion. A representative approach for pixel-space diffusion is JiT
(
Li and He, 2026
)

Here, we describe how we instantiate RePR for learning representations from images. RePR consists of two learned networks: a “Prediction Model” that predicts masked inputs given partial observations (to estimate the PMI), and a “Representation Model” that outputs vectors given a partial input (into which we distill the PMI). ), the Representation Model for patch features (Sec.
5.2
), how we mask views for PMI calculation (Sec.
5.3
), and estimating the PMI with respect to latents for improved performance (Sec.
5.4
).

We distinguish between features that are directly supervised for structure, such as the CLS token of Contrastive Learners, DINO, or LeJEPA, and unregularized intermediate latents, such as the non-CLS tokens of DINO or the latents in an unregularized autoencoder. Such feature instability motivates directly supervising patch features for principled and scalable tokenization.

6.1
Feature Suppression
Figure 2:
Discriminative representation learning can suffer from feature suppression when a small subset of features, such as a watermark, is sufficient to distinguish examples. This degrades representation quality, as reflected by collapsing ImageNet class-probing performance. RePR remains robust to feature suppression.
Existing representation learning methods such as contrastive learning suffer from an issue called Feature Suppression
(
Geirhos et al., 2020
;
Chen et al., 2021a
;
Li et al., 2023
)
where a self-supervised objective might learn only a minimal subset of features necessary to solve the downstream task (e.g. instance discrimination), while dropping the remaining latent variables. This can be disastrous when training tokenizers because the additional latent variables, while perhaps unnecessary for satisfying the contrastive objective, may be essential for reconstructing the data.
To show our method is robust to Feature Suppression, we benchmark on a version of Imagenet that adds a visual watermark to every image patch that uniquely identifies the image in the dataset
(
Enigma, 2026
)
. On such a dataset, contrastive losses become trivialized: merely identifying the image patch watermark is enough to attain a perfect loss. In Fig.
2
, we train LeJEPA
(
Balestriero and LeCun, 2025
)
, DINOv3
(
Siméoni et al., 2025
)
, and our proposed RePR approach on both standard ImageNet and on the watermarked version. On watermarked data, LeJEPA and DINOv3 collapse to only representing the shared watermark. Meanwhile, despite sharing the same PMI factorization guarantees as contrastive learners, our proposed RePR is robust.
6.2
Scaling Laws
Figure 3:
Tokenizer Encoder Scaling Laws:
RePR predictably scales as a tokenizer encoder. When holding size and training duration of a generative model constant, greater RePR size and FLOPs improve generation performance. Iterative feature prediction (Sec.
5.4

In the previous section, we demonstrated that our method resists feature suppression on toy data, where prior representations collapse. In this section, we demonstrate encoder scaling laws: our model captures enough data for generation and predictably improves with scale on real data.
We demonstrate encoder scaling laws using Latent Forcing
(
Baade et al., 2026
)
, which first denoises in latent space and then generates pixels conditioned on the denoised latent. This lets us leverage the improved diffusability of learned representations while retaining generation directly in pixel space. The resulting generative process is lossless, avoiding the reconstruction–generation tradeoff of lossy latent tokenizers
(
Yao et al., 2025b
)
and isolating gains from diffusability rather than compression. Latent Forcing additionally enables controlled FLOP- and parameter-matched comparisons with direct pixel diffusion models such as JiT.

Conclusion
We introduce RePR, a theoretically motivated representation learning method for generative model tokenizers. RePR shares the theoretical guarantees of contrastive learning without requiring negative samples, while remaining robust to feature suppression in settings where prior representation learning methods collapse. We establish empirical scaling laws for diffusability and show that RePR-based generative models outperform direct diffusion on raw data at matched training FLOPs. Together, these results show that representation learning with strong theoretical foundations can coexist with and improve the scaling of generative modeling.

article.headline: RePR：用生成模型估计PMI监督表征
article.lede: RePR用扩散模型估计加权PMI监督图像块表征，ImageNet上FID-50K达2.18。
article.problem: 现有表征学习多面向判别任务，容易出现特征抑制；DINO、LeJEPA在带水印数据上会只编码水印而崩溃。用于生成的tokenizer编码器是否可扩展、以及「先学表征再生成」总算力是否优于像素扩散，仍缺乏清晰答案。
article.method: RePR让预测模型（MAR/MAE编码器+扩散MLP头）估计条件与非条件去噪损失之差，得到加权PMI；表征模型则用patch特征点积去因子化该PMI。为处理高维图像，作者引入时间步加权、将大目标拆成增量patch的bootstrapped PMI，并用相对位置交叉注意力保持空间等变。训练时联合优化两个模型，表征模型每4次迭代才更新一次。
article.results: 在ImageNet上，RePR+JiT-L取得FID-50K 2.18；在1.19×10^20 FLOPs预算下，相比JiT-L像素扩散，无引导FID-10K在条件生成降2.61、无条件生成降4.18。作者还报告tokenizer编码器scaling law：外推显示达到DINOv2水平约需1/7训练FLOPs、达到WebSSL水平约需1/8。用RAE的GAN+LPIPS解码设置时，RePR-173M Iter3的FID-50k为11.13，优于IJEPA-H的12.46和MoCoV3-B的13.84；重建PSNR为21.72 dB，DINOv2-B为18.09 dB。
article.why_it_matters: 若成立，这给出了除放大生成模型之外的又一条scaling轴：把tokenizer编码器本身当作可扩展组件，并按编码器+生成器总FLOPs做预算。它也为「生成式表征学习」提供了可检验的PMI理论框架。
article.limitations: 论文的scaling外推最多只超出实测对数FLOP范围1倍，且ImageNet上width-1024模型在200 epoch后开始过拟合；PMI由扩散VLB估计，只有去噪器最优时才精确，并依赖32步Monte Carlo近似。RAE对比中的GAN+LPIPS解码器还依赖外部模型，其中DINOv1/8预训练GAN使用4.7×10^20 FLOPs，超过作者训练的任何模型。
article.figure_caption_zh: RePR架构：左侧预测模型用MAR与扩散MLP头估计目标patch的加权似然，右侧表征模型输出patch特征并因子化加权PMI。

figure.caption: Architecture. {Left:} 1) Our Prediction Model (bottom) estimates weighted data likelihoods for a target patch $p$ using an MAR architecture, which combines an MAE Encoder $E_ $ and Decoder $D_ $ with a diffusion prediction MLP head $M_ $. 2) The Representation Model $R_ $ (top) outputs vector representations supervised to factorize a weighted PMI. {Right:} We enforce spatial equivariance in $R_ $ by hiding absolute position information but outputting a feature for every patch.

journals.title: Towards understanding and monitorability of reasoning LLMs
journals.summary:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01333-6

Frontier LLMs are trained to solve problems in a step-by-step way, generating reasoning text in human-understandable language. However, these reasoning tokens are not accurate explanations of LLMs’ internal computations, raising challenges for monitorability.
journals.blurb: 《Nature Machine Intelligence》在线发表了一篇关于推理大模型可理解性与可监控性的研究。作者指出，前沿大模型虽然会用人类可读的语言逐步生成推理文本，但这些推理 token 并不构成对其内部计算的准确解释。这一落差给模型的可监控性带来了挑战。

journals.title: Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03313-7

Large language models can mimic thought and feeling with uncanny skill. But evidence from neuroscience suggests that intelligence alone is not enough for subjective experience.
journals.blurb: 《Nature》这篇评论指出大语言模型虽能以逼真的方式模仿思考与情感，但神经科学证据表明智能本身并不足以产生主观体验。作者据此给出三点理由说明当前 AI 并不具备意识、甚至可能永远不会具备，并提示研究生在讨论「模型能力」时区分行为层面的模仿与现象学意义上的意识。
